<meta>This is the title page of a seventeenth-century legal and historical treatise. The work combines the scholarship of Christopher Besold, a prominent German jurist, and Jules César Boulenger, a French Jesuit historian.</meta>

# CHRISTOPHER
# BESOLD,
## <term>Jurist</term> <note>The original abbreviation "JC." stands for *Juris Consultus*, a professional consultant or expert in the law.</note>
# ON THE PUBLIC
# TREASURY
### *DISCOURSE:*

-> Now published for a second time, and expanded in various ways. <-

-> *Attached to the same is,* <-

## [The Work of] JULES CÉSAR
-> BOULENGER, of Loudun; <-

## ON THE <term>TAXES</term> AND <term>TOLLS</term> <note>The original Latin distinguishes between *tributis* (direct taxes paid by citizens) and *vectigalibus* (state revenues from public property or customs duties).</note>
## of the Roman People, a Book.

A small rectangular plaque at the base of the image contains the motto: "SCIENTIA IMMUTABILIS" <note>Knowledge is Unchangeable.</note></image-desc>

-> *Available for sale at Frankfurt,* <-
-> At the Bookshop of the Heirs of LAZARUS ZETZNER. <-
-> THE YEAR 1626. <-

<meta>This page is the formal dedication of the volume. The author, Christopher Besold, is dedicating his work to Martin Chemnitz (the younger, 1561–1627), a significant legal figure and diplomat who served the Dukes of Pomerania. This type of dedication was common in the seventeenth century to secure patronage and intellectual validation from influential peers.</meta>

<image-desc>A rectangular decorative woodcut headpiece featuring a repeating symmetrical pattern of stylized floral motifs and scrolling foliage, similar to fleur-de-lis and palmettes.</image-desc>

### *To the Truly Noble and Most Distinguished Man;*

# LORD MARTIN
# CHEMNITZ, MOST EMINEN-

->TISSIMO, Chief Councilor to the<-
->Most Serene Princes of<-
->Pomerania,<- <note>The "Princes of Pomerania" refers to the Dukes of the House of Pomerania, for whom Chemnitz served as a high-ranking legal and political advisor.</note>

### *His great patron and friend:*

## THESE MODEST <note>The original Latin *exilia* can mean "slender" or "meager," a conventional expression of humility by the author regarding his own work.</note> REFLECTIONS,
## POLITICAL AND
## PHILOLOGICAL,

->FOR THE SAKE OF THE HIGHEST RESPECT AND PERPETUAL<-
->*memory, he deservedly dedicates this, and gladly submits it*<-
->*to his [Chemnitz’s] most refined judgment.*<- <note>original: "censurae... limatissimae." In this period, "censura" referred to a critical review or scholarly evaluation rather than the modern sense of suppressing information.</note>

# C. B. <note>Christopher Besold.</note>

--- Page 4 ---
<meta>This page follows the formal dedication to Martin Chemnitz. It features a commendatory poem by Johann Martin Rauscher, a colleague of Besold at the University of Tübingen. Such poems were standard in 17th-century academic publishing, serving as "blurbs" or testimonials from fellow scholars to validate the importance of the work.</meta>

<image-desc>Decorative horizontal border with repeating floral and leaf patterns across the top of the page.</image-desc>

### To the Reader.

# JOHANNES MARTINUS
## RAUSCHER, OF THE ACADEMY OF TÜBINGEN,
-> PROFESSOR. <- <note>Johann Martin Rauscher (1591–1649) was a noted professor of eloquence, history, and Greek at Tübingen. He was a contemporary and colleague of Christopher Besold.</note>

You, to whom the Mercy of Heaven has granted the royal scepters, <note>original: "fasces." In Ancient Rome, these were bundles of rods representing a magistrate's power. Here, it refers generally to the authority of rulers.</note>
> Or has placed the People under your station in some other rank;
You ask, upon what steady foundation the Republic may walk,
> And by what means you may preserve your Citizen,
When War <note>original: "Mavors," an archaic name for Mars, the Roman god of war.</note> and Poverty alike shall press upon you;
> And neither the one nor the other will abandon their roles?
Will you go to seek oracles at Clarian Delphi, <note>Delphi was the site of the most famous oracle in the ancient Greek world, dedicated to Apollo.</note>
> Where frivolous words seethe from the Priestess for the God?
Or will the sounding of the Dodonian bronze be sought, <note>The Oracle of Zeus at Dodona was famous for its "talking" bronze vessels or rustling oak leaves.</note>
> Or those other voices which the Pythian laurel holds?
There is no need: behold, here are the answers for you in the midst of the Lyceum: <note>The "Lyceum" refers to the school of Aristotle, used here to signify the university or the halls of learning where Besold teaches.</note>
> **THE COMMONWEALTH WILL BE SAFE, PROVIDED THE TREASURY IS SAFE.**
The Republic will be safe with a safe Treasury. So that it
> May flourish, O, apply, apply your strengths!
But let those strengths be easy and moderate, and free from massive weight,
> Lest you, the crowd of citizens, sink under your own burden.
Lest, while you perhaps provide strength and sinew to the Treasury,
> You are entirely deprived of your own strength.
For the Bull rejects yokes that are too constraining,
> And a heavy breeze sinks a slender ship.
Doubtless here a prudent power will know both the goal and the limit,
> Commanding what is owed by an equal law.

<summary>A commendatory poem by Professor Johann Martin Rauscher of Tübingen, arguing that a healthy state treasury is essential for the survival of the republic, provided that taxation is moderate and not burdensome to the citizens.</summary>
<keywords>public finance, taxation, statecraft, Johann Martin Rauscher, University of Tübingen, political philosophy, treasury, justice</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commendatory poem by Johann Martin Rauscher. The previous page established the book as a guide for rulers and citizens seeking stability amidst war and economic hardship, dismissing ancient oracles in favor of the legal and academic wisdom found in the "Lyceum" of the university.</meta>

> From here also the Commonwealth, boasting of its ready coinage,
> Shall not complain of a harsh burden with a mournful voice.
> Do you doubt it? This book will prove it by the witness of authors’ consensus,
> And will bring proof to these words.
> Therefore, Reader, you may learn from the pages of <term>Besold</term> <note>Christopher Besold (1577–1638) was a prominent German jurist and scholar whose works on public law and finance were highly influential in the Holy Roman Empire.</note> a certain method and the just governance of what is Right.
> Calumny, plastered with infamous words, shall not wear these pages down,
> Nor the scraping of a squinting brow. <note>original: "strabi lima supercilii." A metaphor for the harsh, narrow-minded, or malicious scrutiny of critics who look "askance" at a work.</note>
> The Author of the book himself possesses the true heraldry of praise,
> And his reach touches both sides of the Heavens.
> Indeed, he long ago claimed the world as his debtor,
> And holds it bound by eternal obligations.
> This is the shield of Pallas! <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom and strategic war; her shield, the Aegis, offered divine protection.</note> Hang up your black pebble, <note>original: "nigrum suspende lapillum." In ancient Greek courts, a black pebble was used to cast a vote for condemnation or "guilty." Rauscher is telling critics to put away their judgments.</note>
> Aeolus: <note>The god of the winds. Here, it implies that the "hot air" or bluster of critics cannot shake the book's foundation.</note> this book does not stand by your breezes.

-> ### IN TÜBINGEN. <- <note>original: "Antecessor." In a university context, this refers to a formal professor or a predecessor in a specific chair of learning.</note>

-> Anagram, <note>original: "Αναγραμματισμός." Anagrams were a popular intellectual game in the 17th century, where a person's name was rearranged to reveal a hidden motto or truth about their character.</note> through the changing of the Letter <-
-> R. into U. <-

> **I** CARE NOTHING FOR FATE; THIS GOOD CAUSE ALONE TRIUMPHAT. <note>original: "NIL CURO SORTES..." The Latin phrase is an anagrammatic motto derived from the name Christopher Besoldus.</note>

## I N D E X.

...are imposed upon communities. <note>The previous page ended mid-word; the Latin 'tatibus' likely completes 'civitatibus' (cities) or 'communitatibus' (communities).</note> folio 177. n. 127. & the following page, number 129.

**Taxation**. <note>original: "Collecta" — a general term for an assessment or tax collected for a specific public purpose.</note> *See also **Tribute**.*

An **extraordinary tax** is willingly provided by subjects if the Treasury was not previously exhausted through the fault of the Prince, chapter 4. n. 3. and if the subjects are content with their present state. In the same place.

An **extraordinary tax** is only then to be imposed if no other way of raising money can be found. chapter 4. n. 2. v. 4.

A **tax** is more easily borne when no one is exempt from it. chapter 4. n. 20. & v. 2.

The **Imperial Tax** <note>original: "Collecta Imperialis" — taxes owed to the Holy Roman Empire to support its common expenses, such as defense against the Turks.</note> is an ordinary obligation, according to the opinion of some. folio 165. number 97.

What an **Imperial Tax** is. folio 147. number 49.

A **tax** is imposed upon a subject only by reason of the goods they possess within the Territory. folio 167. n. 102.

That **tax** is more approved where not the "heads" or persons, but the goods of the subjects are assessed. chapter 4. n. 18.

The **Estates** <note>original: "ordines" — the representative bodies of the nobility, clergy, and cities that held political rights within a territory.</note> may refuse a tax if the Prince initiates an unnecessary war. chapter 4. n. 5. v. 3. folio 88.

By what means we can ensure that subjects are able to pay an **extraordinary tax**. chapter 4. number 8. & following.

When murmurs of the people follow an **immoderate tax**, they should not be suppressed, but rather ignored. <note>original: "dissimulandæ" — literally 'to be feigned as not noticed' or overlooked.</note> chapter 4. number 12. v. 4.

Whoever possesses **Sovereignty** <note>original: "Superioritatem" — the highest territorial authority.</note> demands the Imperial Tax. folio 151. number 60.

One who does not pay a **tax** is only punished if they have done so deceitfully. folio 189. number 16.

**Out-of-towners** <note>original: "forenses" — people living outside the jurisdiction who might still own property within it.</note> do not pay the tax. folio 164. number 93. & following.

The **right of taxing** <note>original: "jus collectandi"</note> is reckoned among the **Regalian rights**. <note>original: "Regalibus" — rights and privileges belonging exclusively to the sovereign or crown.</note> folio 158. n. 97. & following.

Only subjects are to be **taxed**, by reason of their domicile. folio 165. n. 95. & following.

A **tax** is not paid on precious household goods, idle money, etc. folio 190. number 17.

Whether a **tax** can be imposed on "immovables" <note>The original Latin "immobilibus" is used here, but the examples given—merchandise and furniture—are typically movable goods. The author may be discussing whether these items are taxed as if they were fixed assets.</note>, such as merchandise and precious furniture. chapter 4. number 18. v. 2.

A **tax** imposed due to necessity must be remitted once that necessity ceases. chapter 4. n. 4.

A **tax** ought to be demanded according to the means of the subjects. chapter 4. n. 12. & v. 1.

Whether a **Lord** can tax his subjects for the marriage of a daughter, or for the purchase of a new castle. chapter 4. n. 2. v. 2. folio 73.

In the matter of **taxes**, **custom** is of the greatest importance. folio 149. number 52.

When a controversy arises on the occasion of **taxes**, the **custom** of everyone is especially to be observed. folio 169. n. 106.

A **tax** can be demanded only once. <note>This likely refers to a specific assessment for a single cause.</note> folio 150. n. 55.

The **Estates** do not pay the Imperial Taxes from their own treasuries. <note>original: "Cameris" — the private or administrative exchequers of the rulers.</note> folio 166. n. 98.

If a **tax** is immoderate, it gives rise to rebellion. chapter 4. number 12. v. 1.

# INDEX OF PRINCIPAL MATTERS.
## I N D E X.

The architects of unlawful **exactions** <note>original: "Exactionum illegitimarum" — refers to the forced collection of taxes or fees without proper legal basis.</note> are blamed. chapter 7. number 1. volume 2.

Advisors for new **exactions** persuade the Prince that a new tribute is not heavy for the People. chapter 7. number 1. volume 2. folio 220.

Advisors for unlawful **exactions** look more to their own benefit than that of the Prince. chapter 7. number 1. volume 2. folio 219.

A **tax collector** <note>original: "Exactor"</note> is often more hated than the tax itself. chapter 4. number 20. & volume 1. and the same is held in chapter 7. number 1. volume 2. folio 219.

**Extension** <note>original: "Extensio" — the legal principle of applying a law to cases not explicitly named in the text.</note> has no place in penal matters. folio 191. number 20.

To impose an **extraordinary collection** <note>original: "Extraordinariam... collationem" — a special tax raised outside of the usual schedule, often for emergencies.</note> pertains to the rights of Majesty. chapter 4. number 1. volume 1.

->F.<-

Why there were formerly so many **fiefs** <note>original: "Feuda"</note> in Germany. chapter 1. number 1. volume 3.

The privilege of the **Treasury** <note>original: "Fisci Privilegium"</note> according to the law *bene à Zenone* <note>original: "ex l. benè à Zenone" — a reference to a specific Roman law in the Code of Justinian (C. 7.37.3) regarding the sale of property by the treasury.</note>, whether and when it takes place. folio 195. number 33. and following.

In cases of doubt, one should not favor the **Treasury**. folio 187. number 8.

Whether **unassessed goods** <note>original: "bona incensita" — property not recorded in the official tax registers.</note> should fall to the Treasury. folio 184. number 1. and many following.

Who is considered to have a **Treasury** <note>original: "Fiscum"</note>. chapter 1. number 3. volume 1.

How the **Public Treasury** <note>original: "Fiscus"</note> and the **State Treasury** <note>original: "Ærarium"</note> differ. chapter 1. number 3. and also, numbers 1 and 2.

The **Treasury** in the political body represents the **spleen** <note>original: "lienem refert" — a common metaphor in early modern political thought: if the "spleen" (treasury) grows too large by absorbing all the blood, the rest of the "body" (the people) withers away.</note>. chapter 1. number 1. volume 1.

**Usurers** <note>original: "Fœneratores"</note> are not to be tolerated. chapter 3. number 4.

**Foreigners** <note>original: "Forenses" — specifically those residing outside a particular jurisdiction.</note>: to what extent they may be taxed. folio 165. number 96. and folio 168. number 103. and following.

**Forest authority** <note>original: "Forstliche Obrigkeit" — the legal jurisdiction over forests, including hunting and timber rights.</note>. folio 142. numbers 32. & 33.

**Compulsory labor services** <note>original: "Frondienste" — feudal labor that peasants were required to perform for their lord.</note>. folio 181. number 138.

->G.<-

**Public exchange** <note>original: "Gemeiner Wechsel" — refers to common bills of exchange or public banking.</note>. chapter 3. number 9.

What the **generality of words** <note>original: "Generalitas verborum" — a legal concept regarding how broadly or strictly a text should be interpreted.</note> implies. folio 131. number 4.

**Courts** <note>original: "Gerichte" — specifically referring to jurisdictions or legal tribunals.</note>. folio 179. number 130. and following.

The power of **German Princes** formerly consisted in the multitude of their vassals. chapter 1. number 1. volume 3.

**Lottery** <note>original: "Glückhafen" — literally a "pot of luck," a common term for public lotteries in the Holy Roman Empire.</note>. chapter 3. number 10.

->H.<-

**Death duty** <note>original: "Hauptfall" — a feudal due paid to a lord upon the death of a tenant.</note>. chapter 4. number 14. volume 2.

Why each of the **Swiss** <note>original: "Helvetiorum"</note> serves as a soldier at his own expense. chapter 1. number 1. volume 3.

**High Justice** <note>original: "Hohe Gericht" — the power to preside over capital cases involving the "high" crimes.</note> and what follows from it. folio 143. number 35. and following.

**Homage** <note>original: "Homagium" — the formal ceremony of allegiance by a vassal to a lord.</note>. folio 136. number 12.

**Homicides** are not to be punished with a monetary fine. chapter 3. number 4. volume 2.

->I.<-

The Prince's goods are **immune** from taxes. folio 166. number 99.

One **immune** from taxes, if they once allow themselves to be inscribed in the assessment book, is deemed to renounce their privilege. folio 155. number 68.

No one is **immune** from the **Imperial tax** <note>original: "Imperiali collectâ" — taxes owed to the Holy Roman Emperor.</note>. folio 151. number 59.

No one is **immune** from the **Turkish taxes** <note>original: "Turcicis collectis" — taxes levied to fund wars against the Ottoman Empire.</note>. folio 163. number 88.

REPUBLIC OR ANY PRINCIPALITY <note>The author uses "Republic" in the classical sense of any organized state or commonwealth</note> is a certain civil body; I believe this is clear to everyone. Therein, just as the Counselors hold the seat and role of the Mind—to which the entire nature of man submits—so money is held to be the sinew of affairs to be conducted. <note>original: "pecunia rerum gerendarum nervus habetur." A common legal and political metaphor comparing money to the tendons or "sinews" that allow a body to move.</note> *Law 1, section 20, in the case of questions.* Without expenses, no Republic can stand; it has need of wealth, without which nothing that is necessary can be done. By these sinews of public expenditure, all the offices of the Magistrate receive such vigor that the entire body of the Republic can be both more strongly sustained and likewise more promptly moved. *See Peter Gregory of Toulouse, On the Republic, book 3, chapter 1, at the beginning; Julius Caesar Bulenger, Treatise on the Taxes of the Roman People, chapter 3, at the beginning; Laelius Zecchius, On the Prince, book 2, chapter 3, number 1; Pierre Matthieu, in Sejanus, page 287 and following; Jacob Bornitius, On the Treasury, book 1, chapter 1, page 2; Zacharias Fridenreich, Politics, chapter 17, at the beginning; Hoenonius, Political Disputations 5, thesis 72, in the fundamentals, at the beginning; and most recently Heinrich Klock, in*

# Political Discourses

In his most elegant dispute concerning the Law of Taxes, conclusion 1, he states: **By money the borders of the Empire are defended, the poor are relieved, and those who have served well are rewarded:** to say nothing of other public and necessary affairs of the State, which cannot be managed at all without coins. The legal expert Celsus, *in the law "if a chorus" 79. §. 1. of the Digest on legacies 3*, praises the opinion of the ancient country-folk: **Money without a "peculium" <note>original: "peculium"; a small private reserve or "nest egg" set aside for emergencies</note> is fragile:** calling that a "peculium" which was set aside for the sake of protection, so that they might use it in a time of necessity. If this holds true for country-folk, why should the same not be pronounced regarding Rulers? For Cities stand in need of money and revenues, just as households do; but even much more so: as Aristotle says, *Politics book 1, chapter 11, near the end.* Not only in a Principality, but truly in whatever form of State, money must necessarily be gathered: which are the words of Maecenas to Augustus, in Dio Cassius, *book 52.*

1. Whether a public and perpetual Treasury <term>Aerarium: the public treasury of ancient Rome, here used for any state fund</term> ought to be maintained; or, should Treasures be collected by Rulers? This is usually disputed on both sides. Consult *Nicholas of Cusa, book 3 of "On Catholic Concordance," chapter 39; Bodin, book 6 of "The Republic," chapter 2, number 675 to the end and following; Tholosanus on the Republic, last chapter; Thomas More, book 1 of "Utopia," pages 40 to 43; Jacobus Simanca, book 3 of "The Republic," chapter 15; after Botero, book 7 from the beginning of "The Reason of State"; Apollinaris Calderini, discourse 6.* Also the author of the *Anti-Machiavelli, or Commentaries on the Right and Tranquil Administration of a Kingdom and any Principality, book 3, theorem 32; Bartholomew Keckermann, practical dispute 34, problem 15; Gregor Rolbag, "The Battle of Male and Female," chapter 40 at the end; Hermann Lather, treatise on the Census, book 1, chapter 1.* 

For the negative opinion <note>the argument against hoarding wealth</note>, one may cite the authority of Divine Law; *Deuteronomy chapter 17, verse 17,* where it is forbidden that a King should multiply for himself **gold and silver.** And in *Zechariah, chapter 9, verse 3,* the city of Tyre is reproached: because it heaped up silver for itself like dust, and gold like the mud of the streets. So also <margin>Julian was not greedy for gold</margin> the Emperor Julian was never greedy for increasing money; which he judged was more safely kept in the hands of private citizens: frequently proclaiming that Alexander the Great, when asked where he kept his treasures, kindly responded, "among my friends." *Ammianus Marcellinus, book 25, page 538.* Constantius

# Concerning the Public Treasury. Chapter I.
<note>original: "de Ærario publ. Cap. I."</note>

...also, when his friends reproached him for caring too indifferently for the Treasury <note>original: "Fiscum," referring here to the Emperor's personal or state purse</note>,
<margin>The nature of a good prince.</margin> he replied: "A good Prince, who is loved by his people more than he is feared, possesses whatever the Citizens own." Eutropius, book 10, at the beginning. And concerning the same man, Eusebius, in book 1 of *The Life of Constantine*, chapter 10, narrates this as a true historical event, saying:
<margin>Diocletian's Legates, accusing him of poverty, are shown how great wealth is otherwise gathered by well-wishing subjects.</margin>
"When the rumor had spread everywhere that he was mild and distinguished, that he ardently pursued a life of holiness, and that because of his incredible clemency and kindness toward those who obeyed his Empire, he had stored up no treasure for himself; Diocletian, who at that time held the highest rank of the Empire, sent Legates to him and began to heavily rebuke his loose *negligence in administering* the Republic, casting his poverty in his teeth as a disgrace. To confirm this matter, he used as an argument the fact that he had absolutely no money hidden away in his treasuries. Then he [Constantius] <note>Constantius Chlorus, father of Constantine the Great</note> prayed the Legates who had come from the Emperor to stay for a little while. From all the nations subject to his jurisdiction, he summoned those who overflowed with the greatest abundance of riches. He told them he had need of money, and that this was a timely opportunity for each man to declare his ready zeal and goodwill toward his Lord and King. Upon hearing this, deciding that this was the occasion they had long desired to clearly testify their benevolent will toward him, they cast aside all hesitation and labored to fill his Treasuries <note>term: Aeraria - the public treasury of Rome, as opposed to the private fiscus</note> quickly with gold, silver, and other kinds of wealth and resources. They contended vehemently among themselves with a certain zeal and passion to see who could surpass the other in giving, and they performed this with a very joyful and cheerful countenance. When this was finished, Constantius wished the legates sent by Diocletian to become spectators of his treasure; he ordered them to be witnesses of what they had seen with their own eyes. He reported to them how that treasure, which was presently collected and stored in his Treasuries, had for a long time been preserved by the owners of the money and riches themselves, as if by the safest guardians. These men were then seized with great admiration for what had been done. But the most kind Emperor, after their departure, summoned the owners of that money again; and when he had treated them most humanely for the sake of their obedience and singular goodwill, he ordered them to return home with all their resources recovered. Almost the same thing was made clear long before by Cyrus, the Monarch of the Persians, to Croesus (who was urging him to store up treasures of gold at home), when by asking his subjects and friends for a great sum of money..."

# Political Discourses

<margin>
Cyrus the Persian.
For the King judges that the best way of gathering money and the finest wealth is found in his subjects; a treasury of wealthy citizens and subjects makes a King powerful.
</margin>

...had collected a great force of money; as Xenophon records in the 8th book of the *Education of Cyrus* <note>original: "Cyripædia"</note>, page 2, where he relates that Cyrus said among other things: "Do you see, Croesus, that I too have treasures? But you would command me to expose myself to envy and hatred by collecting them, and to place my trust in hired guards. But I consider my enriched friends to be my treasures, and they are more faithful guardians both of myself and of our goods than if I set hired mercenaries over them." There was also a pithy saying <term>apophthegm: a concise, pointed saying</term> of Alfonso, King of Aragon, recorded by Antonio Panormita in book 4, number 4: that it is the primary zeal and duty of Kings to make their people wealthy; for if the people are made richer, the Kings certainly will not be poor.

<margin>
Louis, King of France
</margin>
Nicolas Froumenteau, in the 3rd book of *The Secret of Finances*, page 410 and following, gives praise to Louis XII, King of France, because although he was involved in many wars, when he was urged to accumulate treasures, he replied:

> that his riches and treasures should be in the purses and in the houses of his subjects; and that the Prince could not better hoard and enrich himself than by enriching his subjects through good treatment and relief;

add also the preface to the 2nd book of the same treatise, page 10 and following.

<margin>
James, King of Britain
</margin>
> Do not enrich yourself, says James, King of Great Britain, to his son in the 2nd book of *Royal Instructions* <note>original: "Instituio Regia"</note>, by imposing new and heavy taxes on the people; but consider the wealth and resources of your people to be your most certain riches.

The true and certain wealth of a Prince (these are the words of the author of the *Anti-Machiavelli*, theory 32, page 678) is situated in the wealth of his subjects, placed almost beyond all risk of danger or loss. For money sought from public taxes and tributes can either slip away through the negligence of collectors, or be diverted by their flight or treachery, or perish by war, shipwreck, or any other accident; but the treasure which the people hold in their own possession is not subject to so many hazards. Therefore, a Prince can increase his resources by no better method than if he treats the people committed to him with clemency, and allows them to grow wealthy in peace through moderate and healthy care and the lightening of their burdens.

<margin>
At Venice, a plan for establishing a treasury is a capital offense.
</margin>
In this manner the Venetians, most skilled in political matters, administer their Republic; indeed, among them it is a capital crime to speak of establishing a public treasury or hoard: otherwise, the citizens are so ample in their family resources that the Republic cannot suffer from want. Philippe de Comines, book 7, final chapter, page 683. Conversely, there was a dispute against a treasury and tax in Scotland in the year 1555, as George Buchanan reports in *Scottish Affairs*, book 16, page 545. Lu-

# Concerning the Public Treasury. Chapter I.

...it is necessary to record his very words, though they are quite numerous.

> This method of raising money, he says, was commonly believed to have been devised by D'Oysel, de Roubay, <note>original: "Osellium, Rubeumque." Henri Cleutin, sieur d'Oysel, and Yves de Rubay were French advisors to the Scottish court.</note> and those few Frenchmen who surrounded the Regent; <note>Mary of Guise, who served as Queen Regent of Scotland from 1554 to 1560.</note> namely, that by conducting a census, records should be drawn up in which the property of all people would be registered. Then, each individual, according to their rated share, would annually pay a small portion into a public treasury destined for this use to cover the expenses of war. From that money, kept in this specific treasury, mercenary soldiers could be hired to guard the borders, while the Nobility remained quietly at home—unless a greater force of enemies should attack than could be sustained by the ordinary garrisons.
> 
> While the lower classes bore this new method of raising money with great bitterness and openly pursued it with stinging words, the greater part of the Nobles muttered in silence; each was looking out for himself, fearing that whoever first opposed the Regent's desire would draw the primary hatred of the refusal upon himself alone. The next rank of men <note>The "Lairds" or lesser nobility and gentry.</note> was no less incensed at the Leading Men—who by their silence were betraying public liberty—than they were at the Regent. When about three hundred had assembled at Edinburgh, they sent two from their body to the Regent to plead against the ignominy of paying a tribute and the confession of public and private poverty involved in taking a census. For they argued that their ancestors had not only defended themselves and their property against the English (who were then far more powerful than they are now), but had even frequently raided their lands. Nor had they themselves now degenerated so much that they would not spend both their property and their lives for their country, should the need arise.
> 
> As for the hiring of mercenaries, they argued it was a matter full of danger to commit the highest interests of the Scottish state to men without property or hope, who would dare anything for money; men whose profound greed might be ignited to plot new schemes as occasion and fortune shifted their loyalty. And even if everything else were well, and those men were more mindful of love for the country than of their own condition, would it be credible to anyone that mercenaries would fight more bravely for others' belongings than owners would for themselves and their own? Would a small pittance, soon to cease in time of peace, stir greater incentives in the minds of the ignoble commoners than fortunes, children, wives, altars, and hearths would stir for the Nobility? *And a little later:* Who will collect this small sum? How much of it will necessarily be lost to the wages of the tax-collectors or gatherers? Who will guarantee that it will be turned toward public use and not into an instrument of luxury? That no such thing will happen, gives us great hope, great...

# Political Discourses

<margin>
The saying of Trajan Caesar: the increase of the treasury is the detriment of the subjects.
</margin>
The integrity and moderation of our most illustrious Princess (in whose hands the supreme power now rests) provides us with confidence; yet, when we recall either the internal deeds of others or our own history, we cannot restrain ourselves from fearing that what we have often seen happen in the past might happen again. Thus far George Buchanan <note>A Scottish historian and humanist scholar (1506–1582) known for his political theories on the limits of monarchical power.</note>. According to the saying of Trajan Caesar: the Treasury <note>original: "Fiscus"; the private or state purse of the ruler.</note> should be regarded in the State as the spleen is in the body; namely, that as it grows, the remaining limbs waste away; because

->*When the Treasury is increased, the poverty of the citizens is proven.*<-

as Andrea Alciatus <note>An Italian jurist and writer (1492–1550) famous for his "Emblems."</note> sings in Emblem 146. This is truly an excellent and memorable sentiment, which Corasius <note>Jean de Coras (1512–1572), a French jurist.</note> in *Miscellany* book 6, chapter 19, wishes were carved and hidden in the innermost hearts of all Princes. "Do you wish, then," he says, "O Prince, for the body to be strong? Ensure that the spleen does not swell. Do you wish, O Prince, for your members—that is, your citizens and subjects—to be well? Do not have a swollen treasury!" And so, Bonfinius <note>Antonio Bonfini (1427–1502), an Italian humanist who wrote the history of Hungary.</note> in *Hungarian Affairs*, decade 2, book 3, reports and praises how Bela, King of the Pannonians <note>Béla I of Hungary.</note>, by relieving the people of all taxes indiscriminately and remitting tributes generally to the provinces, made both the nobility and the common folk very wealthy; so much so that not even the lowliest peasant was found to be needy. Thomas More <note>Author of *Utopia* (1516).</note> likewise rejects a public treasury <note>original: "Aerarium"; the public treasury of the state.</note> for the reason that he believes an enemy is more invited and attracted by an abundance of public wealth. This was also formerly the opinion of the Kings of Egypt, according to Herodotus, book 3; and for that reason, so that they might less invite foreign Princes to invade them, they were accustomed to consume almost all public money in the construction of cities and pyramids, or in the diversion of rivers, or in repairing the embankments of the Nile. See Pliny, book 36, chapter 12, at the beginning; and Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French political philosopher.</note>, in the cited chapter 2, number 675.

<margin>
The reason for establishing a Treasury.
</margin>
2. On the other hand, the argument for a Treasury is supported by the fact that almost all nations have had storehouses of wealth: Zecchius, *Politics*, book 2, chapter 3, number 1, folio 319. Furthermore, Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note>, who did not want his people to have a Treasury, by that very act prevented the Republic from expanding its borders; and when the Spartans sought to take up arms, being destitute of the expenses for war, they were soon forced to borrow money and subsequently fell into extreme danger. See Aristotle, *Politics*, book 2, chapter 7, at the end; and Bodin, in the cited chapter 2, at the beginning. Wisely, therefore, Archidamus, King of the Spartans, as recorded in Thucydides, book 1, when dissuading them from undertaking a war against the Athenians, said: "We have no public money, nor do we readily contribute from our private stores." The Athenians in the time of Themistocles lacked a Treasury; therefore, to provide for the expenses of war, Themistocles had to use a violent remedy—

# Chapter I. Concerning the Public Treasury

<page-num>7</page-num>

Themistocles <note>original: "stocles" - likely referring to the Athenian statesman Themistocles</note> was compelled to act. *Plutarch in his Life [of Themistocles], number 6, page 222 in my French edition.*
Furthermore, in *1 Kings, chapter 3, verse 13*, the Lord God <note>original: "Jehova Deus"</note> promises King Solomon <note>original: "Schelomoni Regi"</note> riches more abundant than those of all other princes, as a kind of distinguished blessing. Likewise, where a public treasury is lacking, the reins of greed are loosened and the pursuit of money is provoked; for when there is nothing in the public store from which citizens can expect relief, everyone scrapes together for themselves against the chance of necessity. And finally, among political thinkers, the people of Genoa in Italy, Antwerp in Belgium, and Cologne and Augsburg in Upper Germany are generally criticized because they are publicly poor while being privately wealthy. *Master Piccart on Aristotle's Politics, book 2, chapter 9, at the end.*

<margin>The Author's Opinion</margin>
3. I believe that in a Republic, effort must be made so that the Treasury is always wealthy. This must be done, however, in such a way that (1) there must be a total proportion between the revenues of the Prince and his responsibilities; and thus, I would wish his revenues to be as sufficient as his responsibilities are various and manifold, and the expenses necessary for their sake. *Keckermann, Politics, book 1, chapter 21, at the beginning, page 328.* Hence, in certain Republics, it does not seem at all necessary for the Treasury to be exceedingly rich. Thus in Turkey, the Emperor has nearly three hundred thousand men bound and obligated to him from the <term>Timars</term> <note>Land grants given in exchange for military service in the Ottoman Empire</note> alone; so that as often as he pleases, and to whatever lands he orders them to go, they set out for war at their own expense. *Lazzaro Soranzo, in The Ottoman, chapter 47.* This is also attested by a certain Venetian Consul in Greece, who says: *In the acquisition that the Ottomans made of their State, they took possession not only of all the direct ownership, but also in large part of the profits of the lands, and these they then distributed to the soldiers for their lifetime as a salary; in such a way that, without other expenditure of public money, that Lord maintains so great a number of horses [cavalry] that to pay for them with money, fifteen million in gold per year would not suffice, etc. Political Treasure, part 1, report on Constantinople, page 216, etc.* So also in the past, the power of the Emperor and the [German] Princes consisted in the multitude of <term>Vassals</term> <note>Feudal tenants who owed military service to a lord</note>; and for that reason so many <term>Fiefs</term> <note>Land held on condition of feudal service</note> were established, to the point that they retained almost nothing for themselves. Today, since wars are waged with voluntary and hired soldiers, and the services of Vassals are restricted by various limitations, new Fiefs are more rarely granted; and there is a need for a wealthier Treasury which may supply <term>Stipends</term> <note>Regular pay or wages for soldiers</note> in case of necessity. Conversely, when the Swiss, having driven out the Nobility, proclaimed full immunity, it was agreed that each man should serve in the military at his own expense. *Bodin, said chapter 2, number 660.* So also

# Political Discourses

Regarding the Chatti <note>original: "Cattis"; an ancient Germanic tribe</note> (whose name Cluverius demonstrates is still retained by the Hessians in *Ancient Germany, book 3, chapter 5*), Cornelius Tacitus, in his book *On the Customs of the Germans*, reveals that they are neither worn down by tributes nor ground away by tax collectors. Exempted from burdens and contributions, and set aside solely for use in battles, they are reserved for wars like missiles and weapons. (2.) It ought not to be within the judgment and power of one or a few men to empty the Treasury <term>Treasury: original "Aerarium," the public fund of ancient Rome</term> when necessity does not press for it; this can indeed be more easily prevented in a free or even a mixed form of Republic.

<margin>
Valerius Publicola is praised
</margin>
And so, among the Romans, Valerius Publicola was formerly praised because, when it was necessary for citizens to contribute money based on the census, he neither wished to touch the administration of the money himself, nor did he allow his friends to do so; nor did he permit the money to be brought into the house of any private individual at all. Instead, he established the Temple of Saturn as the Treasury. *Plutarch, in his Life [of Publicola].* Truly, since the guarding of public money has always seemed difficult beyond measure, the Kings of the Persians, just like the Romans, cast their gold into the shape of heavy ingots <note>original: "laterculorum," literally small bricks or tiles</note> so that they might protect the Treasury more sacredly from plunder and extravagance. Bodin, *book 6, chapter 2, number 675*; Tholozanus, *book 3 on the Republic, chapter 3, throughout, and especially number 8.* By this same means, the Master of Finance for Charles V, King of France, thought the facility of his Lord in spending could be restrained: Bernard Girard, Lord of Haillan, *book 17, folio 424 of the History of France.* Namely, <note>original French: "qu'on ne garderoit plus d'or monnoyé..."</note> that they would no longer keep minted gold inside the King's coffers, but rather they would make large ingots, which would be kept and be more difficult to give away and distribute. But neither the weight of such masses, nor the stone towers of Rhampsinitus <note>An Egyptian Pharaoh mentioned by Herodotus</note>, nor the subterranean caves of Sardanapalus, will be able to protect that public money; nor can the sanctity of temples or tombs, nor deep rivers hide it, if the rare and continued wisdom of Princes or the provident care of the Estates does not do so. The anxiety of amassing wealth is ridiculous and can only turn to the greatest damage of the Republic and individual citizens, unless there is a limit to what is brought in. Xenophon rightly writes in his *Oeconomicus, or book 5 of the Memorabilia*, that this is like drawing water into a perforated jar. See Erasmus in his *Adages* on the "insatiable jar."

<margin>
Gaius Caligula, a massive squanderer
</margin>
And thus Gaius Caligula—surpassing the genius of all spendthrifts with his grandson-like <note>extravagant or wasteful</note> expenses—consumed within less than a full year the immense wealth and that entire fortune of Tiberius Caesar, amounting to two billion seven hundred million sesterces; Suetonius, *chapter 37*. This happened because he lacked a powerful guardian. Monarchies (these are the golden words of the author of *The Secret of Finances*...

# Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter I.

In the dedicatory epistle to the King of France and Poland <note>referring to Henry III, who held both titles</note>, it is said that [finances] will always be in need, unless the key to their Finances is placed and consigned into a good and faithful hand: that is to say, that it shuts with such a strong spring that lock-pickers cannot pick it if possible. For there are hooks <note>metaphorical "hooks" or "claws" used by corrupt officials to snatch funds</note> of all calibers; *twisted* hooks, *delicate* hooks, wasteful hooks, subtle hooks, the hooks of women, and refined hooks, etc. To remedy this evil, a law was passed in 
<margin>
The invention of the "Sacred Treasury" in France.
</margin>
France by Francis I, by which he ensured that four keys to the Sacred Treasury <note>Latin: *Aerarium Sanctius*, the private or emergency reserve of the monarch</note> were manufactured; the King would keep one for himself, and the others would be held by those he had placed in charge of the Treasury. To this law was also added a provision that no money should be moved from the chest unless the Prefect of the Treasury and the Scribe were present. When this custom was abolished by Henry II, all the resources of the Treasury soon lay open to the plunder of the powerful and of flatterers. *Bodin, book 6, chapter 2, number 674.*

II. By the term "Money," I do not only include coins, or even uncoined gold and silver; but everything that can be valued in money: *Law regarding the term "name," 4, and the following law at the beginning; Law regarding "money," 178, at the beginning; Law regarding "money," 222, concerning the significance of words.* <note>These are citations to the Digest of Roman Law</note> These are things which in times of necessity can be sold quickly, or which cannot always be purchased with coins when we lack them. Thus in France formerly, there were public forests in which an innumerable multitude of tall and lofty trees grew for every opportunity; which, if money was lacking in the Treasury during a pressing war, were felled. *Bodin, book 6, chapter 2, number 675.* Likewise in Strasbourg <note>Latin: *Argentina*</note>, and other similar places where the Republic is well-constituted, a great supply of grain <term>Annona: the year's harvest or grain supply</term> is stored up for unexpected cases of war and famine.

And the most learned Lather reports, *book 3 on the census, chapter 7, number 105*, that when a great difficulty regarding the grain supply was feared in the year 1602 on account of frequent hail and rain, Louis the Elder, Landgrave of Hesse, of most happy memory, in an assembly of the nobles...

III. The **Public Treasury** <term>Aerarium: originally the treasury of the Roman people, held in the Temple of Saturn</term> is properly and primarily considered to belong to the People and the Republic, whereas the **Privy Purse** <term>Fiscus: originally the Emperor's personal treasury, though the distinction blurred over time</term> is considered to belong to the Prince. *François Hotman in his Commentary on Legal Terms; Cujas on the preface to the title on the Law of the Fiscus, book 10 of the Code; Rivard, Book 4 of Miscellanies, chapter 4; Coras, Book 6 of Miscellanies, chapter 19.* And they say this is easily recognized from the words of Pliny in his *Panegyric* to Trajan, when he says: "But perhaps you do not restrain the Privy Purse with the same severity as you do the Public Treasury? Nay, with so much greater severity, as you believe yourself to have more license over your own property than over the public's." Thus, even now in most places, there is a difference **between the Chamber <note>the Prince's administrative office</note> and the estates of a Province.** <note>original: "vnder den Cammer: vnd einer Landschafft Gütter"</note>

In Democracies and Aristocracies <note>original: "Popularibus & Optimatum Imperiis"</note>, nothing that pertains to the City can be called Private; but in a Monarchy, the demesne lands <note>lands owned directly by the ruler</note> differ from Public lands, and the Privy Purse differs from the Public Treasury. *Bodin, chapter 2, number 641.* Add the most celebrated jurist of the Netherlands, *Paulus Busius, Book 3 on the Republic, chapter 1, number 3; and Political Disputations 11, questions 22 through 26;* who proves that legal authors understand the Public Treasury and the Privy Purse differently than other Latin writers. *This is also evident from the final paragraph of the Institutes on Usucaption.* However, Universities and Corporations are thought to possess a common chest or purse, not a Public Treasury or a Privy Purse: *see Christoph Coler, Parerga, chapter 28.* For the "Fiscus" properly belongs to those who recognize no superior, and who thus possess fiscal rights. *Marc'Antonio Peregrini on the Law of the Fiscus, Book 1, chapters 1 and 2.*

# On the Public Treasury, Chapter I.

...they designated these for the necessities of the state. <note>Citing Jean Bodin, *Six Books of the Commonwealth*, book 6, chapter 2; Pierre Grégoire (Tholosan), *On the Commonwealth*, book 3; *The General Guide to Finance*, part 1; and Jacob Bornitz, *On the Treasury*, book 1, chapter 3.</note> I also touched upon this in my own *Politics, book 1, chapter 4, number 32.* From this, the origin of **land-tithes, divisible estates, ground rents, etc.** <note>original: *Landtgarben / theilbaren Gütter / Bodenzinß*</note> seems to descend. If the land is subject to tax <note>original: "si ager vectigal"</note>, see the titles in the Digest regarding the leasing of civil or fiscal estates, and the entire title on manorial lands and forests, etc. See also the sections on the lands and forests of the Lord’s estate, the lands of the Divine House <note>A Roman legal term for the Emperor's private property</note>, and the collection of taxes from patrimonial and leasehold lands in Book 11 of the Code. Likewise, buildings are found in some places constructed by magistrates, serving the uses and opportunities of private business. *On these, see Bornitius, On Revenues, chapter 6.*

VI. However, the Prince or the Republic has the right to build a Treasury <note>original: "Ærarii"</note> not only from public lands; but also those who are the appointed guardians of the laws and the public state, and who devote themselves entirely to this, rightly seek from that source their livelihood and whatever else is necessary for the administration of such a difficult office—and even those things pertaining to their honorable recreation. *As I said in Book 1 of my Politics, chapter 4, number 31.* From this descends the ordinary collection of taxes (**Stewer / Schoß / Schatzung**) <note>German synonyms for various types of taxes, assessments, or "shots" (contributions)</note> which the rulers demand annually as a support for expenses and labors, and for the general protection of the realm. *See the arguments in Matthew chapter 17, verse 24, etc.; and chapter 22, verses 17 and 21; Mark 12, verse 17; Luke 20, verses 22 and 26; Romans 13, verse 6 and following, where see Tremellius in his notes on the Syriac version; and as I have said in Book 1 of my Politics.*

For which cause it is considered not only necessary, but also most equitable, that he should contribute something from the profit and gain of those goods into the common fund. They seem to expend for their own sake whatever they contribute to public use. <note>original: "causâ impendere videntur, quicquid conferunt in publicum usum." There is a unanimous consensus among historians and political theorists that Taxes and Tributes were born almost at the same time as Kings, and that there has been almost no nation that did not pay tributes from the public purse to its Kings and Magistrates. <note>Citing various authorities including Bulenger, Aegidius Thomatus, Heigius, Caspar Klock, and the author's friend Gottfried Engelhart of Silesia.</note> But indeed, among the Romans, "tribute" <note>Latin: *tributum*</note> was called by this name because that money was commanded from the Tribes, tribe by tribe, or from individuals among the People according to the valuation of their Estate <note>Latin: *Patrimonium*</note>. Gilkenius teaches this in *his commentary on the law 'it pleases,' number 20, etc., in the Code on the Most Holy Churches; and Hænon in Political Disputations 5, b. 90.* I shall also speak *concerning extraordinary tributes* myself below in *Chapter 4.*

VII. Likewise, the fruits of Jurisdiction and the revenues serving the Commonwealth are reckoned here; the profits from punishments and fines—***Fines / Trespasses / Penance*** <note>original German: "Brüch / Frevel / Bůssen"</note>—and whatever other things are enumerated as <term>Regalia</term> <note>Royal rights or prerogatives belonging to the sovereign</note> in the *single chapter of Title 56, Book 2 of the Feuds.* Add also *Choppin’s treatise on the Domain, throughout.* I have also reviewed these in part in *Book 1 of my Politics, Chapter 4, numbers 35 and following, up to number 42.*

<margin>Bornitius here, Book 3, Chapter 1.</margin>
These are called "incidental returns" because they fall to the treasury by chance and accident; commonly, these rights of the King are pointed out by Jurisconsults as "Regalia." And here, almost every Commonwealth has its own unique customs, nor are all things approved and adopted by everyone; indeed, new ones are devised daily, or old ones extended, as Juvenal once complained in *Satire 4*:

> Whatever is conspicuous and beautiful in the whole sea,
> Is a matter for the treasury, wherever it swims. —

And yet it is done unjustly if new burdens are introduced under the name of Regalia, as I warned in *Politics Book 1, Chapter 4, number 41, under verse 2, page 174.* Just as the Regalia are not uniform for all Commonwealths, so also, in general, a different system of the Treasury and Domain exists in different places. In Turkey, the Treasury consists almost entirely of Gifts, which are conferred upon the Emperor by other Princes (especially Christians) and also by his own Subjects and Servants; for no one is permitted to come into his sight with "empty hands," as the saying goes. They attribute this to Magnificence, though it brings immense utility with it. And if anyone looks more deeply into all the acts of the Turks...

# Political Discourses

If one wishes to look closely, they will recognize that these officials are solely intent on plundering wealth from all sides in great abundance, so that they may give what has been snatched away to the Emperor; often through their hands, as if through a kind of aqueduct, all those treasures of this Empire flow away and discharge themselves into the Ocean of the Emperor's greed. <note>The author uses the metaphor of an aqueduct to describe how wealth is systematically funneled from the provinces directly to the Sultan.</note> *Lazaro Soranzo, chapter 47. Achille Tarducci, in The Vincible Turk <note>original: "Turcâ Vincibili"</note>, on Royal Revenues and Treasuries, page 238 and following. Henning Arnisaeus, Politics book 2, chapter 5, page 563 and following.* The Lord <note>The Sultan</note> extracts one hundred and sixty thousand scudi in distributions and pensions from various Princes, says the author of the *Political Treasury: part 1, report on Constantinople, page 122.* And he orders those gifts to be displayed from a high and lofty place in the sight of everyone, as if they were the tributes of subjects. *Jean Bodin, book 6 of The Republic, chapter 2, number 645.* Likewise, in Turkey, all Christians or Jews who live there pay tributes; on the contrary, it is provided by Muhammadan Law that no tribute be exacted from Muslims. *Pierre Belon, book 3 of his Itinerary, chapter 28. Tarducci, page 239.*

2. So too the Roman Treasury <term>Ærarium; the public treasury of ancient Rome, housed in the Temple of Saturn</term>, while the Republic was flourishing, consisted of the spoils of enemies and the tributes of the conquered. For although it was lawful for soldiers to pillage enemy cities captured by force, the public monies were nevertheless brought into the Treasury. But when cities surrendered, or when money was promised by treaty or formal agreement, the soldier received nothing beyond his pay; unless the amount of money was so great that the pay seemed worthy of being doubled on account of the soldiers' outstanding valor. *Bodin, book 6 of The Republic, chapter 2, number 643. Arnisaeus, said chapter 5, page 564, etc.* The Romans also, having conquered peoples and fined them a portion of their land, were accustomed to send colonies of needy and poor citizens and assign that portion of land to them; from which incredible utility and glory accrued to the Empire and the Roman name. Bodin discusses this at length in *said chapter 2, number 644.* Indeed, the provincials were compelled to contribute not only tributes, but also grain, oil, pork, beef, etc., for the feeding of the Roman people. *Bulenger, chapter 9.* And when Perseus, the King of Macedonia, was defeated by Aemilius <note>Lucius Aemilius Paullus, who ended the Third Macedonian War in 168 BCE</note>, the Roman people were freed from the burden of tribute; for at that time such a great force of gold and silver was brought into the city that there was no need for any extraordinary collection; indeed, the old tribute ceased to be paid until the consulship of Hirtius and Pansa <note>43 BCE</note>, which was near the beginning of the first war waged by Augustus against Antony. *Pliny, book 33, chapter 3. See Plutarch, Life of Aemilius, number 19.* For even before then, Caesar had exposed treasures, untouched until 그날 <note>original: "illum diẽ"</note>, to the pillaging of the soldiers. *Whence Lucan, book 3:*

## CHAPTER II.

Regarding the Treasury, a threefold inspection occurs: namely, how the revenues destined for the Sovereignty are to be preserved; how they are to be increased, and others created in times of necessity; and finally, by whom the Treasury is to be administered.

I. THE PRINCIPAL METHOD OF PRESERVING REVENUES AND THE TREASURY consists in the method of allocating them well and sparingly. For parsimony <term>frugality or thrift</term> increases wealth: *Proverbs 13, verse 17.* And as the proverb has it, it is the greatest tax <note>original: "summum... vectigal," likely referencing Cicero's "Magnum vectigal est parsimonia."</note>. *Rule is worth more than rent; and where there is none, it places itself there;* which is an excellent warning of the Spaniards. *The Curious Forest by Julian Medrano, folio 21.* It is especially true, as is commonly said: profit consists in the making of expenditures. And therefore, let that saying of Horace be held here as an Oracle:
> *If you enjoy things rightly, there is no greater abundance*
> *That could be given to you by Jove,*
Maecenas said rightly to Augustus: Great riches are not so much...

# Political Discourses

Wealth is gathered not so much by receiving many things as by not making many expenditures. *Cassius Dio, Book 52.* <note>Dio refers to the Roman historian's advice on imperial finances.</note> Therefore, the most efficient method of increasing the census <note>The public treasury or state revenue</note> is to subtract from expenses and to restrain lavish gift-giving. Likewise, when King Ptolemy asked one of the seventy translators <note>Referring to the legendary translators of the Septuagint</note> by what means he might remain wealthy, he received this answer: if he did nothing beyond the dignity of the Kingdom and if he spent nothing on luxury or on empty and useless things. *Aristeas in his History.* Among the Spaniards, there is a proverb that he who observes a rule in spending cannot be in want: *a despesa concertada nô pueda faltalle el pan* <note>original Spanish: "with arranged expenses, bread cannot be lacking."</note>. The warning of an anonymous ancient philosopher to the Emperor Theodosius and his sons regarding the restraint of generosity seems entirely worthy of being brought forward here, as reported by the most illustrious *Marquard Freher in his treatise on coinage, at the end of Book 1, folio 25*, where among other things he says: "If immoderate generosity pours out what should have been saved, the depletion of resources—unprecedented by any ancient custom—will no longer be able to assist in times of necessity. For which reason, we must recall for a moment the foresight of our Fathers, which they held in times of poverty, or what might be seen now in such a license of resources: Afflicted Poverty, ignited into various attempts at crime, holding no reverence for the Law or affection for piety before its eyes, has committed its vengeance to evil arts. It will therefore be a care for your Prudence, Best Emperor, by repressing generosity, to both look out for the taxpayer and to propagate the glory of your Name for the future, etc."

I. It is common to all types of domestic administration that it be considered first and foremost that expenses are not greater than the fruits <note>The income or revenue</note>. *Aristotle, Book 2 of the Economics, from the beginning.* Let it hold a measure and look toward the end: therefore, as *Juan de Mariana* says in *The King and the Education of the King, Book 3, Chapter 7*, the cares of the Prince should be directed so that, by removing superfluous expenses, there may be a limit to the taxes. And what frugal men are accustomed to advise in managing family affairs should be carefully considered: that public expenses, if not smaller, should certainly not be larger than the Royal census; lest he be forced to borrow—

# Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter II.

...to act, and with interest increasing daily, to pour out the resources of the Empire. The great and primary care ought to be that individual expenditures are made equal to the means and abundance available; the calculation of the Taxes <note>original: "Vectigalium ratio"</note> and the necessity of spending should agree with one another. Otherwise, if they exceed due measure, the Republic may be entangled in greater evils. If Royal expenditures are much greater than the Taxes for a long time, an indubitable plague will follow; with the necessity of commanding new tributes daily, the ears of the Provincials will grow deaf, and their spirits will be embittered. This was also embraced in a few words by **Alphonso, King of Naples** <note>Alphonso V of Aragon, known as "the Magnanimous" (1396–1458)</note> in *Apophthegms, book 3, number 16.* He says that for Kings who measure their expenses by their revenue, all good things fall into place; they are loved by their Citizens, not feared. The citizens themselves, relieved from the suspicion of new burdens, act with alacrity and display their own goods, and finally seek the life of the Prince with prayers and supplications. And when John, Cardinal of Saint Angelo, had come to Austria as a Legate of the Apostolic See, and had learned what the revenues and expenses of Emperor Frederick were, he said: "There was a rumor that Frederick was too attentive to money; but in my judgment he is very liberal, for he measures his expenses by his means." *Aeneas Sylvius <note>Pope Pius II</note> in the Parallels.* In all things, frugality, parsimony, and the rule of reason should be preserved. And it should always be turned before the eyes of the one who presides: that it is not fitting to arrange expenditures beyond the strength of ordinary revenues; and that just as each person does privately, so also a Prince ought to "measure himself by his own foot" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to live within one's means</note>, which **Gregorius Tholozanus** writes word-for-word in *The Republic, book 8, toward the end.* If Princes would so establish their Courtly Economy and administration that there was always a surplus, rarely would anything be lacking for the use of unforeseen necessity; and if they did not allow expenses to overcome the strength of their resources, there would never be an occasion for burdening subjects with provincial collections. *Heresbach, On Educating the Children of Princes, book 2, chapter 5, near the end.*

**22.** Here, Princes frequently err through ignorance of their revenues and the ledgers of receipts and expenses. Thus **Thomaso Costo** writes concerning the ruin of illustrious families in the Kingdom of Naples, in *The Last Journal of Fugillozzio, folio 555:* "I am not at all surprised that so many houses in Naples have come to a bad hour (I do not speak of those that suffered this either through lack of succession or through change of states), but rather that they do not all go that way; since almost all the Lords of Naples, trusting in that swollen and vain name of 'income'—concerning which they usually rely on the reports of others—strive to spend far and wide: without ever checking the debt against the credit, drawing themselves..."

# Political Discourses

...today one desire, and tomorrow another, they live, as the saying goes, by chance: which is exactly what leads them to ruin. To remedy this destructive disadvantage of the Great <note>original: "Magnatum"</note>, the most illustrious Hero of Belgium, **Maurice, Prince of Orange**, attempted to apply a medicine through an ingenious invention; who, in a singular treatise, taught how to adapt Courtly Economy to the methods of business negotiation. *Simon Stevin, in the work "Mathematical Memoirs of Maurice": There is nothing with which a Monarch can more properly occupy his thoughts than in the distribution of his Finances: and there is no speculation that can serve the great as a wider field in which to exert themselves, to maintain their thoughts, to withdraw from themselves, and then to recover themselves, than the totality of their funds: not to set their heart on avarice, for that is entirely unworthy of a magnanimous Prince; but to dispose his spirit toward a just distribution of his revenue:* as the Author of the *Secret of Finances* elegantly writes in the dedicatory Epistle to the King of France and Poland <note>Henry III</note>. It is also helpful that gifts and bounties be made only by the Prince's own hand. And so of the Marquis of Rosny <note>Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully</note>, Pierre Matthieu writes in *Book 1, near the end: He made himself difficult, and refused many things: to the end that the granting of them should be reserved for the King, and the favors received and recognized from the hand of His Majesty alone, and no other.* And likewise of Livia, Cassius Dio writes in *Book 58*: if she granted anything to anyone, she ordered it to be paid out immediately under her own observation: taking great care lest the same thing happen to her as happened to Augustus; from whose gifts the dispensers <note>treasury officials</note> were accustomed to subtract a very large part. *See Canonhiero, in "Politics," chapter 12, book 8, page 452.* And a Prince is rendered more frugal if he sees for himself what departs from him and the Republic through inconsiderate profusion. Even the smallest things in this area a Prince ought to value: and there is an apothegm of Cosimo de' Medici on this matter, *if I did not take account of small things, I could not do great ones.* *Botero, "Sayings," book 1, page 31b.* If the Prince does not neglect these and other similar warnings, the proverbial sentiment will not apply to him: "thrift is too late at the bottom of the jar" <note>A reference to Hesiod; meaning it is useless to save only when the resource is almost gone</note>. Indeed, the crowd of spendthrifts is usually accustomed to be frugal only after they see that very little remains. Which also, in the *Trinummus* of Plautus, the servant Staphinus blames in his master's son: *Late and foolishly, he considers the account only after he has devoured his property, though he ought to have been cautious before.*

# Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter II.

The Prince should strive to ensure he has no occasion or necessity to extort money from his subjects, nor to vex the people with new burdens <note>The author uses "aggravationibus," referring to additional taxes or legal hardships</note>, as Reinhard Lorichius <note>A 16th-century German humanist and educator</note> beautifully teaches in his *Institutes for a Prince, chapter 60.* Here, truly, one must first set aside the pursuit of external Reputation <note>original: "Reputationis"</note> which destroys internal greatness. In this manner, Alexander Severus <note>Roman Emperor, reigned 222–235 AD</note> purged the City, the Provinces, and his own Court of unnecessary men. He said that an Emperor was a "bad ward" <note>original: "malum pupillum," implying a poor guardian of the state's resources</note> who would nourish unnecessary people, useless to the Republic, from the very vitals of the Provincials. He also said it was a crime for a public steward to convert that which the provincials had given into pleasures for himself and his own circle. *Lampridius in his Life of Severus.* Therefore, the Salaries <note>term: Salaria (regular payments or stipends)</note> which we see idle or useless men receiving must be withdrawn. Indeed, nothing is more foul, or rather more cruel, than if those who have contributed nothing to the Republic by their labor should gnaw away at it; as the Emperor Antoninus Pius once said, *according to Capitolinus, page 147.* So too Almansor the Arab <note>Al-Mansur, the second Abbasid Caliph</note> used to say that flatterers and all useless men—with whom Courts everywhere swarm—are like wasps; as Botero records in *The Sayings, book 1, page 57b.*

Public parsimony <note>frugality or thrift</note> does not consist in stripping Kings of their domestic servants; this cannot be done without contempt for Majesty itself. Such a thing usually excites foreigners to despise the Prince and subjects to revolt. We read that this once happened to Louis XI, King of the French; he not only drove the Patricians and Nobles from his household and service—using a tailor as a Herald, a barber as an Ambassador, and a doctor as a Chancellor—but also, to trample upon the magnificence of other Princes, he dressed in the most foul clothing and attire: a greasy hat, filthy with small images and shells, and woolen clothing of the cheapest price and a gloomy color. *Bodin, book 6, chapter 2, number 677.* 

Nevertheless, the innumerable multitude of Offices and the profuse magnitude of expenses, which everywhere grow almost to infinity, must be recalled to moderation and, in some part, pruned away. In this manner, Pope Innocent VI, a man of most upright life and great constancy and severity, diminished his domestic expense, reducing his household to a fixed and honorable number. He did not wish to have anyone at home except the most proven men. He commanded the Cardinals to do the same by a most sharp edict, saying that his life and the lives of all churchmen ought to be an example to others. *Platina in his Life of the Pope.* A Prince must indeed direct all things toward the splendor of the Empire, yet he must not undergo the infamy of...

# Political Discourses

...of being stingy or tight-fisted: but it is nevertheless fitting to apply diligence and judgment, and to measure pomp and the courtly retinue by the standard of the Province, and always by the poverty of the subjects. *See also Latherus, On the Census, book 1, chapter 11.* Why, I ask, are so many court officials necessary—those useless title-holders who, in the manner of harpies, devour what is set before them to the ruin of the subjects? Why so many secretaries, when two or four clerks <note>original: "amanuenses"</note> might suffice for dispatching business? To what end is there such a great number of kitchen attendants, to whom cling, like moths, assistants, and other assistants to those assistants, and to these servants, and servants of servants? Why are so many leeches nourished on the blood of the people? Flatterers, courtiers, fools, or true morons, dwarfs, and monsters of nature? These are held as delights: mossy followers of the retinue, and unarmed bodyguards—a mere number, a useless weight upon the earth, born only to consume the harvest. For we see all of these nourished at public expense to the public prejudice, etc. These are the words of *Peter Gregory of Toulouse, On the Republic, book 22, chapter 5, number 2, where he has many other things on this.* A Prince should provide by all means that idle men and empty titles of offices—such as Harbingers <note>original: "Metatorum," those who go ahead to arrange lodgings</note>, Historians, Royal Priests, and extraordinary Councilors—do not hold the Republic up to mockery and prey through annual salaries, while providing no benefit. *Mariana, book 3, chapter 7.* Concerning Burgundy, the author of *The Secret of Finances* writes: <note>original: "du Secret des Finances"</note> that the ancient revenue of the Dukes of Burgundy was not enough to pay half of the wages of the officers who are there now. *In the dedicatory epistle; and the same in book 2, folio 45* asserts: that he would much prefer the wages of all the officers newly created in the Kingdom of France than the entire ordinary and extraordinary revenue of the crown during the time of the good King Louis XII. To whom, therefore, would it seem a wonder that there the debt and the exactions from the poor subjects have grown to an immense degree?

4. A good Prince should not define the height of Fortune by luxury, as boy-kings and ignorant youths do, and those who are accustomed to corrupt them with such persuasion. *See the Notes of Jan Gruter, in Flowers of the Law, part 1, folio 643.* It is a kind of small-mindedness <note>original: "pusillanimitè"</note> in Monarchs, and a testimony of not feeling enough of what they are, to labor to make themselves valued and seen through excessive expenses. *Michel de Montaigne, book 3 of the Essays, chapter 6, folio 911 in my copy.* It is a trait of Nero to think that reputation is situated in profusion. # On the Public Treasury, Chapter II.

...profusion: that those who kept a strict account of their expenses were sordid and stingy, while those who squandered and wasted were truly elegant and magnificent. <note>original: *Sueton. cap. 30.* Referring to Suetonius's biography of Nero, who viewed frugality as a vice.</note> But does not Seneca prophesy concerning our own age when he writes thus (in *Oedipus*):

> *Throughout the whole world a most great evil has arisen,*
> *Luxury, a seductive plague; to which long time*
> *And grievous error have given strength and vigor.*

It is a most certain sign of the depravity of our age that nothing is now deemed magnificent unless it is superfluous and luxurious. Both publicly and privately, we imitate the foolish pride of Heliogabalus <note>A Roman Emperor notorious for his decadence.</note>, who never dined for less than thirty pounds of silver, and who loved to be told that the prices of the items placed upon his table were higher than they actually were: saying that this was the "appetite" of the banquet—that those things please more which are bought for more. <note>original: *Lamprid.* Referring to the historian Aelius Lampridius.</note> Regarding Vitellius, Dio records (*Book 65, at the beginning*) that the entire time of his Principate was nothing other than drunkenness and gluttony; this may truly be said of certain Courts today as well. To this point belongs the saying of Scopas the Thessalian, the sculptor; when someone wondered why Apelles had so many superfluous things in his house, he replied: "Nay, it is by these superfluous things that we are happy and blessed, not by those that are necessary." The same can certainly be pronounced now concerning Kings and Princes, who are accustomed to define their greatness almost entirely by superfluities. But a good Prince should remember that Sovereignty consists in virtue, not in decoration and pomp: as Alexander Severus used to say. <note>original: *Lamprid.*</note> Indeed, all luxury ought especially to be exiled from the Court of a Christian Prince. And a question truly seems worthy of being discussed with diligent care by Court Theologians and those who write on cases of conscience: Whether eternal life may be promised to one who, by himself, has uselessly squandered more than the care and sustenance of all the poor, orphans, widows, and other miserable and abandoned persons would have required. Luxury is certainly a seductive evil. And although it may be easier to accuse luxury than for a Prince or a ruler—who wishes to outshine others—to avoid it; nevertheless, wisdom, which is proper to a rational man, ought so to temper his acts that, by exercising caution, he appears more prudent than the rest. He should use a temperate diet and clothing, and by a laudable parsimony <term>parsimony: the quality of being careful with money; thrift</term>, spare the public treasury, as Tholosanus advises (*Book 22 of The Republic, Chapter 5, at the beginning*).

Therefore, the manifold occasions for pouring out money must be avoided, such as the useless display of horses, dogs, and similar things; one must abstain from foreign—

# Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter II.

was not much more costly than that of the common man; he wore shirts <note>original: "Pfaiten," an archaic term for a shirt or smock</note>, tunics, and waistcoats, which had to fit closely to the body everywhere, making them no wider or larger than his limbs were. It was trimmed with silk and featured a rough breastplate; he always wore linen trousers. His uppermost daily garment was a gray cloak—as was the custom of the German soldiers at that time—made almost like a mass-vestment <note>a chasuble</note>, as one still sees in old pictures. He did not esteem the clothing of foreign nations or other fashions, though they were costly, but rather despised them entirely. The Germans and Franks, because they commonly used to wage war among the Italians <note>original: "Wahlen," referring to Romance-speaking peoples, particularly Italians</note> and the French, quickly adopted their short cloaks and little tunics. When Emperor Charles <note>Charles V (1500–1558), Holy Roman Emperor</note> saw this, he became angry and cried out: "O you Germans and Free Franks, how are you so thoughtless and inconstant that you adopt the clothing of those whom you have conquered and fought, and over whom you are lords? It is not a good sign; it bodes nothing good. You take their clothing from them, and so they will take your heart from you. What use are these foreign <note>original: "Welsche," meaning foreign/Romance</note> patches and rags? They are good neither for heat nor for cold, neither for rain nor for wind." He therefore issued a provincial edict that such French clothes should be neither bought nor sold in Germany.

While he lay in Friuli <note>a region in northeastern Italy</note> one winter and saw that the Germans were buying foreign, costly furs from the Venetian merchants and parading about in them, he forced them, dressed as they were, to ride out to the hunt just as it began to rain. He led them with diligence through thick bushes and thorns, so that such clothes were not only ruined by the rain but also torn to pieces. Afterward, he led them back home; they had to eat immediately by the fireplaces, where the clothes were ruined even further by the heat of the fire. He intentionally delayed the meal long into the dead of night. He let his own wolf-skin dry in the air, and in the morning, nothing was wrong with it. When the Germans had to appear before him with their costly furs, which were all ruined, he showed his own pelt and said: "You foolish people, which garment is more useful now? Mine, which cost me a shilling, or yours, for which you have squandered your entire paternal inheritance?" *Francis Robortello <note>a renowned Italian Renaissance humanist (1516–1567)</note> also relates this in his funeral oration for Charles V, saying: when he once saw in the court one of his followers indulging too much in dress and an almost womanly finery, he immediately ordered that he return to his own, that is, military dress...*
