# Political Discourses

If one understands the established customs and methods, they will easily find the source of this abundance. Your frugality, O Augustus <note>The author addresses the Emperor or a generic sovereign using the title "Augustus" to signify supreme authority</note>, provides you with the greatest Revenue <note>original: "Vectigal"</note>; for whatever others used to squander on lavish desires, all of that is now reserved for public use. O, how praised is the mind of the Prince, and by Hercules, it is all the more praiseworthy because whatever was paid by the public was expended by him for the public good. Even Septimius Severus <note>Roman Emperor (reigned 193–211 AD) known for his administrative and military reforms</note> used the public wealth so sparingly and moderately that he left the Roman state by far the wealthiest and filled with all necessary things. *Lampridius.* Other examples, including those from Germany, have been collected by Lorichius. *See "On the Instruction of a Prince," chapter 59, page 170; and see Matthias Castritius, "On the Virtues of German Princes," book 3, chapter 6, and book 4, chapter 6, numbers 4, 16, 21, 22, 23.*

Thus, a Prince ought never to despair of acquiring sufficient riches, provided he is willing to exercise diligence regarding expenses and does not allow himself to be persuaded that Frugality <note>original: "Parsimonia"</note> is a rustic or unrefined thing. Those who act otherwise seem to desire to perish amidst pomp and dancing. This was once said to Charles VII, King of France, by the vigorous military leader La Hire <note>Etienne de Vignolles, a French military commander during the Hundred Years' War</note>, when he had been sent from the army to inform the King of the state of affairs while the English were successfully waging war in France. He found the King entirely occupied with the women's quarters, dancing, banquets, and other such delights. Struck by this blunt remark, the King finally began to wake as if from a long lethargy; rejecting his pleasures, he turned all his thoughts toward reclaiming his kingdom from the enemies. *Gaspar Ens, "Epidorpides," book 1, page 13; Botero, "Aphorisms," 1, page 34b.*

To this also fits what they relate concerning Heinrich Glarean <note>A Swiss music theorist, poet, and humanist (1488–1563)</note>; when asked by a friend how he lived and fared, he said: "I live the life of Princes and Great Men." When the other asked what kind of life that was, he replied: "I drink and indulge my inclinations, and meanwhile, I am and remain in everyone's debt." *Gaspar Ens, "Epidorpides," 2, page 238.*

II. A treasury exhausted by ambition and bribery is usually replenished through crimes; and every extravagant Prince either is, or will become, an extortioner. *Richter, "Economic Axioms," 78, 83, 122 and following.* He who is prodigal with his own property is also prodigal with the property of others. Rapacity is joined to extravagance. *Guicciardini, book 12.* For it is familiar to Princes that, when they are in need, they devise unjust taxes to relieve their poverty and lay their hands on the property of others. *Vincentius Castellanus, "On the Office of a King," book 3, chapter 10.*

He who pours out much wealth is almost necessarily forced to suck the blood of the People. <note>original: "Qui multa profundit, necesse est ut ferè Populi sanguinem exsugat."</note> *John Calvin, on Daniel chapter 11, number 20.* We justly flee from poverty (says King Theodoric in Cassiodorus, *Various Letters, book 1, letter 17*) which persuades one to excesses; for scarcity is a ruinous thing in a ruler: and as someone rightly said; a poor King is a dangerous animal. Poverty follows a prodigal Prince; and extreme tyranny follows poverty. And so Gaius Caligula, who was convinced that one must be either a frugal man or a Caesar: at last, exhausted and needy, turned his mind to plunder through various and most exquisite kinds of false accusations, auctions, and taxes. *Suetonius in his Life [of Caligula], chapter 37 and following. Caelius, Ancient Readings, book 2, chapter 24.* Likewise Nero, who as I have said before, thought there was no other fruit of wealth and money than profusion; and holding no limit in giving or spending: first he searched for the treasures of an ancient hoard, of which a Roman knight had given him a vain hope; afterwards it became necessary to delay and postpone the soldiers' pay and the benefits of the veterans, and soon he turned his mind to false accusations and plunder: finally, he delegated no duty to anyone without adding:

> You know what I need; let us act so that no one has anything.

*Suetonius, chapter 30 and the two following.*

So also Vitellius, since he restrained neither luxury nor greed; having turned to prey and cruelty, a polluted and cowardly Prince, he perished shamefully: when he had ruled for one year, minus ten days. To this I could add the examples of Domitian, Commodus, Bassianus <note>Also known as the Emperor Caracalla.</note>, and other Roman Princes: who, laboring under two different vices, greed and luxury, used the one to amass money and the other to pour it out; they had ends equal to the slaughters of Nero, Caligula, and Vitellius. # Political Discourses

<margin>Page 36</margin>

When a ruler realizes that he has made himself vulnerable to barbarians through his actions, and nonetheless remains stuck in the process of explaining away all his financial burdens, he thinks nothing of plundering by every possible means. The goods of both the living and the dead are seized everywhere, regardless of the accuser or the crime; it was enough to be charged with any deed or word whatsoever against the majesty of the Prince. Inheritances from the most distant relations were confiscated, even if there was only one person to say they had heard from the deceased, while he lived, that the Emperor was his heir. Zonaras <note>Joannes Zonaras, a 12th-century Byzantine chronicler</note> reports in *volume 3* concerning Monomachus <note>Byzantine Emperor Constantine IX Monomachos, r. 1042–1055</note> that he squandered the wealth of the Empire with such monstrous bribes and immoderate expenses that the ruin of the State arose from it. For once the treasury was exhausted, he was forced to impose taxes on those peoples who held immunity from such things on the grounds that they kept watch over the narrow passes at the borders of the Republic. Therefore, once the burdens were changed—since the Emperor preferred money instead of the border stations—he opened the way for enemies, from which disasters for the State followed.

It is also worthwhile to know the outrages of Emperor Michael; for since he was a man of the greatest intemperance, he poured out such a force of money that, afterwards becoming destitute, he was forced to devise unjust taxes and lay hands on the property of others to relieve his poverty. So writes Joannes Curopalates <note>John Skylitzes, a Byzantine historian</note>. And concerning Robert, Duke of Normandy, son of William the Conqueror, Bernard de Girard writes in *book 7, page 584 of the History of France*:

> The revenue did not suffice for the prodigal expense he made; to satisfy which, he imposed great taxes <term>tailles</term> <note>A direct land tax often associated with the French monarchy</note> upon the People: the ordinary custom of prodigal Princes, who, to sustain their prodigality, are constrained to demand from and trample their People.

Prodigal Princes also wish to be the heirs of themselves, of the State, and of their subjects while still living. They possess the mind of Heliogabalus <note>Roman Emperor known for extreme decadence</note>; when he was still a private citizen and someone, admiring his luxury, said: "Are you not afraid of becoming poor?" He replied, "What is better than that I should be the heir to myself and my wife?" as recorded by Lampridius in his *Life*. However, it must never be presumed that such impious thoughts would enter the mind of a Christian Prince.

### III. On the other hand, Liberality is the proper trait of Princes; and it must always be exercised by a Prince, especially toward the well-deserving and the needy.

Regarding the Emperor Alexander Severus <note>Roman Emperor, reigned 222–235 AD, known for his moderate rule</note>, the historian Lampridius writes: He never let a day pass without performing some act of gentleness, civility, or piety; yet he did so in a way that did not overturn the Treasury. I desire that the Beneficence of a Prince be Public, and joined with the utility of his Subjects and the Kingdom: for if it is done in such a manner, it will draw the souls of the Subjects toward his love far more effectively than any Magnet attracts iron. On the contrary, if he neglects those things which ought to be done liberally for the Public, and instead pours out benefits upon his Courtiers or other domestic favorites rather than Public men; he will be publicly judged as greedy, and will prepare for himself both hatred and contempt among his Subjects. ->*That kindness of a King is sinister,*<-

->*If it rains upon specific men, but not upon the human race.*<-

And to this point belongs the celebrated journal of Crates <note>A Cynic philosopher</note>, found in the writings of Laertius, which goes in this manner: "Set down ten minas <note>A unit of currency</note> for the cook, a drachma for the doctor; ten talents for the flatterer, smoke for the counselor, a talent for the prostitute, and three obols for the Philosopher." Therefore (as Cardinal Aldobrandini <note>Pietro Aldobrandini, a powerful patron of the arts in the late 16th century</note> was accustomed to say, as reported by Farnese in his *Apophthegms*, title 10, number 11): The Muses must be nourished by the Liberality of Princes; as well as others who excel in all varieties of arts and sciences. Apollinaris de Calderini speaks beautifully on this in *Discourse 10 and following*. Primarily, as Keckermann rightly advises in *Politics*, book 1, chapter 3, page 91, a Prince ought to exercise public beneficence toward two types of men: namely, toward men of outstanding learning and excellent artisans; and secondly, toward those Soldiers who have served the Republic illustriously through some remarkable deed. For if he holds the hearts of Wise and brave men devoted to him, he can easily either hold or disregard the others. Regarding Pope Leo X, Paolo Giovio <note>An Italian physician and historian</note> reports that he panted for the glory of liberality more ardently and profusely than for anything else, judging those to be unworthy of being a Prince who did not use the gifts of fortune with a beneficent hand. For there was no one, whether citizen or foreigner, who held the reputation of a slightly more noble art—no Poet, even if half-mad, no one who was not ignorant of some part of the best literature—who did not feel the humanity of this most humane Prince.

...he conjectured it to be so: because the poor make a feast of it. <note>original: "perche i poveri ne fan festa."</note> *Botero, On the Sayings of Great Men, folio 33, verso.* Thus, the memory of **Bishop Otto of Bamberg** is celebrated because in the year 1124, when there was a great dearness of provisions <term>annonæ caritas: a high price or scarcity of grain</term> and a very great famine was increasing everywhere on earth, he was most liberal toward all his subjects in distributing grain, so that none of his people perished from hunger. Furthermore, he supported, nourished, and aided foreigners whom he saw were in need of crops with the greatest and most pious liberality. *Hedio in the Chronicles.* Likewise, **Nicholas, Bishop of Constance**, during a period of extreme scarcity of grain, daily satisfied three thousand men with alms out of his pious liberality. *Bruschius, On the Bishops of Germany.* **John, the 26th Abbot of Fulda**, born of the illustrious family of the Prince-Counts of Henneberg, was of such great liberality toward the poor that every day, when he took his food, he would send one dish along with a silver platter from his table to the bed of some well-known needy person. *Bruschius, On the Monasteries of Germany.*

And indeed, to me, looking more closely at human affairs, no families, no Princes, and no Empires seem to have flourished so much in wealth and victories as those which have taken the greatest care of the needy and the weak. **Saint Louis, King of France**, founded twenty-eight colleges of Divine and Human learning with his own resources, even though he also daily sustained one hundred and twenty poor people who followed him, most humanely and with the same food as himself. Therefore, it ought not to seem a wonder if he ruled for forty-four years with the highest glory to his name; so that he was held formidable to his enemies, dear to his friends, a god to his subjects, and a saint to all.

And thus pious men have often judged: that the **Republic of Strasbourg** <note>original: "Argentinensem Remp."</note> would be safe from more serious evils as long as the poor and other wretched people are supported so generously and without regard for cost. Nor should we omit **James V, King of Scots**, he who is surnamed the "King of the Commons" <note>original: "Rex egentium," literally King of the Needy</note>: who, although he surpassed all the Princes of his time in kindness, nevertheless far exceeded his ancestors in the magnitude of his wealth.

In section I, it is said of Charles IV <note>Holy Roman Emperor, reigned 1346–1378</note> that he was the "stepfather and squanderer of the Empire" (because he pledged the customs duties and taxes of the Empire to the Estates) and that a more pestilential plague never befell the Germans. *Spiegel on Book 1 of Gunther the Ligurian; Arumæus, discourse on the Golden Bull 1, number 3 and discourse 3, number 43; Lather, book 1, chapter 16, number 29, etc.* Sturmius says that today the Emperor has no tributes; the Monks have them, the Priests have them, the Nobles have them, and Kings, friends, allies, and Princes have them. *Sturmius, Sermon 2 on the Perpetual Administration of the War against the Turks, page 114.* Schneidewin reveals that the revenues of the Roman Empire under Frederick Barbarossa <note>reigned 1155–1190</note> were still sixty tons of gold. *Schneidewin, Institutes on Intestate Succession, under the rubric on the succession of the Treasury, number 5.* This was a sufficiently large sum of money for the standards of that time. # Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter II.

Taxes should be remitted, or even ordinary tributes suspended, during times of public calamities and sudden disasters; see *Novel 163* <note>A "Novel" refers to a new law issued by a Byzantine Emperor, in this case regarding the relief of public taxes</note> on the relief of public taxes; add also Philippus Hoenonius, *Disputation 5, Question 90, page 293*; Jean de Chokier, *Political Aphorisms, Book 2, Chapter 10, page 6*. 

Following the example of the Emperor Nerva Cocceius: who, for those Roman citizens struggling in great poverty, not only distributed lands to provide financial relief, but even sold his own personal clothing, silver vessels, and gold items, along with the rest of his furniture. He distributed these to others with the highest benevolence, as Dio <note>Cassius Dio, the Roman historian</note> says. Likewise, when a most bitter plague struck the people of Sardinia, Tiberius Caesar promised ten million sesterces and remitted for five years as much as they were accustomed to pay to the Public Treasury and the Imperial Privy Purse. Tacitus, *Annals, Book 2*. 

In the same way, Hadrian remitted an infinite sum which was owed to the state by private debtors in the City <note>Rome</note> and Italy; in the provinces, he also remitted huge sums from the arrears. Spartianus <note>One of the authors of the Augustan History</note>. Since the goodwill of the subjects stands as the treasure and safeguard of Princes (Plutarch, *Life of Aratus*), a Prince ought to take diligent care to retain or acquire it. 

Herodian writes similarly of Pertinax in *Book 2*: that he remitted all the taxes which the previous tyrants had devised for the purpose of extorting money. For unless you frequently take up the needle and thread in a disturbed Empire and sew up the rupture, neither you nor the Republic will be able to flourish. Waremund von Ehrenberg, *On the Subsidies of the Kingdom, Chapter 7, Number 38*. 

Thus it is recorded above in Number 4, that Julian, through his liberality, raised up cities that had been exhausted by taxes and almost deserted, restoring them to their former splendor with money contributed from the treasury. Those who wish to lay down their reign in peace and secure it for their descendants ought to especially observe this kindly relief of tributes (Perez, *Aphorisms, page 160, number 80*); or those who have newly occupied an Empire, lest they be more harsh than is conducive to a new reign—a fault Tacitus found in Mithridates. 

Thus it was the custom of the new Kings of the Persians to grant the first year immune from taxes to their subjects to win their favor; the Kings of the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> were also accustomed to do this. Herodotus, *Book 6*. Likewise, when the Romans reduced Cappadocia to a province after the death of King Archelaus, they diminished some of the royal tributes so that the Roman Empire might be hoped for as a milder rule. Tacitus, *Annals, Book 2*. 

It also seems to pertain to equity to remit all or part of the tributes to subjects on account of their merits or by special privilege. For the services of the faithful ought not to perish,

# Political Discourses

It is fitting that expenses incurred during sad times should be recovered in better fortune. <note>The author argues that subjects who suffered for the state should be relieved of taxes once peace returns.</note> **Cassiodorus**, in the 3rd book of his *Various Letters*, letter 32, where he writes concerning the people of Arles who endured a siege on behalf of King Theodoric, records the following decree: "Let those be satisfied in liberty who preferred to hunger in distress for our sake. Let those be joyful who faithfully endured sadness. It is not fitting to be immediately anxious about taxes from one who, out of loyalty to us, could scarcely avoid extreme ruin. We demand such things from those at peace, not those who have been besieged. For what would you demand from the master of a field when you know he has not been able to cultivate it? They have already given us the most precious tax of their own loyalty. It is unjust that we should demand cheap coins from those who have offered us their glorious consciences." <note>original: "Satientur in libertate... gloriosas conscientias nobis obtulerunt."</note>

### § 3.
It will contribute greatly to the **Treasury** <term>Ærarium: the public treasury of ancient Rome</term> to restrain the embezzlements of the **Treasurers** <term>Quæstors: officials overseen by the state to manage finances</term> and the agents of the **Exchequer** <term>Fiscus: the emperor's private or state purse</term>, as well as the crimes of extortion. For this reason, certain Princes have continually participated in person in the auditing of the administrators' accounts. **Lather**, book 1, chapter 15, throughout the discourse. Thus also among the Romans, one did not escape a judgment of embezzlement <term>peculatus: the theft of public or ecclesiastical money</term> even if accused of stealing only a tiny amount. **Furius Camillus**, because a Tribune of the Plebs complained that fifteen thousand pieces of copper were missing from the treasury, was sent into exile. **Plutarch**, in his *Life*. And **Scipio Africanus**, who had restored the Republic—shattered by the arms of the Punic War and then almost bloodless and dying—as the Mistress of Africa, punished himself with voluntary exile because forty million was demanded back from him, though he had brought two thousand million into the Treasury. **Livy**, book 38; **Valerius Maximus**, chapter 3, number 3.

Likewise at Rome, all who handled public money were prohibited from private trade. **Aerodius**, book 2, title 11, chapter 5. Diligent care must be taken lest the taxes be diminished by various and depraved men who know all the ways of money and undertake all frauds for the sake of money; whether they be **Tax-farmers** <term>Publicani: private contractors who collected taxes for a profit</term> or those to whom the care of the Royal Taxes is entrusted; a plague than which hardly any more foul can be devised. How heavy it is for the Republic, and how hateful to good men, that most people approach that administration "juiceless" and without wealth, yet the same men emerge within a few years as wealthy and blessed. From these men, surely, an exact accounting of their acquired riches should be demanded. **Mariana**, book 3, chapter 7, folio 262. Thus formerly at Rome, **Cato the Younger**, as soon as he was appointed Treasurer, immediately established a new system for the administrators and scribes of the Treasury. He was the first to bring to that office not only the title and honor, but a spirit and method worthy of the Magistracy, treating the scribes as they truly were...

Let other Princes imitate this: for they will act wisely if, like him, they begin their reign with such a censorship. # Political Discourses

It increases one's wonder, he says, that although there were many smaller taxes then, and necessary expenses were much greater than they are now, the state was nevertheless in a condition of great wealth. Now, with taxes increased and new ones added daily, and new debts contracted, Kings are placed in a state of extreme poverty. Thus, it is necessary to praise the faithfulness of the ministers of that time and, conversely, to accuse the greed and plunder of those who are in power now. *But concerning the administrators of the Treasury <note>original: "Fisci"</note>, I shall discuss them at greater length below in Chapter 7.* 

Pietro Bembo <note>A Venetian cardinal and historian (1470–1547)</note> also mentions in his *History of Venice, Book 12, page 496 and following*, that during a shortage of public money, it was decreed by the Venetians that those in charge of the Republic's revenues must provide a certificate, confirmed in writing by four magistrates, stating that they have paid what they owed. Anyone who does not produce this certificate may neither hold nor apply for any office of the Republic. Furthermore, if any of those magistrates certifies that a citizen has paid when he has not, that magistrate shall pay the citizen's entire debt to the Republic as a fine; the scribe who prepared the document shall be expelled from his office. However, the Council of Ten <note>The high governing body of Venice</note>, judging that this law was not sufficient, met in a fuller assembly and decreed that debtors to the treasury should be detained and handed over to custody.

4. Fiefs <note>original: "Feuda"</note> which return to the Lord when a family of vassals dies out should not be granted to others, but should be applied to the "table" <note>meaning the ruler's personal or state maintenance fund</note>, as they say. Infinite donations and grants of immense sums of money made to the most unworthy men are to be revoked. *Jean Bodin <note>French political philosopher (1530–1596)</note>, Book 6, Chapter 6, number 657.* Nero had squandered twenty-two hundred million sesterces <note>An ancient Roman currency</note> in donations. For that which is taken from the public through unfair and immoderate bribery—not for merits toward the Republic nor as a reward for labor—can hardly be free from the charge of embezzlement <note>original: "peculatu"</note>. And you will find examples everywhere of Royal gifts which were revoked and abolished by the Court of Paris <note>The Parlement of Paris, the highest judicial body in Ancien Régime France</note>. <margin>Clapmarius, Book 5, Chapter 13, citing Conanus.</margin> For in this way, precautions are taken so that the Nobles do not further lay greedy hands upon the public wealth; thus their greed and audacity are reined in. Truly, I think there would be very few who would wish to petition Princes, or take what is offered to them of their own accord, if they thought the gifts could be revoked or if they were forced to render accounts. <margin>Which may be seen in Mariana, *On the King and the Education of a King*, Book 3, Chapter 7, page 263.</margin> This was followed by Henry III, King of Castile, who, by a memorable but somewhat violent example, liberated the taxes that had been seized by the Nobles. The author of *The Secret of Finances* <note>A reference to Nicolas Froumenteau’s *Le Secret des finances de France* (1581)</note> urges the same; <margin>In the dedicatory epistle.</margin> he promises to free the King of France from all debt if even a tenth part of the illicit grants and alienations <note>The transfer of state property or rights to private individuals</note> were revoked. And in France also, so that the robberies of the courtiers might be met head-on, it was established by law that the gifts of the Prince were void unless the recipient included in the records of the gift all previous largesse granted to his ancestors. Likewise, no gift made by the Prince would have force unless it was recorded in the acts of the <term>Chamber of Accounts</term> <note>original: *Rationalis Curiae*; the sovereign court overseeing public finances</note>, though these laws have long since fallen into disuse. <margin>Bodin, Book 6, Chapter 2, number 674.</margin>

II. At all other times, all shortcuts to profit should be absent from the purity of the Treasury; as noted by *Symmachus <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus (c. 340–402 AD), a Roman statesman and orator known for his traditionalist views.</note> in Book 10, Letter 54.* For many Princes, by harshly acquiring money, add more hatred to themselves than strength. # Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter III.

Someone once asked what kind of letters <note>original: "litteras"; here meaning both literature/learning and formal documents</note> a certain man possessed or brought with him. When the other replied, "Hebrew, Greek, Latin, etc.," he responded, "I would prefer 'Banker's letters' or 'Money-changing letters.'" <note>original: "Argentarias sive Collybisticas"</note> This is recorded by G. Ens in *Epidorpides*, book 2, page 255.

In the same way, Trajano Boccalini, in *The Ragguagli di Parnaso* <note>original: "Pietra del Paragone"</note>, reproaches the greatest King of our century. To a certain learned man who had suggested how a famous province of his Kingdom might regain its former splendor, the King gave a gift of only 20 Ducats. But to another man, who had supplied a method by which that same region could bear an intolerable yoke of taxation, he assigned 12000 annually.

Yet these "letters" and little tricks—which certain Princes value highly, and through which many men become "great" in their eyes—were once festively exposed and summarized in a single word by a Spanish Knight. For when Ferdinand of Aragon, King of Naples, was commending the invention of a new Customs Duty <note>original: "Portorii"</note>—which was of this sort: that whoever received a salary from the Royal Treasury should pay back four gold pieces into the Treasury for every hundred received—the Knight who was then present said: "O King, so that I might be much more highly commended by you, I would give you this advice: that you should simply snatch away the food and clothing from all of us whom you feed and clothe."

As Giovanni Pontano writes in *On Social Intercourse* <note>original: "De Sermone"</note>, book 5, chapter 1: It would certainly be better if a magistrate snatched everything from his subjects all at once, rather than reducing them to destitute misery by slowly twisting them with various cleverly devised schemes. If there are any Advisors <note>term: Consiliarii (political counselors)</note> who think they ought to serve not Justice, but only the profit of their Lord: these men, by attracting Divine malediction, harm the Prince much more than they help him.

"You may possess wealth," says Seneca in *On the Happy Life*, chapter 23, "but let it be taken from no one, nor stained with another's blood; acquired without hatred toward anyone, and without filthy lucre; wealth whose exit is as honorable as its entry, and over which no one groans except the spiteful." This is a rule common to all ranks of men, but it is one that must be most carefully observed in the enriching of the treasury <note>term: Fisco (the state or imperial purse)</note>, according to the opinion of Heinrich Klock in *On Taxes*, question 6. But concerning the "Arch-schemers" <note>note: "Arcigogilantibus" refers to those who devise complex, often deceptive, financial plots</note> and the architects of exactions, I shall speak below, <margin>Chapter 7, specifically.</margin>

The warning with which he concludes that treatise deserves to be engraved upon the mind of a good Prince, when he says: *It is only reasonable that those matters undertaken with the favor of the divine will always turn out better and more happily for the Republic.* <note>original: "Reipubl."</note> But truly, although Henning Arnisaeus <note>A 17th-century German political theorist known for his work on the sovereignty of kings.</note> thinks that such methods of raising funds should not be sought out too scrupulously—since they seem to possess neither a fixed number nor a systematic science, and can be devised from the circumstances according to each person's prudence (*Book 2 of Political Doctrine, chapter 1, page 566*)—it is nevertheless helpful to keep the examples of others before our eyes; so that we may either imitate them, or avoid them, or at least adapt them in part to each specific Republic.

IV. And indeed, if fitting penalties were exacted from Usurers <note>original: "Foeneratoribus"</note> (concerning whose destructiveness see *Bodin, On the Republic, Book 6, chapter 2, number 667; add Master Lather, Book 3, chapter 23, number 71 and many following*), Drunkards, Blasphemers (*Lather, Book 2, chapter 4*), Slanderers, and others of a similar kind; and if we returned to the wisdom of the Ancients to prevent boldness in lawsuits (*see what I have said, following Bodin in the aforementioned chapter 2, number 662, in my treatise On Appeals, chapter 13, section 6*); Lather, Book 2, chapters 5 and 7; **Engelhard**, *On Taxes, thesis 4, page 7*; then both our public morals and the Treasury <note>original: "Aerario"</note> would be better provided for today. Thus Charles IX, King of France, imposed a Tax <note>original: "Vectigal"</note> on the "itch" for litigation; however, it was not heavy enough to uproot those old and great evils (*Lipsius in Admonitions, Book 2, chapter 10, number 4*), nor was it long-lasting (*Choppin, On the Laws of Anjou, on the customs of Gaul, precept number 3*). But nevertheless, the greatest care must be taken here lest we proceed further through the enticement of profit, and appear to love money more than the punishment of crimes: or lest we allow a place for wicked Informers <note>original: "Delatoribus"</note>. Hence Antoninus the Philosopher <note>The Emperor Marcus Aurelius.</note> rightly despised those denunciations by which the Imperial Treasury <note>original: "Fiscus"</note> might be increased (*Capitolinus*). Among bad Princes, on the contrary, it was often a crime simply to be wealthy.

# Chapter II. Concerning the Public Treasury

The Romans were accustomed to confiscating the property of those they executed for particularly grave crimes, designating those assets for public use; thus, the execution of the master was followed by the forfeiture of his goods. <note>original: "Domini supplicium, bonorum publicatio sequeretur"</note> <term>Alexander ab Alexandro, Genial Days, Book 3, Chapter 23.</term> Today, however, the penalty of total confiscation remains only in the crime of High Treason <note>Lese-majesty; an offense against the dignity of the state or sovereign</note>: <term>Law "Quisquis" regarding the Julian Law on Treason; Chapter 1 on Regalian Rights; Bocer on the Crime of Treason, Chapter 3, Number 16 etc., also Number 111 etc.</term> This applies even if there are descendants or ancestors surviving, since the aforementioned Law <term>Quisquis</term> speaks in general terms. In other crimes, by common custom, the right of confiscation has fallen into disuse. However, political thinkers quite rightly debate whether it is better for the goods of the condemned to be awarded to their relatives rather than to the State, or whether the ancient law should be restored. <term>See Bornitz, Book 3, Chapter 6; Lather, Book 2, Chapter 9, Number 9 etc., and Chapter 10, Number 11 etc.; add Friedrich Martini, Treatise on Tributes, at the end, folio 534</term> where he interprets <term>Article 218, Section 6 of the Criminal Constitution of Charles V.</term> Certainly, [confiscation] is seen as ill-advised because it is cruel for the treasury to seek profit from mournful circumstances, and because otherwise, judicial rulings might incur sinister suspicion, and punishments might be transformed—contrary to their purpose—into mere greed.

And it is a most wretched thing that many judges and officials, according to Ventura de Valentiis <term>Book 1, Parthen. litig. Chapter 14, Number 2 and following</term>, serve their own passions and avarice; they rejoice in imposing and exacting fines, and impiously say:
> *God be praised and thanked, the fines and penalties have brought in a respectable sum this year.* <note>original German: "Es haben dieses Jahres vber die Bruche oder Geltbuͤssen / Gott sey lob vnd danck / ein Ehrliches getragen."</note>

This is something that citizens and peasants experience everywhere, and all too often. A Hessian Secretary once replied to a Treasurer who was boasting of and amplifying the profit from fines:
> *Many a peasant complains about that.* <note>original German: "da beclagt sich mancher Bawer vber."</note>

For it is better to give an account for mercy than for cruelty. Scottus most justly established <term>Commentary on the Annals of Tacitus, page 293</term>: Justice requires that if someone's goods are confiscated because they are guilty of extortion (or another crime), the goods should be returned to those from whom they were previously unjustly extorted. If a Prince acts otherwise, he is said to have condemned the thief only so that the theft might fall to him; and as the <term>Proverb</term> says, he has skinned the sow only to clothe himself in its hide. That is a most foul thing, and to be avoided by a Prince.

### V. The Republic ought to apply itself with all its might
to ensure that no part of the Region remains deserted or is destined for less useful purposes. This is so that it may earn the praise given to Massinissa <note>The first King of Numidia (modern-day Algeria), famous for turning nomads into farmers</note>, of whom it is read: that he rendered all of Numidia, which had been uncultivated and deserted, most abundant in all manner of fruits. *See Botero, On Illustrious Politics, book 7, chapter 4; Lather, On the Census, book 3, chapter 3.*

It is rightly judged that deserted and uncultivated places that have been distributed to no one—such as mountains and similar areas which are occupied neither by private citizens nor by towns and villages—belong to the domain of the Republic. *I, in my Politics, chapter 4, number 37.* For the investigation of these areas, diligent Inquisitors <note>In this context, state investigators or surveyors rather than religious officials</note> were most correctly appointed, who, having found such lands, joined them to the domain of the Emperors. The Princes or Republics then divided the sterile and deserted fields they found among colonists to be cultivated; at first, indeed, for free, but later with a fixed rent established. *Peter Gregory of Toulouse, book 3, chapter 2, number 9.* For they believe this holds the weight of an oracle: that all the riches of nature, by which the common life of men is sustained, are contained within the most diligent cultivation of the earth and are returned with multiplied interest. *See the discourse of Lather, book 3, chapter 6.*

Thus, as I think, it would be most fitting and useful if subjects were compelled to plant apples, pears, plums, cherries, peaches, and other fruit-bearing trees on their estates; and that this should not be neglected even in public places: so that there would be no part of the region which was not shaded by trees according to the nature of the soil. ...so that they may have a means of sustaining life. For if we, in addition to the resources of the Empire, also intercept the profits of commerce, from where then shall the subjects obtain their livelihood? <note>original: "undè nam subditi victum comparabunt?"</note> *Zonaras, Annals, volume 3.* <note>Johannes Zonaras was a 12th-century Byzantine chronicler and theologian.</note> Furthermore, a dispute occurred some years ago between the citizens of Stettin and their Prince; namely, whether he was compelled to sell grain to his subjects, or whether he could instead export it and sell it in foreign places. *Georgius Everhardus, volume 1, counsel 14.*

Otherwise, provided it does not harm the subjects, commerce does not seem to be a disgrace to Royal dignity. I (says *Bodin*) <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and political philosopher known for his theory of sovereignty.</note> if I had to decide, do not want a Merchant Prince; but if given the choice, I prefer a Merchant to a Tyrant: and I prefer that noblemen trade rather than plunder. And thus the Kings of Portugal, since they were confined by the very narrow borders of their Kingdom and could neither conveniently maintain the rights of their Majesty nor wish to prey upon their subjects, exercised a most abundant and profitable commerce without disgrace, and to the greatest benefit of the Commonwealth. However, it seems there is a need here for the following cautions and limitations:

( 1. ) That trade and the convenience of buying and selling are not thereby rendered more difficult; but rather that the subjects are freed from the deceptions of merchants.

( 2. ) A Prince ought not to involve himself in any commerce except that which brings profit to foreign merchants rather than to the local inhabitants. Indeed, it does not seem to be disapproved if the public treasury, rather than foreigners, perceives a utility of this kind.

( 3. ) The whole body of the Commonwealth exercises most honorably that commerce which individual members could not. *Bornitius, book 2, chapters 1 & 2.* <note>Jacob Bornitius was a 17th-century political economist.</note> And so it is said of *Solomon*, *1 Kings 10:22 and 2 Chronicles 8:18*, that he engaged in maritime trade with King Hiram; the expenses of which, surely, the subjects could not have borne. This reasoning also pleases *Xenophon* in his *Treatise on Revenues*, where he persuades that the State, with funds collected from all sides, should establish commerce and long-distance voyages. But I think it more advisable if, to help the fatherland with necessary foreign goods, Princes contribute money to industrious merchants; whereby they may increase their own utility along with the public's. For commerce demands the whole man, and Princes are frequently deceived by their agents. Here it should be noted what the *Compiler of the Political Treasury* writes concerning the Kingdom of Portugal, *part 1, page 110*: These... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence as the catchword "Queste" indicates the start of the next page in Italian.</note>

# Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter II.

Such vast quantities of merchandise, coming from India and all parts of the world to this city (Lisbon), are spread throughout Europe to the great profit of the Portuguese. The King’s profit would have been much greater—as he held the spice trade for his own account—had he not been cheated by his own ministers. But it can truly be said that for some years now, the King has grown poorer despite the merchandise being highly profitable; for this reason, he has granted private individuals the right to trade them, reserving certain duties for himself. From these, he has gained seven hundred thousand Ducats <note>A gold coin used throughout Europe</note>, over and above all expenses related to the merchandise.

(4.) A Prince may buy up grain and similar necessities exported by foreigners, so that he may later sell them to his subjects at a tolerable price when they are in need. This was the counsel provided by Joseph to Pharaoh <note>A reference to the biblical story in Genesis where Joseph stores grain against a coming famine</note>. Trajano Boccalini also persuades Princes toward this in *Reports from Parnassus*, book 2, report 7, page 34:

> They should leave the trade of selling and buying the fruits and yields of their lands, and the profits of their traffic, free among their subjects; but they should employ every industry in the glorious and rich commerce of filling the storehouses of their States with grain and every sort of corn necessary for human life, purchased in distant countries—a most happy and wealthy traffic.

We experienced this in the year 1614 throughout Swabia <note>A region in southwestern Germany</note>; when the harvest failed, the subjects were entangled in great debt, and a vast amount of money was carried away to neighboring places. If the great lords had possessed grain ready at hand, they could have enriched themselves with a most favorable profit. See also Boccalini, report 7, page 39, and consult Lather, book 3, chapter 7, on the remedies for the high price of grain.

On the contrary, King Alfonso of Naples made himself equally hated by his own people and by foreigners because he would buy up whatever oil and grain grew in Apulia at the lowest possible price, so that during a great scarcity and want of food, he could sell it at his own whim—not permitting the lords to sell their own wheat and oil until he had sold his own. See Comines, book 2, *On the Neapolitan War*. Indeed, that kind of forced purchase is entirely detestable, when provincials are compelled to buy food supplies from the Treasury, or are forced to sell them to the Treasury at market prices. See Sitzman’s commentary on Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, book 1, page 148; and Bulenger, *On Taxes*, chapter 7.

From these things, I believe it follows that many have rightly viewed as not only sordid, but also cruel, the type of business used by Antonio de Leyva <note>A Spanish general and governor of Milan under Charles V</note>, who, when appointed governor of Milan by the Emperor Charles V, prohibited by law any citizen from grinding wheat or making bread for themselves. Instead, they were forced to buy from shops marked with the sign of the Eagle for that purpose. *Sabellicus, in the Supplement.* A nearly similar situation exists if a Lord commands his subjects not to buy beer from anyone but himself, or not to grind grain or bake bread anywhere (the "Ban-Mill" or "Baking-Fee" <note>original: "Bann Mühlin / Backkuchen." These were feudal monopolies where peasants were forced to use the lord's facilities for a fee.</note>) except in his own mill and oven; or if he commands anything similar which ought rightly to be left to the will and free choice of the individual. *See the excellent Andreas Rauchbar, Legal Questions, part 1, question 27; the most distinguished Rutger Rulant, decision 24; Johannes Köpen, decision 20.* To this category belongs the salt monopoly, or the tax on it, which burdens the subjects in France. *See Heinrich Klock on taxes, chapter 3, letter a.* Cujas, citing Athenaeus, reports that Lysimachus, the King of Thrace, first instituted this tax; but that kind Nature, indignant at the baseness of the deed, afterwards denied the benefit <note>This refers to a legend that the salt springs dried up after the tax was imposed.</note>. *Cujas, Observations, book 3, chapter 31; Choppin on the Domain, book 1, chapter 15, number 15.* In Rome, too, monopolies were once quite frequent: namely, where the Prince granted to a certain body or person the right to sell a specific commodity, under the burden of paying a certain pension into the treasury. *Bulenger, chapter 4.* This pertains to burdens which are heavy for subjects and should not be easily employed; I shall speak of this matter below in its proper place.

3. Great advantage can also be perceived from the admission and care of foreigners; Xenophon, in his *Treatise on the Methods of Revenues*, considers this among the best sources of income; there he explains at length how this ought to be done. *Consult also Bornitius, Treatise on Coinage, chapter 8.*

VII. Bornitius persuades us, in *The Treasury, book 1, chapter 4*, that Princes should restore the use and capture of wild animals to the Law of Nations <note>term: Law of Nations (Jus gentium). The legal concepts considered common to all prestige cultures, often implying that natural resources like wild animals should be accessible to all, rather than restricted by feudal law.</note>; provided, however, that the Royal Right remains undiminished, with a tax reserved for the Prince on every head of game.

> This would surely be more beneficial to the public and more pleasing to God than for the subjects to be harassed by hunting parties (as is currently the more frequent practice). *Wehner, in Metamorphosis, chapter 13, folio 215.*

# On the Public Treasury, Chapter III.

Philip, King of Macedonia and father of Perseus: He increased the revenues of the Kingdom not only through the produce of the fields, but also by reopening old, abandoned mines and establishing new ones in many locations. <note>original: "Macedoniae Rex Philippus, Persei pater"</note> *Livy, Book 39.* This profit is the true "merchandise" of Princes, which no one except the Prince may lay a hand upon. <note>The author argues that mining rights are a regalian right, exclusive to the sovereign.</note> *Rauchbar, question 22; Arumsaeus, Discourse on the Golden Bull, thesis 5; Lather, Book 3, chapter 9.* Indeed, any Republic ought not to neglect this. *Xenophon in his treatise On Revenues, number 14,* where he teaches how we ought to conduct ourselves in silver mines if we wish to perceive great fruit rather than loss from them. From these revenues, the Electors and Dukes of Saxony, within 79 years, collected 41,118 tons of gold <note>A "ton of gold" was a unit of account representing 100,000 thalers, not a literal weight of gold.</note> from the veins of Schneeberg, through the tithes and the hallmarking of silver. *Albinus* in **The Mining Chronicle of Meissen,** *title 4, folio 31 and following; Bornitius, Book 1, chapter 5, and the same in his treatise On Coins, chapter 8.*

IX. Furthermore, for the sake of accumulating public money, a *Mount of Piety* <term>Mons Pietatis: a charitable pawnbroker run by the state or church to provide low-interest loans to the poor</term>, as they call it, can be established: see *Bornitius, On Coins, chapter 8 at the end,* who likewise in his work *On the Treasury, Book 1, chapter 7,* reviews various methods for it. From this institution, public money can be granted as a loan at legal or slightly higher interest rates, provided a pledge (of gold or uncoined silver) is given: **A Public Exchange.** <note>original: "Gemeiner Wechsel"</note> By this method, it seems that the frauds of usurers can be countered at the same time. *Bodin, Book 6, chapter 2, number 665; Lather, Book 3, chapter 23; Molina, disputation 325.*

To this I also refer what is customarily practiced in certain places: that the Treasury receives a certain sum of money from a private individual and grants them either sustenance or a pension (higher than common interest) for the duration of their life. **Purchase of a Prebend.** <note>original: "Pfrundtkauff" - a life annuity or pension arrangement.</note> In some places, especially in Italy, a man to whom a daughter is born is permitted to pay whatever dowry money he wishes into the Treasury of Piety under this law: that he cannot reclaim it, but when the girl reaches her 18th year, the girl's husband receives ten times the money from the Treasurers as a dowry. *Bodin, number 665.*

# Political Discourses

X. We truly disapprove of the public Pot of Fortune (**Lucky open Lotteries** <note>original: "Glückhaff offne Lottereyen"</note>). See *Bornitius, book 2, chapter 4*, with whom *Lord Latherus* also agrees, *book 3, chapter 15*, since not only the end, but also the means, ought to be honorable. The Belgians <note>referring to the people of the Netherlands</note>, however, establish those public drawings of lots in order to collect revenue for the Poor; and the profit which they take from there, they contribute toward building hospitals <term>nosodochia: Greek-derived term for hospitals or infirmaries</term> and establishing their endowments. *Keckermann, Politics book 1, chapter 21, page 342; and the same, chapter 22, page 361.*

XI. Experience likewise teaches, against *Bornitius, book 2, chapter 5*, that the use of Alchemy is employed in vain for the purpose of procuring public money. Today, that which the most prudent writer *Tacitus* judged concerning Nero in the *16th book of his Annals* fits many Great Men. Luxury, he says, meanwhile increased with empty hope, and old wealth was consumed as if new riches had been offered which he might squander through many years. Indeed, he was already giving bounties from that source. And the expectation of riches was among the causes of public poverty. Furthermore, we consider that it should be decreed here that private individuals everywhere, moved by the greed for profit, should [not] study Alchemy; as *Keckermann* says, it is an altogether wise Law which was passed in the Kingdom of England, that no private person may practice Alchemy without the consent of the King. *Politics book 1, chapter 22, page 362; and see his practical disputation 32, question 9; La Noue, discourse 23; Lather, book 1, chapter 11.* Truly, Diocletian burned the writings of the ancients concerning the smelting of silver and gold in vain, lest the Egyptians, becoming wealthy from that art, should rebel: *Suidas.* He would have left those books to them more safely, so that they might receive Poverty as the reward for this folly.

Without the Spagyric <term>Spagiricâ: another term for alchemy, specifically the paracelean method of separating and recombining plant or mineral components</term> art or Alchemy, one solicits the secrets of Nature in vain; only those whose eyes are clouded by darnel <note>lolio: a weed believed in antiquity to cause blurred vision or hallucinations if eaten in bread</note> will deny this. But the "purse-catchers" must be fled; those who first snatch for themselves the gold which they afterwards promise to others, and if any place faith in them, they are falsely [deceived]...

# Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter III.

See Georg Rollenhagen <note>A German writer (1542–1609) known for his satirical epic "Froschmeuseler" (The Battle of the Frogs and Mice).</note> in the *Froschmeuseler*, book 1, chapter 15. This disease is the companion of certain poverty and fruitless labor; it is familiar to curious and greedy minds, to whom the following process is not infrequently sold at a high price (as mentioned by the most illustrious Remus, in his notes on Themistius, page 181):

->Take this, I know not what;<-
->Put it there, I know not where;<-

Ferrandez de Eyçaquirre, in his *Moral Concepts*, number 219, calls Chemistry <note>original: "Chymiam"</note> a "graduated folly"; and in the play *Turbo*, Andreas de Valentia <note>A pseudonym for Johann Valentin Andreae, a key figure in the Rosicrucian movement.</note> writes in Act 4, Scene 1:

That is the art without art,
Whose mother is idleness,
Whose vow is to be blackened,
Whose proof is to lie,
Whose labor is to puff up,
Whose end is to despair,

Whose sum is part with part,
Whose words are trifles,
Whose fame is to be noted,
Whose path is to be hindered,
Whose fruit is to beg,

Likewise, Du Bartas writes beautifully concerning the Alchemists in *Eden*, page 30, etc., in the commentary by Simon Goulart. All these things, however, are to be understood as referring to vagabond counterfeiters, not to the diligent searchers of nature; for nature is surely open to no one except the <term>Spagiric</term> <note>A term for an alchemist who follows Paracelsian methods, focusing on the separation and recombination of natural elements.</note>. The old man <note>A theological reference to the unregenerate human nature.</note> takes all his lust and joy in it, making it his treasure, comfort, and indeed his God. In searching, he has no rest; when he finds something, his heart is entirely captured and possessed. But sink yourself deep into Christ, into His holy cross, into His death, as you were baptized into it; then God will teach you that this art is indeed a gift of God to whomsoever God reveals it, etc. Yet, whoever has it and knows it must not let it be noticed by men at all, and must only take from it with fear what is strictly necessary to sustain himself and his own, and to help the poor."

# Chapter 11. Concerning the Public Treasury

Regarding Caligula <note>Gaius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, the third Roman Emperor, known for his erratic and often cruel fiscal policies</note>, we must be careful to avoid his practice of rescinding the wills of those who neglect the Prince, treating them as "ungrateful." *Nicolaus Betts, On Family Pacts, final chapter, page 732.* But how and when can the Treasury <term>Fiscus: the private or state purse of the ruler</term> take anything from a Will? *Lather* treats this extensively in *Book 3, Chapter 2*, where he also inquires at *number 37, etc.*: Whether it can be arranged by law or statute that individual testators <note>those making a will</note> must leave something to the Church and the State in the name of a legacy?

XIII. In former times, the riches of very many people consisted in a multitude of Slaves. The Prince could also acquire these for himself if thieves and other delinquents—to whom life can be granted without violating Divine Precepts, and who are otherwise punished fruitlessly by Exile or Flogging—were instead condemned to the Mines <note>original: "in Metallum"</note> or other public works, either for a time or in perpetuity (as was formerly done in Rome. *Bulenger, Chapter 35*). Alternatively, their labor could be assigned for a fixed fee to private individuals who stand in need of their service. This is also favored by Thomas More in *Book 1 of Utopia, page 25 and following, where he discusses the Republic of the Polylerites* <note>A fictional people in More's Utopia who used criminals as public bondmen</note>. Following the laudable institution of the Belgians and other Republics, the profligate, the disobedient, and wicked or vagrant men could be compelled to some labor useful to the State, or be trained in a unique way in a certain public prison, in a **House of Correction** <note>original German: "Zuchthauß"</note>. In this way, they might earn their sustenance by the labor of their hands, and having finally returned to a more honest and better life, they might be released as reformed, gentler, and more accustomed to hard work. *See Hippolytus a Collibus, On the Growth of Cities, Chapter 23; and Isaac Pontanus, in the History of the City of Amsterdam, Book 2, Chapter 9 and following; and Lather, Book 3, Chapter 19, number 61 and following.* How much profit and gain might be procured for the Treasury from the works of such men can easily be guessed. Furthermore, through fear of this punishment, very few sturdy beggars, idlers, spendthrifts, and that sort of "useless weight upon the earth" would be found in the streets.

# Political Discourses

There is also an acute discussion in Xenophon <note>original: "d. redit. rat." referring to *De Vectigalibus* or *On Revenues*</note> regarding how a Republic might increase its income through slaves purchased and leased by the state. He explores how, in times of peace or war, these slaves might assist the Republic and how they might perform labor specifically in the silver mines. Likewise, Linschoten <note>Jan Huygen van Linschoten (1563–1611), a Dutch voyager</note> testifies in chapter 29, page 56, column 2, that many Portuguese in India still provide for their own food and expenses through the labor of slaves. So too in former times, Phaleas <note>Phaleas of Chalcedon, a Greek statesman</note> suggested—as noted in Aristotle's *Politics*, Book 2, Chapter 7, at the end, where Piccartus <note>Michael Piccart (1574–1620), a commentator on Aristotle</note> comments—that public craftsmen should be appointed from among the slaves of the Republic.

XIV. But these and all similar methods of increasing the Treasury <term>Aerarium: the public treasury of a state</term> are only to be employed if the reason of the Republic and the nature and condition of the Region and the People permit it; each of these must first be judged with mature judgment. For there is a vast difference between **Civil Art**, which relies on almost general precepts, and **Civil Prudence**, which applies those general categories to specific instances (which are infinite and varied, depending on changing circumstances) and transfers them into practice. When this distinction is not observed, many are deceived by a massive error, as if any precepts and methods could be adapted to each and every Republic. Bornitius <note>Jacob Bornitz, a 17th-century political theorist</note> discusses this in his final book, chapter 3.

Aristotle recounts many of these (though for the most part they are Tyrannical) throughout Book 2 of the *Economics* (which John Case <note>An English Aristotelian scholar</note> denies were written by Aristotle) and Tholosanus <note>Pierre Grégoire, a French jurist</note> in Book 3 of *The Republic*, chapter 6. I believe these methods fall into two categories: they are either demanded extraordinarily from the subjects, or by some other means...

# Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter IV.

Money is acquired [for the state]. Among these methods, those which appear least burdensome to the subjects are always to be pursued. For first and foremost, I protest here in the words of Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse <note>A 16th-century French jurist and professor of law</note> in his *On the Republic*, Book 3, Chapter 2: It is not my intention to advise Tyrants on the ways they might harass their subjects with tributes for their own benefit rather than for the sake of the Commonwealth. Indeed, I detest such men, and I consider their advisors to be the leeches of the people, destroyers, predators, wolves, murderers of the poor, instruments of demons, the worst scourges of God, and slaves to greed. And what I have set out to propose, I believe should only be imitated in the greatest necessity, when faced with two evils: namely, when the defense of the people urges it, and to avoid worse schemes by which the wretched common folk are flayed alive.

Since urgent causes and public necessities occasionally arise which require far greater expenses, Princes and Republics have, by excellent counsel, reserved for themselves extraordinary impositions. These they proclaim contrary to custom, only for a certain period of time; or they increase old tributes and taxes. <note>original: "vectigalia" — taxes on goods or transit</note> *See the argument in Book 1 of the Code on Taxes; Bornitz, Chapter 6, Section 1.* And they ascribe this power to Royal prerogatives and the highest law. *See my own Politics, Book 1, Chapter 4, number 43; extensively discussed by Lord Bocer in his treatise on collections, Chapter 1, number 20, etc.; also Chapter 4 from the beginning, and Chapter 5, number 7, etc.; and Winckeler, observations 2 and 3.* Hence Cicero says, without doubt, in *On Duties*, Book 2: because of the thinness <note>poverty or depletion</note> of the Treasury, a tribute must be contributed, so that all may understand that necessity must be obeyed for the safety of the Commonwealth. And in such a case, in the court of conscience, subjects are not excused if they refuse tributes, collections, etc., or circumvent them by fraud. *Molina, On Justice and Law, Volume 3, dispute 674; Covarruvias on the chapter "Sin," section 5; and myself above in Chapter 1, number 6.* (Among the Romans, this was called a "rash tribute" <note>original: "temerarium tributum" — an emergency tax levied in times of sudden crisis</note>; *Bulenger, Chapter 11 from the beginning*; or even an "indiction" or "collection.") Although a Republic acts more wisely if, in time of peace and when it is not in want, it collects those funds without burdening the People and places them in the Treasury; with these, it can relieve the common fatherland when the time requires, without the proclamation of new Tributes. Effort should therefore be made so that, on account of the thinness of the Treasury and the persistence of business, a certain and annual Tribute be contributed; which, being small, does not weigh heavily, and when collected and stored away over a long time, increases the Treasury: and so in time [of need...]

2. Necessity makes whatever tends toward the Public Good just; and this necessity rendered the so vast and violent exactions of the Romans tolerable. The burdens of the Empire compelled the institution of most taxes: as much for the common utility as for the injury of individuals; as Pliny writes in his *Panegyric*. In Spain, there are *derramas* <note>assessments</note>, *fintas* <note>property taxes</note>, *perdidos* <note>losses</note>, and *emprestidos* <note>forced loans</note>, never to be repaid, etc. See Molina, *On Justice and Law*, dispute 661, number 8, etc.

In Germany likewise, such various names are imposed on extraordinary contributions that, just as in other places, one struggles with the names: Imperial tax, Land tax, Redemption, New assessment, Grant, Turkish tax <note>A tax raised specifically to fund wars against the Ottoman Empire</note>, Roman expedition tax, War tax, Maiden tax <note>A traditional levy for the dowry of a lord's daughter</note>, Final tax, Forest money, Soldier money, Fattening-pig tax, Mast money <note>Fee for grazing livestock on acorns/nuts in forests</note>, Cargo money, Beam money, Mast-tree money, Wine-purchase tax, the "best head of cattle" <note>A death duty where the lord took the best animal</note>, Plow money, Emergency money, Pasture money, Tithes of meat, wine, grain, peas, etc. Cattle tax, Bushel tax, Acreage money, Timber-carriage, Drink tax, Chimney or Hearth money, Rafter money, Protection money, Freedom money, Excise <note>original: "Ungelt"</note>, Bridge money, Way money, Surcharge, etc. Waremund de Erenberg, *On Kingdom Subsidies*, chapters 4 and 5. Haenon, dispute 5, theorem 88, b. folio 284. Caspar Klocke, *Disputation on Contributions*, theorem 3. Regarding the exactions of the Romans and their various names, one can read Bulenger, *On Taxes*, throughout; Heigius, part 1, question 17, number 10 and following. Altogether, what Davus says of Geta in Terence’s *Phormio*, Act 1, Scene 1, seems to fit this situation perfectly:

For in a similar way, some people seize various occasions to collect taxes from their subjects. And not infrequently, burdens that are imposed outside of the ordinary routine are accustomed to degenerate into ordinary ones. For it is a trick far too well-worn among the secrets of ancient tyrants: to seek out occasions for war so that they may always press upon their subjects even after the war has ended. *Bodin, Book 6, chapter 2, number 664.*

II. When money is milked from the subjects, there is need for caution, lest the harshness of the business—with no result—only summons offenses; which are to be avoided by no one more than a Prince. *Symmachus, Book 10, epistle 27.* Care must be taken lest it be said:

> To him (and may it not turn out well) we send these kids. <note>original Latin: "Hos illi... mittimus haedos." A quote from Virgil's Eclogues, implying a gift given under duress or with ill will.</note>

*Facius, Political Livy, part 1, article 40, folio 175.* This, however, will not happen if it is brought about that the subjects are as willing as they are able to contribute. Subjects are not usually unwilling to contribute to the public good, and they endure patiently under the burden: *see Nicolaus Besold, on family pacts, last chapter, folio 734, etc., where he reviews four precautions which a legitimate Prince ought to observe in extractions of this kind for the sake of procuring the safety of the people and winning and preserving their goodwill.* (1) If public necessity is present; which is thought to have this quality: that it often persuades one of the impossible. *Symmachus, in the said epistle 27.*

Indeed, violent extractions are considered so ruinous that the Kings of the Persians were accustomed to demand nothing from their subjects and shake nothing out of them, but only to take those things which were given spontaneously: *Facius, Political Livy, said article 4, folio 171 and following; Engelhart, thesis 22, letter a; just as in Ethiopia nothing is commanded, but all things are offered spontaneously. Bodin, in the often-cited chapter 2, number 64.* So also the ancient Germans were accustomed to contribute whatever they paid of their own accord. *Tacitus, on the Customs of the Germans.* It is the custom, he says, for cities to contribute to their Princes voluntarily and man by man, either of their herds or of their crops: which, being accepted as an honor, assists with necessities. # On the Public Treasury, Chapter IV.

Regarding the State: What the People provide in response, they weigh more as a matter of honor than as a burden. *Henrique Farnese, in the Sayings of Aldobrandini, title 24.* There is a similar contribution in the Kingdom of England, which is called a **Benevolence** <note>A "voluntary" gift to the Crown, though often expected</note>; which the King indeed seems to request in a certain way, yet almost everyone stands ready to provide it, lest they seem to be deprived of the King’s love and favor against their will. *Polydore Vergil, books 24 and 26.* Take the example of Edward IV, who dealt with his friends so that they would spontaneously expend money for the costs of War; because he himself would measure the goodwill of each individual by that act. Likewise, Charles V, when the French were using the aid of the Turks, requested something from each person, committing it to their own judgment whether and how much they wished to give: a practice which Philip later imitated in Spain. *Molina, dispute 661, number 8, at the verse "when however the Prince."* And I just advised above in number 1, verse 2, that the hateful names of "Tributes" are to be avoided.

2. One must never resort to the extraordinary exaction of Tributes unless the highest necessity compels it. *Molina, on Justice and Law, volume 3, dispute 667; Bocer, on Collections, chapter 1, number 3, and chapter 6, number 53.* A Prince ought to strive for nothing with such great zeal and seriousness as that no one be burdened by a new tax: *New Constitutions 43, chapter 1, section 1.* Unless he wishes to be pointed out as a leech of the People, a rapacious wolf, a murderer of the Poor, and a harpy. *Althusius, Politics, chapter 11, number 25; Klock, on Contributions, thesis 46.* See also by all means the *Counsel of Lord Dr. Johannes Brentius, which is among the Theological Counsels of Lord Felix Bidembach, decade 6, counsel 9: Whether and when a Christian Magistrate may tax their subjects with a good conscience.* <note>original: "Ob / vnnd wann ein Christliche Obrigkeit / ihre Vnderthonen mit gutem Gewissen schätzen möge."</note> The Hebrews, the wisest of men, hint at this, for they designated collections as <term>Mas</term> <note>Hebrew: מס, meaning tribute or forced labor</note>: from the root <term>Masas</term> <note>Hebrew: מסס</note> meaning "it is melted away"; because they melt down or consume the Subjects. Hence, when collections are exacted from Subjects without a just cause, Rebuffus says that the Lords collecting them are perpetually tortured with the punishments of hell. *In the Law "He who," on the Signification of Words.* Worthy of commemoration is the grave and effective exhortation of Saint Louis, King of the Franks, to his son Philip, which he commanded to be inserted into his Will in these words: "Son, be religious toward God above all; be kind and liberal toward the needy; be a most sharp guardian and avenger of the Laws and customs of this Empire; abstain from Taxes and tributes, unless the highest force of necessity and the most just cause of Public utility impels you to it. If you do otherwise, consider that you will be a Tyrant rather than a King, etc." *Bodin, chapter 2, number 655.* Princes ought not to think that the People are so dull that they are readily held...

It could be asked here whether Subjects can be compelled to pay off the **debt** <note>original: *aes alienum*, literally "another's copper"</note> of their Lord; and whether for this reason an extraordinary contribution may be rightly imposed upon them? *See Daniel Haunonius, political disputation 5, thesis 90, page 294; Lather, chapter 7, number 7, etc.* This, *Thomas Maullius, in his treatise on homage, chapter 7*, denies. To such an extent that even if the Lord is imprisoned because of debt, the Subjects still cannot be compelled to pay or act as a guarantor for him. This he understands to be true only if the Lord contracted that debt by spending money on Horses, houses, clothes, or other superfluous delights. For if the debt arises from a necessary cause, no one would doubt that the citizens can be compelled to dissolve it. *Bocer, on Taxes, chapter 6, number 23.* But since a People cannot enjoy full happiness as long as the Territory is not liberated from every bond of pledge <note>referring to lands put up as collateral or mortgaged</note>; as *Pierre Matthieu* writes in *book 2, narration 3, folio* **342**, prudent Estates, therefore, in this regard, toward a contribution...

# Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter IV.

We know that because of the heavy burden of taxes, half of the Kingdom revolted from the King of Judea. <note>original: "ob graviora Imperia Tributorum... à Judææ Rege defecisse." Referring to the division of Israel under Rehoboam, 1 Kings 12.</note> *1 Kings, chapter 12.* This same error destroyed the Carthaginian Republic, concerning which Polybius, in *Book 1, chapter 72*, records the following details, which are plainly worthy of memory. They were themselves the primary authors of so many and such great evils for themselves: namely, those who during the previous war had ruled the peoples of Africa cruelly. They seemed to think they had found a sufficiently just cause when they demanded from all others half of their annual produce; and they compelled the inhabitants of the cities to pay twice as much in the name of tribute as they had paid before the war. Furthermore, in the collection of these taxes, they granted no mercy or favor to the poor. They admired and valued those Governors of provinces not for treating their subjects with kindness and humanity, but for those who prepared the greatest resources for the Republic to maintain the army, ships, and public works, while treating the rustic and country folk most bitterly; one of these men was Hanno. <note>Hanno the Great, a Carthaginian leader often criticized for his harshness toward the peasantry.</note> And so, when the men in Africa had no need for encouragement—I will not even say a message—to rebel; even the women, who had previously often suffered their husbands and parents to be led to prison by the tax collectors, then conspired among themselves in each of their cities that they would hide none of their possessions. They contributed their jewelry, stripped from their persons, toward the soldiers' pay without any hesitation. Soon, Matho and Spendius (who were the leaders of the conspiracy against the Carthaginians) abounded with such a force of money that they not only paid the remaining wages to the mercenaries—which had been the agreed price of the rebellion from the start—but there was also a large supply to continue those expenses thereafter. Thus, if anyone desires to enter upon a right path of counsel, he must take account not only of the present, but also of the future. And everywhere other examples occur of many seditions having arisen for this reason. ->*The riches of the common people are the praise and glory of the King;*<-

I wish to add the golden words of *Bernard de Girard, volume 2 of the History of France, book 18, page 509.* It is a failing of the men of the long robe <note>referring to lawyers or magistrates</note> that they do not demonstrate to Princes the iniquity and injustice of such impositions. For Princes, who never feel the pains and burdens of the People, deliberate lightly on that which they do not know the importance and consequence of. But God holds his People in singular affection and recommendation; and Princes can be certain that if they treat their subjects badly, God will take vengeance for it: and that Princes never receive punishment from God except for the great oppressions they inflict on the People. A Lord sins mortally if he imposes a burden or taxes by an unjust reckoning. Those who flay their subjects, draining their blood and scarcely leaving them a borrowed breath; they are said to commit violence, and are held to restore it as a debt: likewise they shall render an account of these things on that great day of judgment. From which also the same Princes may dread retribution from the Highest [Judge] of all things...

...with God as the parent and moderator, who is accustomed to come to the aid of the afflicted, and as a just Judge, renders to each according to their merits. <margin>Antonio Borrini, *The Cavalcade*, part 6, near the end.</margin> To this also pertains what Nicolaus Betsius writes <note>Nicolaus Betsius was a 17th-century jurist known for his work on family pacts and public law</note> in the *aforementioned treatise on family pacts, final chapter, pages 742 and following*: Mehmed, the Emperor of the Turks—the one who occupied Constantinople—having composed his Will, left a testament in great liberty, confessing that he had commanded money from his provinces outside of the usual order <note>original: "extra ordinem," referring to extraordinary or emergency taxes levied without traditional consent</note>. *See Commines, book 6, final chapter, page 590.* This Piety, says Betsius, if it is to be admired in an infidel Prince, how much more execrable must be the opinion of those "New Politicians" returning from Italy; who think it right and lawful to extort money from subjects for Princes by any fraud whatsoever. They mostly abuse the precepts of **Machiavelli** and the examples of Princes (whose true motives they do not grasp) for this purpose. Great is the iniquity of certain Princes (as Commines <note>Philippe de Commines (1447–1511), a writer and diplomat known for his cynical but realistic political analysis</note> complains elsewhere) who, compelled by no necessity, command money according to their own lust, and maintain a large bodyguard to keep the wretched multitude in fear; and then they pour out that money rashly and for pleasure, with no good to the Commonwealth, reducing nothing of their daily expenses, exhausting their people, and surrounding themselves with a crowd of flatterers.

But there is a God, who allows no wickedness to go unpunished, and who especially detests cruelty: who, although He does not speak to men today as He did in those ancient times, has nevertheless left clearly written down what His opinion is and what He wishes us to do; so much so, that clearly no one of sound mind, who has reached a just age, will have any room for excuse. Only bad Princes increase tributes <note>term: tributes (tributa) — general taxes or levies paid by subjects to the state</note>. For as each ruler is better, so he is either content with former tributes, or even diminishes them further. Most gloriously, the **Emperor Julian** <note>Julian the Apostate (reigned 361–363 AD), known for his efforts to reform the Roman administration and reduce the tax burden</note> said to the people of Antioch: "None of us has bought a field or a garden among you, nor built a house, nor taken or given a wife from among you; nor have we loved those things which are considered beautiful among you, nor sought Assyrian wealth, nor fed upon the prefectures; nor have we allowed the magistrate to abuse his power toward us; nor have we been the authors of splendid banquets or theaters for the people. On the contrary, we gave them such immunity and abundance of all things that, free from the fear of want, they played anapests <note>a type of poetic meter often used in satirical or mocking songs</note> against those who bestowed so many goods upon them. We did not command gold, we did not exact silver, nor did we increase tributes, but..."
