# Chapter IV. Concerning the Public Treasury

<margin>The Emperor Valens</margin>
...furthermore, regarding the remaining balance not yet paid, we have waived a fifth part of the customary taxes. Moreover, concerning the Emperor Valens <note>Flavius Valens, Roman Emperor from 364–378 AD</note>, *Ammianus Marcellinus* writes in *Book 31, Chapter 40*: He was a most fair guardian of the provinces, each of which he kept unharmed as if it were his own home. He softened the burdens of tribute with a singular zeal, allowing no increases in taxes. He was not troublesome in demanding arrears of debt. To thieves, and to judges caught in embezzlement <term>peculatus: the theft of public or state funds</term>, he was a harsh and vehement enemy.

I shall conclude this section again with the words of Reinhard Lorich of Hadamar <note>A 16th-century German humanist and educator</note>, who writes thus in his *Education of a Prince, Chapter 72*: When many ordinary tax levies cannot fill the "leaking jar"—that is, the Prince’s treasury <term>fiscus: the personal or state purse of a ruler</term>—war is used as a pretext. The generals collude, and the unhappy people are sucked dry to the very marrow, just as if the Princedom were nothing other than a massive business venture. 

But those worthy of the title of Prince are not those who claim the Commonwealth <term>Respublica: the state or public affairs</term> for themselves, but those who dedicate themselves to the Commonwealth. For he who conducts his empire for himself, and measures all things by his own advantages, is certainly a tyrant and not a Prince, regardless of the titles he holds. With what face, then, do they claim the title of Prince for themselves, who choose a few men—and those the most wicked—from among their number, through whom they exhaust the strength and wealth of the people? They do this by artfully devised pretexts and repeatedly renewed titles, converting it into their own treasury; whether they mercilessly extort it, or wickedly squander it on pleasures, or cruelly spend it on wars. 

And whoever can act the part of the old fox most effectively in these matters is valued most highly; just as if the Prince were the enemy of the people, not the father, so that he is seen to consult the Prince's interests best who most hinders the welfare of the people. *Aristotle* reports in his *Politics* that in some Oligarchies <note>Rule by a small, elite group</note> it was the custom that those about to enter office would swear an oath in these specific words: *I shall pursue the common people with hatred, and I shall strive with all my might that it goes badly for them.* 

But a Christian Prince, when entering office, will swear far different things to his people. And yet we hear that some are such toward the people as if they had sworn according to that barbaric custom: that they would be enemies to the people's affairs in every way. It plainly tastes of tyranny whenever it is best for the Prince only when it is worst for the people, and when the happiness of one grows from the calamity of the other. For it does not matter if he is called "Prince" or "Father of his Country" by flatterers or by the oppressed, if in reality he is a tyrant. And even if his own age flatters him greatly, posterity will not be so compliant. You see the names of once-formidable Kings, whom no one while they lived—or...

...or dared to offend even with a nod, with what great hatred their descendants pursue them, and with what great liberty they detest even their very names. That is not true praise which is extorted by fear or bestowed by flatterers. And it goes poorly with the reputation of a Prince if his protection is placed in a silence induced by threats. Even if the present age remains mostly silent, certainly (as I have said) posterity will speak. For who was ever so formidable a tyrant that he could restrain the tongues of everyone? And all cases in which subjects are held to a contribution must be understood to apply only if the Lord cannot assist the public from his own revenues without a notable diminution of his property, and is found powerless to meet the expenses through no fault of his own. <note>Citing Thomas Maullius on Homage and Henry Klock on Taxes.</note> And so, if a subject of any Lord immediately subject to the Empire says that he is burdened by collections beyond measure and the strength of his means, he can obtain penal mandates against the one burdening him from the <term>Imperial Chamber</term><note>The Reichskammergericht, the highest judicial court of the Holy Roman Empire</note>, as infinite legal precedents prove. # On the Public Treasury, Chapter IV.

...be harassed more than is fair or right. <note>Latin: *debite & plus æquo divexentur*. References to legal scholars Andreas Gail and Joachim Mynsinger.</note> And if any Commander were to do this, he could easily acquire the authority and favor of all. Indeed, even in a state ruled by many <term>polyarchic: a government where power is invested in multiple people</term>, more is often achieved by example and imitation than by punishment. That is to say: those who are highest in honor ought also to be the first in contributing, if they wish the common people to be ready to give.

In the writings of Livy <note>Roman historian, Book 26 (cited here as Decade 3, Book 6)</note>, the Consul Levinus, when deliberating on the burden to be imposed on private citizens due to the Macedonian War, and seeing that the common people were not obeying the decrees, gave this opinion: "Just as the Magistrates stand above the Senate, and the Senate above the people in honor, so they ought to be the leaders in undergoing everything that is hard and harsh. If you wish to enjoin anything upon an inferior, if you first establish that law for yourself and your own kin, you will find everyone more easily obedient. Nor is an expense felt as heavy when the people see each of the Leaders taking more than a man's share of the burden upon themselves. Therefore, so that the Roman People may have the fleet we wish to equip, let us first command ourselves to provide private rowers without refusal. Let us all, as Senators, bring our gold, silver, and coined copper to the public treasury tomorrow. Let each man leave only rings for himself, his wife, and his children, and a <term>bulla: a protective amulet worn by Roman boys</term> for his son; and those who have a wife or daughters may keep one ounce of gold each. For those who have sat in a <term>curule chair: a high-ranking magistrate's seat</term>, let them keep the trappings of their horse and a few pounds of silver so they may have a salt-cellar and a dish for the sake of the Gods <note>Religious offerings were traditionally made using these silver items</note>. For the rest of us Senators, let us leave only one pound of silver and five thousand pieces of coined copper for each head of a household. Let us carry all the rest of our gold, silver, and copper to the bankers <note>Latin: *triumviros mensarios*, public bankers of Rome</note> by our own example, before any decree of the Senate is even made. Thus, a voluntary contribution and a competition to help the Republic may excite the minds of the Equestrian order first, and then the rest of the common people, to emulate us. This one way we Consuls have found, after much talk among ourselves. Enter upon it, with the Gods' good help. A safe Republic easily keeps private property safe; by betraying public interests, you would preserve your own in vain." There was such great spirited agreement to these words that thanks were spontaneously given to the Consuls, etc.

# Political Discourses

The foundations of the Republic are established. We pray to your saving Divinity <note>original: "Salutare Numen tuum"; a formal address to the Emperor</note> that in this offering, which adds something to those that came before, you may understand that this has been our care: that we should not seem to have less capability under your rule; our zeal has grown through our love for you. These are the words of Symmachus <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus (c. 340–402 AD), a Roman statesman and orator</note> in his 10th book of *Letters*, epistle 26, to the Emperor Theodosius. But if, on the other hand, they endure the Empire of their Prince with an uneasy mind, not only do the taxes seem heavier, but he also seems to rule only precariously—that is, for as long as an enemy does not offer them a more tolerable yoke. <margin>As I have already mentioned somewhere above.</margin> Salvian <note>Salvian of Marseille (c. 400–470 AD), a Christian writer who critiqued Roman corruption</note> refers to this in his 5th book *On the Government of God*, page 156, when he says: "There is one and the same prayer among the Roman commoners there: that they might be allowed to live the life they lead among the Barbarians. And we wonder why the Goths are not defeated by our forces, when the Romans would rather be with them than with us," etc.

Regarding how much the wasteful luxury of a Prince harms the levying of new taxes, Charles VI <note>Charles VI of France (r. 1380–1422), known as "the Beloved" and later "the Mad"</note> learned this by experience in Paris. Guagninus <note>Alexander Guagninus (1538–1614), a chronicler</note> writes of this in his 9th book of *French Affairs*: "A humble man from the Parisian common folk," he says, "driven as if by new furies, complained that he was being crushed by the magnitude of the taxes. Therefore, approaching the provost of the merchants, he forced the man to come to an assembly, where one of the bolder commoners, on behalf of the multitude, demanded that the payments and taxes be abolished; because they had requested this long ago and had not been heard, the time had now come when they must be satisfied. Many, wishing to resist the excited multitude bravely, thought that if the matter were deferred until the next day, the fury could be restrained, and so they postponed the business. Understanding this, a certain cobbler <note>original: "veteramentarius futor"; a repairer of old shoes</note> rising up rashly, said: 'Let it be set down: the arrogance and pride of the Courtiers fall back upon the shoulders of the People, and the goods squandered by them on luxury become our losses and calamities.' By this commotion, it happened that after they were ordered to go home by the King's mandate, the taxes were abolished." Maecenas <note>Gaius Maecenas (70–8 BC), an advisor to Augustus Caesar</note> spoke most truly to Augustus Caesar in Dio's *History*, book 2: "Who, seeing that you live temperately and waste nothing, using the greatest thrift in your private affairs while being most liberal in public, would not willingly contribute something; since he considers your riches to be his own security and abundance?"

# On the Public Treasury, Chapter IV.

II. Between flocks and shepherds, there is a mutual relationship of benefit and duty; in the same way, there is a mutual exchange between the Prince <note>The term "Prince" (Princeps) here refers generally to any sovereign ruler or head of state.</note> and the people. The People owe the Prince tax, they owe him obedience, and they owe him honor. In turn, the Prince owes the People mercy and vigilance. Therefore, when he demands a tax from his own people as if it were a debt, let him first examine himself to see whether he has paid the "tax" of his own duty to them? *Lorich, Institutes for Princes, chapter 72, at the beginning.*

IV. The willing inclination of subjects to contribute is also encouraged: (4.) If a pact of remission is involved, so that the Prince binds himself to remove the Tributes in good faith once a certain time has elapsed. *See below in this chapter, number 7.* (5) If promises are added regarding the granting or preserving of Privileges—such as Religion, Liberty, etc.—by way of compensation. *Bornitius, in this book, book 6, chapter 1, at the end.* (6.) If the People see that they are being dealt with candidly.

Therefore, a Prince must not use pretexts or offer false and simulated causes. *Discussed at length by Bornitius, in this book, book 8, chapter 3.* Comines <note>Philippe de Commines (1447–1511), a writer and diplomat known for his memoirs on European politics.</note> rightly rebukes the English for inventing necessary wars so that they might have money, which they afterwards wastefully consume. *Comines, book 4, chapter 1, page 279, and chapter 11, page 343.* One must avoid the trick used by some: while they propose the utility of repairing Cities or the gathering of an army, they feign an urgent necessity and stir up fear of the enemy in the People; then, after the money has been exacted, they leave the works unfinished or claim that peace has been granted. *Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse, book 3 on the Republic, chapter 6, number 32; Boccalini, 1st Advertisement, 90, page 434, etc., where he treats Constantius Albicius.* To this pertains what Aristotle relates in the 2nd book of *Economics*: Mausolus, the Tyrant of Caria, suborned certain people who immediately promised they would contribute and named a sum. Once this was done, the wealthier citizens—partly out of shame and partly out of fear—promised and contributed more. If such deceits are employed, tax collections are usually burdened with a double hatred.

V. Furthermore, it is not only necessary that a Public necessity exists, but it must also be publicly approved by the Estates <note>The "Estates" (Ordines) refers to the representative assembly or social ranks of a realm whose consent was often required for extraordinary taxation.</note>. For there is no Prince, as Comines says (book 5, last chapter, pages 472 and 477), who has the right to exact even a farthing <note>original: "teruncium" - a tiny Roman coin, used here to mean the smallest possible amount.</note> from his subjects,

# Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter IV.

...Kings, because they impose taxes with the greatest humanity and moderation, with the approval of the Procurators of the Kingdom, the Tribunes of the People, and the Subjects, in the Assemblies <note>original: "Comitiis" - referring to formal legislative gatherings like the Cortes or Parliament</note>. Parladorius, *Book 1 of Everyday Matters, chapter 3, folio 57.* Although Vasquius reports that a tax on wool was once imposed on subjects without summoning the Procurators of the Kingdom or holding an Assembly, it was afterwards revoked in the Assembly. *Book 2, section 17, number 102, on the succession of creatures.* Whence the author of the Political Treasure, *Report on Spain, part 1, folio 92,* writes:
> *The Princes, Cities, and Peoples do not consent to be burdened with extraordinary impositions: but they desire that their indulgences and privileges be fully observed.* <note>original: Italian</note>

Hence the Emperor Maximilian I of Austria used to say that he was a King of Kings; and the King of Spain a King of Men; and the King of France a King of Asses, etc. <note>This famous quip suggests that while the Emperor ruled over other sovereigns and the Spanish King over free men, the French King ruled over people who bore any burden like beasts of burden.</note> Bodin attests to a similar privilege in France: *Book 1 of the Republic, chapter 2, number 656,* and Froissart brings forward an example. *Volume 1, chapter 155.* Indeed, the Monk Aymon attests that the Kings of France, since the age of Charlemagne, could not institute new taxes except by the supporting decree of the General Estates. *Book 4, chapter 116 and following.* Charles VII was the first to exact collections at his own pleasure, of whom Comines writes thus, *Book 6, chapter 7, folio 543:*
> *And at that time there were great matters, as much for garrisoning the conquered lands as for dismissing the men of the companies who were pillaging the Kingdom: and to this the Lords of France consented, for certain pensions that were promised to them, for the money that would be raised in their lands. If this King had always lived, and those who were then with him in his council, he would have advanced much at that hour: but by what has happened since and will happen, he heavily burdened his soul and those of his successors, and inflicted a cruel wound upon his Kingdom, etc.* <note>original: Middle French</note>

Furthermore, concerning the Assembly of Blois held by Henry III, it is reported in the *General Guide of Finances, part 1, folio 196:*
> *That he said to the deputies of the Estates, whom he had come one after another before him; that he intended, after the Estates had granted him what was necessary for the maintenance of the expenses of his house and payment of garrisons, that he would make no levy of taxes <term>tailles</term> <note>The "taille" was a direct land tax in France from which the clergy and nobility were exempt.</note> upon his People without the consent of the Estates, etc. He even promised that the money would not be handled by his officers and accountants, but by those who would be commissioned for this by the Estates, etc.* <note>original: Middle French</note>

# Political Discourses

...to exercise cruelty against the property and money of subjects, as Philippe de Commines <note>original: "Cominæus"; 15th-century French diplomat and historian</note> notes in book 5, final chapter, page 464. But indeed, although the Estates of the Kingdom of Naples are likewise held under the rule of their King by very strict laws: nevertheless, if the King has a need to demand some extraordinary subsidy <note>a financial grant or tax</note> from them; so that all suspicion of coercion may be removed, and their votes may be freer, the Estates are usually summoned to Naples. In their Assembly (held not in a fortress or Royal palace, but in the Monastery of Saint Lawrence) the King himself, or the Viceroy in his name, delivers a speech adapted to the present matter; he explains the cause and the driving necessity for holding the Assembly and seeking the extraordinary subsidy, and then he is accustomed to declare how much the King expects from the Estates. See Betsius <note>original: "Betſium"; likely Jean Betz, a legal scholar</note>, in the said final chapter, page 736. 

But nevertheless, these things are to be understood with a grain of salt; not so that we take away from the Prince the power of imposing tributes in a full Kingdom (which is ascribed to Royal prerogatives, as I said above in number 1), or that we consider those contributions to be merely gifts. Rather, we adapt these things to his duty and prudence; which always suggests a mitigation of strict law, and sometimes a remission. *Bartholomäus Keckermann, Practical Dissertation 3, Problem 8.* So also in the German-Roman Empire, various rulings have been handed down against subjects refusing an announced tax. *Roland, On Commissions, part 3, book 3, chapter 8, number 6; Winzeler, Observation 5, near the end.* They also say that if some of the leading men of the People do not present themselves at the assemblies called (so that the tribute may be discussed in them); the part of those present, being the majority, also burdens the rest. *Winzeler, Observation 6.* In a similar way, *Otho Casmannus, Politics, chapter 32, page 175,* says: If the Magistrate can obtain the tribute by persuasion, it would be better; although (as Tacitus cleverly noted) persuasion from one who can command carries the force of necessity. Otherwise, let him say with Themistocles <note>Athenian general and politician</note> to the Ambassador regarding money: that he comes accompanied by two Goddesses, Persuasion and Violence. But then they might respond to him: that they also have great Goddesses among them, Poverty and Impossibility, because of which it was not permitted to give what was requested. 

Whenever subjects say this same thing truly; the Prince more rightly acquiesces in it: lest he run into the inconveniences of which mention has already been made above in this chapter, number 1. I have found this out by experience myself (says Betsius in the said Family Pact, final chapter, page 737) that a certain Prince, to be compared to the highest Princes in lineage, kinship, and the breadth of his principality, when he undertook a non-necessary war, solely for the enlargement of his territory, [threatened] wealthy subjects with the threat of prison and other punishments...

# Political Discourses

In the case of an unnecessary tribute, one should plead against the disgrace; and in the conducting of a census, one should plead against the confession of public and private poverty: *From Bucanus and Waremundus, on Subsidies, chapter 6, near the end.* It is not to the credit of Superiors to play fraudulently with the hides of the poor <note>A metaphorical expression meaning to profit at the expense of the vulnerable</note>. Furthermore, the Estates <note>The "Ordines" or representative bodies of the social classes</note> can deny the granting of funds if the Prince wishes to initiate a non-necessary war. This is proven by the bold refusal of the Flemish given to Charles of Burgundy <note>Charles the Bold (1433–1477), Duke of Burgundy</note>, when he attempted to impose a levy to restore the costs of the Swiss war. *In Guillaume Paradin, History of Burgundy, last book, page 976:*

> That they recognized him as their Prince and natural Lord, and that if they heard he was a prisoner, or enclosed by his enemies, they would sell everything they had to recover and deliver him: but to continue the war, which served only to destroy his lands and his neighbors, and to irritate God against him, they were not at all determined to help him, etc.

The Lusitanians <note>The Portuguese</note> also observed that wars moved against the Moors, even when funded by the common people, always brought calamities upon the Kingdom: a point that was repeatedly and fruitlessly urged upon Sebastian <note>King Sebastian of Portugal, who disappeared at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir in 1578</note>. *Conestaggio, On the Union of Portugal and Castile, book 1, page 43.* But can tributes be denied to a Prince, and can he be resisted in practice, on account of prodigality or denied justice? This is discussed by Keckermann <note>Bartholomäus Keckermann (1572–1609), a prominent German Reformed theologian and philosopher</note> *in the said practical disputation 34, problem 13, at the beginning*; it is not for this place, but pertains to the care of the Republic.

VI. And furthermore, the money that is exacted from the subjects must be converted to the purpose for which it was intended. *Meteren, History of the Netherlands, book 21, page 76; Molina, On Justice and Law, Volume 3, disputation 667; Bocer, On Collections, last chapter, number 16; Caspar Klock, On Contributions, letter a; Hænon, Political Disputations 5, theorem 90, page 292.* For far be it from Princes to hold the opinion that what is contributed from the common fund should be seen as belonging to the Law of the Treasury <note>original: "in Jure Fisci"; meaning the Prince's private or state purse</note>. *Symmachus, Book 1, Epistle 40.* And it seems a most excellent precaution, which renders exactions as pleasing as possible, if it appears that previously collected money was spent on the intended uses. To this end, Princes sometimes either give an account of the exacted money to the Estates, or permit it to be administered by deputies of the Estates. This ought to seem by no means shameful to a Prince, since by it he demonstrates his integrity and frankness.

...to those who devour the flesh of the People. Nor will this sin be forgiven them when they say at the moment of death: *Lord, have mercy on me.* The sin is not forgiven unless that which was taken away is restored. Let no one think, says Saint Augustine <note>A reference to Augustine’s famous rule on restitution in Letter 153 to Macedonius</note>, that he who has unjustly taken the property of another—which he is able to return—can truly repent of that sin and obtain pardon unless it is restored; for as long as the thing on account of which the sin was committed is not returned, if it can be, then repentance is not being performed, but merely feigned. *See Ægidius Bossius, Ethical Questions, century 2, decade 3, question 8; William Perkins, On the Right Manner of Living, page 120; and this matter of restitution is treated extensively by Covarruvias in "On the Rule of Law" in the 6th book, and by those who write on cases of conscience and the manner of confessing: such writings are not as foolish as some married men <note>original: "mariati"; likely a typo for "maritati" or "morati" (the sophisticated), or perhaps a jab at secular men</note> judge them to be.* Savonarola encompasses much in a few words in *Book 4 on Simony, conclusion 8*: Kings and Princes, and their wives and children, who do not live simply but spend everything on their displays, and horses, and superfluous dogs, and luxuries, and because of this burden the people with great exactions—how shall they be saved? # On the Public Treasury, Chapter IV.

The King of France, having secured peace with the Spaniard, remitted the extraordinary taxes <term>vectigalia; taxes on goods or services</term> to his subjects. A truly praiseworthy saying of his is circulated: *“We release you from what you owe from the past.”* <note>original French: "Nous vous quittons ce que vous devez du passé."</note> *Pierre Matthieu* mentions this in *Book 1 of his History.* Indeed, the Justice of Tribute <term>Tributum; a direct tax</term> also requires this: that from the beginning it be exacted according to due proportion and according to the estimation of expenses which public necessity requires; nor should more be demanded than necessity is seen to command. <note>References to the Code of Justinian (l. omnes. 12) and Molina’s "On Justice and Law."</note> And there exists the *163rd Novel of the Emperor Tiberius* regarding the relief of future debts; where that most pious Emperor says he was moved (on the occasion of the Passion of Christ and His Resurrection, following the likeness of the liberation from the Servitude of Egypt) by Justice and Philanthropy; so that there might be a relief not only of past fiscal debts, but also of future ones. From which *Joachim Stephani, in his exposition of the New Constitutions,* rightly gathers: that the relaxation of Tributes, Payments, and Rents <term>Canones; fixed annual payments</term> proceeds from the Justice of the Prince: and these things must be moderated by mercy and humanity alone, lest the Subjects be too greatly burdened. <note>See also above, Chapter 2, number 4, verse 2.</note>

VIII. Subjects can assist the Commonwealth <term>Respublica; the state or public affairs</term> with resources; if (1.) they are driven to labors and idleness is removed: so that they themselves are compelled to sell to others, and not buy everything. And therefore, concerning the inhabitants of the modern City of Rome, it is held in the *Political Treasury, part 1, page 34,* that almost all are either burdened by debt or pressed by poverty. *“As it necessarily must be, where there is no proper craft of one's own by which men can sustain themselves: because almost all things that are used are brought from foreign countries.”* <note>original Italian: "Secondo che necessariamente conviene essere, dove non vi sia alcuna propria arte..."</note> Whence, he who desires to exact much from his Subjects has a necessity to create for them the opportunity for sustenance and wealth. For this reason, in the Free Cities of the Empire, although the burdens are almost heavier than those which Princes impose on their Subjects: yet they bear them with a more level mind; not only in view of common Liberty, but also because, by good laws of Commerce <term>Mercatura; trade and mercantile activity</term> and other things necessary for life, provision is usually made there with almost greater zeal.

Let Belgium be our example; in which there are no gold or silver mines; indeed, several provinces are not even abundant in grain. Nevertheless, it is today far more fortunate in opulence and riches than Hungary or even that "Blessed Arabia": it grew, of course, by the industry of men and by the most fruitful commerce of every kind. Florence, Lyon, and Nuremberg can also serve as examples for us; where more people live by art <note><term>Art: refers to "Ars" or skilled craft and technology rather than just fine arts.</term></note> than by nature. I say further here, that Princes and governors of Republics should forbid raw materials of a simple nature to be exported from their regions to foreigners: for that material, when polished and worked, yields more profit than when raw and natural; the former fills the Prince's treasury more, and the cities with inhabitants more. For where there is an abundance of material, there will also be inhabitants and profit. But I cease to mention more here: I add only this as a conclusion; that such great riches reside in the arts, skill, and industry of men, that you can by no means compare the Indian gold and silver mines, nor the golden mountains of Hungary or Blessed Arabia, to them. *Thus far Elver.*

# On the Public Treasury, Chapter IV.

IX. If (2.) the extortions of Officials are restrained. *Anti-Machiavelli, Book 3, Theorem 32, page 682 and following.* <note>The "Anti-Machiavelli" was a popular genre of political literature in the 17th century arguing against cynical power politics in favor of moral governance.</note> Whence Henry the Great, King of France, most wisely used to say: *My people are made to pay a double tax; one is to me, and the other is to the Officers. > ->*What will the Masters do, when thieves dare such things?*<- <note>original Latin: "Quid Domini facient, audent cùm talia fures."</note>

If Justice is administered promptly, and if it is not sold, as it were, under the spear <note>A Roman metaphor for a public auction or sale of spoils.</note>; if those things which are sometimes offered to Officials for the sake of "remuneration" (to say nothing more severe) are forbidden; if the expenses spent on Advocates and other administrators of lawsuits are cut short by a summary expedition of cases; it seems that the wealth of the Subjects can be properly looked after. Indeed, the author of *The Secret of Finances*, Book 3, page 429 etc., demonstrates that the multitude of Judges, Advocates, and Procurators harms France more than those many Civil Wars. He claims 50,000 useless men exist there, each of whom daily consumes at least one gold crown uselessly. Memorable is the opinion of Maecenas to Augustus, found in *Dio Cassius, Book 52*: It is not hidden from me that some will take it poorly that Tributes and Taxes are established; but these very people—if they are not afflicted by any other damage besides, and if they find by experience that these are exacted for the sake of their own safety and so that they may safely enjoy the rest of their goods—will even give great thanks to you. This is especially true since most of them will receive that money back, some as magistrates, others as Governors of Regions, others as soldiers; thus, by contributing a small part of their income to you, they can receive all the rest without loss. So too can Subjects bear the costs of wars, if the soldiers are not insolent toward the property owners. Let the soldier live with the Provincials according to Civil Law; and let not that spirit grow rank which feels itself to be armed. Because the shield of your army ought to provide peace to the Civilians. <note>original Latin: "Paganis," referring here to non-combatants or civilians rather than religious heathens.</note> *Cassiodorus, Variae, Book 7, Letter 4.* Do not permit soldiers to be insolent to owners. Let them receive their provisions under moderation: let them not involve themselves in outside cases. Let him who glories in being armed know that he was chosen for the security of all. *Ibid, Book 6, Chapter 22.*

# Political Discourses

X. If (3.) private wealth is preserved through sumptuary laws <note>Laws intended to restrain luxury and extravagance, particularly in food and dress.</note> and other similar statutes: if a curb is quickly placed upon the spendthrift, and if it is brought about by every possible means that money cannot flow to foreigners. What, I ask, would be added to the Treasury if that which is wasted on luxury and clothing—beyond necessity and decency—were instead collected there? For indeed, private individuals ought to retain their money, not only for the sake of "friend, doctor, and enemy," as the common proverb says, but also for the sake of the Commonwealth; the necessity of which must always be preferred above all others. Those who delight in banquets, public distributions of meat, and luxuries, and pour out their money into these things—which contain the memory of only a single day—these should be considered gluttons <note>original: "heluones"</note> not only of private property, but of public property as well. They are citizens of a small mind, wasteful not only of money, but also of their reputation, esteem, and nobility. It is in the interest of the Commonwealth to provide that no one uses his property badly: and I judge that such men should be restrained by laws, lest they pour out money into foul things of no importance. *Laurentius Grimaldus, On the Best Senator, book 2, page 217 and following.* 

But the decree of the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note> was perhaps too harsh; it required that for one day, the masters, the household, and the beasts of burden should fast, and as much as they would have consumed if they had not fasted, they should grant to the Samian exiles who were seeking to recover their homeland. *Aristotle, Economics, book 2.* Which nevertheless was reported by Wehner to have been repeated in Lorraine in the year 1594. *In the Metamorphosis of Public Affairs, chapter 12, page 148.*

A Prince ought to strive with the greatest zeal not only to have those goods by which he may attract the currency of foreigners to himself (as mentioned above in number 8), but also and especially to ensure that money is not carried away to foreign nations under the pretext of exotic goods. Thus, Buchanan reports concerning James I, King of Scotland, in his 10th book: Since through constant wars—which for nearly one hundred and fifty years after the death of Alexander III had shaken Scotland—with cities so often plundered and burned, and the youth turned toward the pursuits of arms, the other arts were neglected; the craftsmen...

# On the Public Treasury, Chapter IV.

He summoned skilled craftsmen of this kind from Flanders <note>Modern-day northern Belgium and parts of France, then famous for textile production</note> by offering rewards and tax exemptions. He filled the cities—which were nearly empty because the nobility, following ancient custom, remained on their country estates—with this class of men. In doing so, he not only restored the former appearance and population of the towns, but also led a great multitude of idle people away from laziness and toward labor. He ensured that what could be manufactured at home at a low cost was not purchased abroad at a high price. But I know not by what fate other nations have become accustomed to absorbing our Germany, while on the other hand, no profit flows from them to us.

<margin>See Lateranus, book 3, chapter 10, throughout the discourse.</margin>
This very same calamity of Germany was long ago deplored with serious lamentations—and pointed out as if with a finger—by Dr. Martin Luther, *in the Treatise "On Commerce and Usury," printed in the year 1525:*

> That foreign trade, which brings goods from Calicut <note>A major port in India</note> and India and such places—namely, such costly silk, gold-work, and spices, which serve only for pomp and have no practical use, and which suck the money out of the land and the people—should not be permitted if we had a government and princes.

And a little later:

> God has cast us Germans aside so that we must shove our gold and silver into foreign lands, making all the world rich while we ourselves remain beggars.

<margin>Lather, book 2, chapter 2.</margin>
A warning must also not be neglected: that subjects should not be prohibited from placing their money at legitimate interest outside the territory. However, the Prince should not borrow money from foreigners:

> So that the interest stays in, and does not go out of, the country.

<margin>Book 1 of the Politics, chapter 2, near the end.</margin>
II. I have already investigated by what remedies luxury might be restrained. Regarding the same James I <note>James I of Scotland (1394–1437), cited here as a model of frugality</note> mentioned above, what Buchanan <note>George Buchanan (1506–1582), a Scottish historian</note> records in that same place is worthy of memory. Against this plague [of luxury], he says, the King resisted as much as he could, both by passing laws and by his own domestic example. For he not only restricted himself in his personal dress and frugality to the manner of a well-to-do private citizen, but if he saw anything immoderate in any part of anyone's life, he showed by his expression, and often by his words, that it was displeasing to him. Thus, the course of widely spreading luxury was checked, rather than new intemperance being extinguished or ancient parsimony fully restored. Pierre Matthieu <note>French historian and advisor to Henry IV</note> also discourses prudently on this matter *in Sejanus, page 289, etc.:*

> It is not enough that those who have the oversight of the Finances keep their eyes open to ensure that expenses do not exceed receipts; the State has a great interest in ensuring that the means of private individuals are managed without excess, with order and modesty.

# Political Discourses

...just as they ought to be acquired without shame. The disorders that one notices in dress, at the table, in buildings, and in the delightful superfluities of private houses, are symptoms of a state that is not only sick, but dying. And indeed, later inquiring into the reason why the Emperor Tiberius did not correct such luxury, <note>Tacitus, Annals 3.53-54</note> he writes thus: on this point, he did not wish to begin the example of reform with his own house, which was overflowing with excess; or perhaps the disorder had already hardened into custom and discipline; or he did not wish to draw public ill-will upon himself subtly and to no effect. His greatest reason was to avoid exposing his commands to contempt, or "opening a vein before having the bandage ready to stop the blood." <note>original: "aperire venam premier que d'avoir toute preste la bande pour arrester le sang." A metaphor for starting a reform without the means to control the resulting social unrest.</note> I likewise subjoin this caution: that only those things should be prohibited which pertain to luxury and pomp, not those which can serve as honorable recreation. In this way, Julius Caesar exercised the sumptuary law <term>sumptuary law: laws intended to restrain luxury or extravagance, particularly regarding food and dress</term> with sufficient severity; having stationed guards (as Suetonius writes in chapter 43) around the market to seize prohibited delicacies and bring them to him; sometimes even sending lictors <term>lictor: an officer attending a Roman magistrate</term> and soldiers who, if the guards had been deceived, would carry away items already served from the dining room. It must also be judged prudently whether, while the luxury of the wealthy is being prevented, the means of living are being withdrawn from the artisans and other citizens of humbler fortune who sustain their lives by it.

XI. If (4.) the Republic is not to be strangled by the chains of tributes—as if by the hands of robbers—except in cases of necessity; as Salvianus says in some place, *Book 4 on the Governance of God*, page 103: <note>Salvianus was a 5th-century Christian writer who critiqued Roman social injustice.</note> something should be reserved for necessity. And in this respect, what the Emperor Constans used to say is true: "Public wealth is better held by many private individuals than reserved within the enclosures of a single Prince." *Eutropius*. For if, as Juvenal says in *Satire 3*, "every tree now pays a fee to the People"; if the blood of the subjects is first consumed to moisten the cement of insane constructions; then nothing can easily be imposed when a new necessity arises.

# On the Public Treasury, Chapter IV.

The wealth of the subjects must be carefully estimated. *Clapmarius, Book 5 on Secrets, chapter 14; Bornitus, book 4, chapter 3.* Let Princes always remember that golden saying: "It is the part of a good shepherd to shear his flock, not to flay them" <note>original Latin: "Boni Pastoris est, tondere pecus, non deglubere"</note>; which the Emperor Tiberius said to Aemilius Rectus, the Governor of Egypt. *Dio Cassius.* And indeed, not only should the sheep not be skinned, but their skin should not even be nicked: *that they should not only not skin them, but that they should not nick their skin at all.* <note>original Italian: "che non solo non lo scorticassero, ma che punto non intaccassero loro la pelle."</note> *Boccalini, report 2, ragguaglio 6, folio 29.* *To skin one's vassals is nothing other than to cut down a forest; although for one time, a piece of more substance and more help is extracted, the owner of the forest remains, from then on, without a forest and without a plant.* <note>original Spanish: "Dessollar los vasallos, no es otra cosa, que atalar un bosque..."</note> *Antonio Perez, aphorisms from the second letters, 356, page 320.* If we wish to gather fruit from trees, they must not be devastated; the woods should be thinned, not uprooted. "I hate the gardener who cuts away the vegetables by the roots": which was the response of Alexander the Great when someone advised him that far more taxes <term>vectigalium: revenues or customs duties</term> could be carried off. *Maximus Tyrius, sermon 13; Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse, book 3 on the Republic, chapter 9, number 15. And what I said above in this chapter, number 1, regarding the inconveniences of exactions, pertains to this at length.*

Hence Cypselus of Corinth, when he had made a vow to Jupiter that if he gained possession of that City, he would dedicate all the wealth of the Corinthians: he ordered a census to be recorded, and when they had declared their holdings, he took a tenth part of their goods from each individual; regarding the remainder, he ordered them to trade and build their wealth. As the year turned, he did the same. It happened, therefore, that in ten years, he himself held all the goods of the Corinthians and consecrated them, and the Corinthians meanwhile sought and prepared everything anew. *Aristotle, Economics, book 2.* Therefore, to speak with Plautus, a Magistrate should not carry off the matter "along with the dust." <note>A metaphor for taking everything down to the last grain.</note> Let the Treasury <term>Aerarium: the public treasury of Rome</term> not be for him, as Pliny says, a "morgue of the citizens" <note>original Latin: "spoliarium," a place where the clothes of dead gladiators were stripped</note> and a receptacle for bloody spoils. Let him not clip the wings so closely that they cannot grow back. He who wipes the nose too hard draws blood. Which Chokier also teaches from Guicciardini, *Aphorisms, book 2, chapter 10, folio 92 and following.* Ludovico Sforza, having sent an envoy to the Genoese to demand a great sum of money from them, and that envoy having been sumptuously received at dinner by a certain nobleman of the City; it happened by chance that from the dining couch...

...while he was walking in the gardens, and having noticed that herb which is called **Basil** <note>original: "Basilicum"</note>, he said to the ambassador: "My Lord, touch this herb lightly," etc. When the ambassador complied, he found the herb to be sweet-smelling. Then the host said: "Now press the herb firmly in your hand and smell it." Upon doing so, he confessed that he was struck by a very unpleasant and disagreeable odor. Then the nobleman said to the ambassador: "My Lord, if Duke Ludwig treats this City with the gentle hand of his power, he will find it sweet and obedient; but if he presses it too hard, he will undoubtedly perceive the unpleasant scent of rebellion and impatience." A Prince should not be like **Rehoboth** <note>The biblical King Rehoboam, whose harshness caused the ten tribes of Israel to rebel; see 1 Kings 12</note> and say: *My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke.* Rather, one should keep in memory what Capitolinus writes concerning **Antoninus Pius** <note>A Roman Emperor known for his peaceful and fiscally responsible reign</note>: *He took no pleasure in any gain that resulted from the oppression of a provincial.* If the head should wish to draw all the blood, marrow, and nourishment of all the members into itself, nothing else would surely follow but the collapse and ruin of the entire body.

<margin>Adam Keller, *On Juridical-Political Office*, chapter 8.</margin>
An extraction is clearly intolerable and impious when it so exceeds the fruit of labor that the owners would rather surrender the things themselves than provide the payment imposed and taxed upon them, or which takes away from the owner all hope of obtaining a free livelihood.

<margin>Althusius, *Politics*, chapter 11, near the end.</margin>
Such was that tax imposed under the Emperor **Justinian**, which, as Suidas asserts, was called *epibole* <note>Greek: ἐπιβολὴ; a "supplementary tax" or "imposition" that forced landowners to pay taxes for neighboring abandoned lands</note>, as if you were to say "an addition"; it was an unforeseen plague upon estates.

<margin>Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book 5.</margin>
There were also at one time such heavy and novel descriptions <note>tax assessments</note> ordered by **Chilperic**, King of France, to be made in every part of the Kingdom; decreeing that an owner should provide one amphora of wine annually for every *aripentum* <note>a half-acre measure of land</note> of his own land, and many other things. Because of this, many left their cities and their own property, deeming it better to wander in other Kingdoms than to be subject to such danger.

<margin>Thomas Maullius, *On Homage*, chapter 7.</margin>
A subject is not bound to nourish his Lord if he himself is in want.

<margin>Cicero, *Letters to Atticus*, book 5, letter 16.</margin>
Consider a Province lost and utterly overturned forever where nothing is heard but the inability to pay the commanded *epikephalia* <note>Greek: ἐπικεφάλια; a "poll tax" or "head tax"</note>; the possessions of all are sold; the groans and weeping of the Cities; these are the monstrosities not of a man, but of some savage beast.

<margin>*The Secret of Finance*, page 5b.</margin>
Such as Normandy declares itself to be to France: *A true anatomy of the human body, in which nothing remains but the bones and the skin, and even those are crushed.* Just as if the nerves are stretched too tight, the body must necessarily contract; so also it is with Tributes...

2. The Statesman should measure the method of taxation by the guidance of civil prudence; which, above all, weighs the nature of the Region and its revenues. As I shall advise from Mariana <note>Juan de Mariana, a Spanish Jesuit historian</note> below in chapter 7, number 3. A "Cynosure" <note>A guiding star or focal point</note> can be found if we examine whether a country supplies more to foreigners than it is forced to buy from them. And first of all, it must also be considered: are the contributions kept and consumed outside or within the Kingdom? Thus Commines <note>Philippe de Commines, a Burgundian-French diplomat and chronicler</note> writes concerning the exactions of Louis XI in book 5, the final chapter:

-> "Surely it was a matter of compassion to see or know the poverty of the people. But our good master had one virtue in him: he put nothing into a treasury. He took everything, and he spent everything." <note>original: "seurement c'estoit compassion de veoir ou sçavoir la pavuretè du peuple..."</note> <-

It is no wonder that France, above other Kingdoms, bears tributes with a calm mind, since it is able to sell many things to others.

-> "It has no mines of gold or silver; nevertheless, money is never lacking in France, brought in from various sides by those who make use of the things of that country: because Portugal has always been open, etc." <note>original: "Non ha Minere d'oro, ne d'argente..." from *Thesoro Politico*, part 1, report on France, folio 179.</note> <-

In this respect, Hybreas once said to Mark Antony: "If you want two harvests of taxes, give us two harvests of grain." <note>Plutarch, *Life of Antony*.</note> A Prince should not explore the resources of his subjects in the manner that Dionysius, the Tyrant of the Syracusans, did. When he was in a state of poverty regarding money, he commanded a Tribute from the Citizens. When they said they had already contributed often and could do no more, he did not think force should be used against them. But after a few days had passed, he ordered the Leaders to take the Votive Offerings (with which the Temple of Aesculapius was adorned, which were many, made of gold and silver) from the shrine and offer them for sale in the Forum as if they were secular items. The Syracusans bought them up with great zeal, so that a great force of money was collected. Having gained possession of this, Dionysius ordered an Edict to be proposed: "If anyone has bought a votive offering belonging to Aesculapius, let him return it to the Temple immediately, or suffer the penalty of death." <note>Polyænus, *Stratagems*, book 5.</note>

This is usually done in recognition and as a fruit of victory. <note>Engelhard, *On Taxes*, thesis 2; see also Molina, *Disputation* 674, at the beginning.</note> However, War is not to be moved for that reason...

### XIII.
Not only is something exacted from subjects through extraordinary contribution (which we commonly call a "collection" <note>original: *collectam*</note>; the Romans called it an "indiction" or even a "super-indiction"), but there is also a very ancient and most common method of increasing the Treasury: the **TOLL** <note>original: *VECTIGAL* — a tax on goods</note> imposed on things which are exported and imported. See Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse, *On the Republic*, book 3, chapter 6; and on tolls, consult Becht, *Disputation on Security*, thesis 56 and many following; likewise the individual dissertations of Heinrich Klock and Gottfried Engelbart.

Lord Bocer teaches what an ordinary and what an extraordinary collection is in *On Collections*, chapter 6, from the beginning. Thus also Winceler, in Observation 1, number 12, etc., distinguishes one collection as extraordinary and another as ordinary; and so the "ordinary" would be the same as a Tribute. See above, chapter 1, number 6. But in truth, the Latins use the term "Toll" <note>original: *Vectigal*</note> generically for any profit that benefits the Treasury. <note>Citing various legal authorities including Alberico Gentili and David Argenteus.</note> Sometimes it is used for Tribute. Sometimes it is contrasted with Tribute and Collections. Hither also belong "Port-dues" <note>original: *Portoria*</note>, or the revenues which come from ports or transit...

XIV. **Tolls** should be imposed on various items rather than proceeding directly to **Tributes** <gloss>direct taxes</gloss>; so thinks Arnisaeus, because where someone hopes for profit, they may more graciously allow something to be trimmed away. Therefore, it is proper to impose them on those things from which profit is perceived. Likewise, the import of those things which subjects cannot do without should be lightened; conversely, the export of things which foreigners need should be burdened. For it is less harmful for superfluous things not to be exported than for necessary things not to be brought in. <note>Citing Bodin, On the Republic, Book 6</note>

# Political Discourses

<margin>Hænon, Political Disputations 5, thesis 88, at the end.</margin>
In the collection of taxes <note>original: "vectigalium"</note>, not only Justice but also prudence must be applied. A tax must be moderated so prudently that, if possible, it is imposed on exported goods and burdens foreigners more than citizens. In this way, the wealth of the Jewish people grew from the tax on balsam <note>original: "opobalsami"; a highly prized aromatic resin used in ancient medicine and perfume</note>; because it was produced only in that province, it was repeatedly carried from there to others. <margin>Justin, book 36.</margin> Likewise, the Emperor of the Turks takes a tenth of exported goods from foreigners leaving the port, but only a twentieth from his own subjects. Accordingly, the custom of France is rightly disapproved of by Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1529–1596), a prominent French political philosopher</note>; <margin>Book 6 of The Republic, 2, number 651, etc.</margin> where an excessive amount is demanded from subjects, while almost nothing is required from foreigners as a tax fee. And although the salt mines in France itself are considered the most abundant and excellent in all of Europe—from which the Belgians, Britons, and Danes are accustomed to seek salt—it is nevertheless sold much more dearly to the French than to them; indeed, it is even secretly brought back by foreigners into the borders of the French Empire. Yet reason sometimes seems to require that foreigners be enticed by the leniency of taxes, namely when the health of marketplaces <note>term: "Emporiorum" (trading hubs or commercial centers)</note> depends on the readiness and abundance of arriving foreigners. <margin>See Keckermann, Practical Disputations 34, question 9.</margin> Thus also Plato, <margin>Book 8 of the Laws.</margin> removed all customs duties from his Republic so that merchants would be enticed to bring in an abundance of goods. A Prince also ought not to burden goods carried through his territory with too heavy a tribute, lest he arm those burdened in this way against himself and his people. <margin>Busius, Political Disputations 11, thesis 32 and following; and Political Book 3, chapter 1, number 6.</margin>

2. I have said that it is necessary to impose taxes on those things from which profit is felt. And thus Trajan <note>Roman Emperor, r. 98–117 AD</note> imposed the twentieth-part tax on inheritances (established by Augustus <margin>Engelhart, thesis 4, page 7</margin>)—a tolerable tribute and easy only for foreigners, but heavy for citizens—upon the former, while exempting the latter. Clearly, it was manifest with how much pain men would bear—or rather, would not bear—having something stripped and scraped away from goods which they had earned by blood, kinship, and finally by the fellowship of family rites; and which they had never hoped for as if they were someone else's, but had always possessed as their own, to be passed on to their next of kin. On the contrary, where you acquire wealth generously and often unexpectedly, what is the bitterness in having something taken away? <margin>Pliny, Panegyric, page 74, with Lipsius's commentary.</margin> <margin>Bulenger, On Taxes, chapter 21.</margin> This law, being neither unjust nor heavy and therefore to be recalled into use, is urged by Waremundus <margin>On Subsidies, chapter 5, number 54, etc.</margin> following Johann Sturm <margin>Sermon on the Turkish War, page 174b.</margin>, and Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), a famous humanist scholar</note> agrees in the same place. Neighboring to this is...

It also examines the inheritance tax, suggesting it is more bearable when applied to unexpected windfalls rather than family property.</summary>

### On the Public Treasury Chapter IV

The tax on the inheritance of one's own people; <note>original: "vectigal hereditatum hominum propriorum"</note> **the principal case of inheritance tax** <note>original: "der Hauptfall"</note>: which in some places is extended to others of free condition as well; though I do not know if this is done justly.

3. Thus, even today, a certain tax (**deduction** <note>original: "Abzug"</note>) is taken from the inheritance of a citizen when it is passed to a foreign place—that is, to a non-citizen; and it is usually a tenth part. *Jacob Curtius, Volume 1, Conjectures, book 1, chapter 51.* Likewise, in certain places, subjects who move elsewhere with their families are similarly forced to pay a tenth part of their alienated property (they call this the **migration tax**, or **departure tax** <note>original: "Nachsteuer"</note>). *Bornitius, book 5, chapter 9. Klock, On Taxes, theorem 63.* **Arrival / Departure** <note>original: "Auffahrt / Abefahrt"</note>: whether this tax <note>term: Gabella (a general term for taxes or duties)</note> is lawful by right is debated by *Köpen, question 11.*

However, this burden has been remitted in this Duchy by a special privilege; and they are accustomed to call this immunity **the right of free passage** <note>original: "den Freyen Zug"</note>. *Ernest Cothman, Academic Responses, 19*, generally exempts academics from these tenths. Just as the ancient "twentieth" tax on inheritances <note>note: referring to the Roman *vicesima hereditatium*</note> was waived for the closest relatives, so here too the first degree of immunity from the inheritance tenth ought to be that children are released from this necessity regarding the goods of their parents; and likewise parents regarding the goods of their children. *Jacob Curtius, Volume 1, book 1, chapter 51. Andreas Rauchbar, part 8, question 15 and following. Andreas Scheffer, Legal Questions, part 2, question 10. Maullius, On Homage, chapter 10, number 39.* It even seems more equitable that this tenth should not be paid on the dowry and festive garments of daughters who marry outside the territory, regardless of what *Johann Köpen* says in *Decision 6, number 6 and following*; compare *Rosenthal, chapter 5, conclusion 34.* This right belongs to the Magistrate, even regarding movable property (**chattels** <note>original: "in der Fahrnuß"</note>) and debts owed; but not regarding those things which the deceased possessed outside the territory. *Rauchbar, question 17.* It is also accepted that a foreigner or alien to whom something has been bequeathed must accept this deduction from the legacy; the heir is not bound to redeem it or provide the legacy in full to the legatee. *Rauchbar, part 1, question 16.* Regarding various questions concerning **the departure tax** <note>original: "die Nachsteuer"</note>, one may consult *Rauchbar, question 15; Scheffer, part 2, question 10; Berlichius, part 3, final question; Köpen, decision 5; Scheplitz, on the Constitutions of the March, part 3, title 8; Klock, On Taxes, theorem 62 and following.* Close to these rights is the **Right of Albinage** <note>term: Jus Albinagii (the right of a lord or sovereign to the property of a deceased foreigner)</note>, which is counted among the Royal rights in France, as I said in *Politics, book 1, chapter 4, number 36 and chapter 11, number 17. See Fr. de Clapperiis, in Decisions, case 1, single question, page 4; case 2, question 1, page 14.* By virtue of this, the inheritances of foreigners fall to the Treasury.

**Henning Arnisæus** <note>A prominent 17th-century German political theorist</note> also discusses the tax on foodstuffs in his *Treatise on the Rights of Majesty, book 3, chapter 7, under number 5*, where he says: "Indeed, matters have reached such a point in several provinces of Germany that we are compelled to pay a tax for the grain brought to the mill, and for that which we eat, that which we drink, and that by which we sustain body and life—effectively forced to buy back those things which are already ours." <margin>Public Duties</margin> For the future, they should as little as possible burden those things necessary for the food and clothing of the poor, who sustain their lives through the industry of perpetual sweat; and they should apply a greater rigor of impositions on those things which belong only to the delights, luxuries, and superfluities of the wealthy, who, living idly off their rents, only attend to the art of being immersed in games and the exercise of perpetually inventing new vices. For it is a general precept: <note>original: "Generale namque est præceptum"</note> those things which we do not wish to be imported into or exported from the Republic, on those the Tax <term>Vectigal: a general term for taxes, duties, or tolls</term> should be increased; on others, it should be diminished. If it cannot be avoided that a new tax be demanded (these are the words of Jacobus Simanca, <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist and bishop</note> book 9 on the Republic, chapter 24, number 10), let foreign and barbarian goods be burdened, which do not serve the necessity of life so much as luxury and delights, and the use of which is peculiar to the rich: such as spices, ointments, gems, and other things of that kind. For from this, only those will feel the inconvenience whose fortunes can bear it; nor will they be reduced to want because of this loss, but perhaps they will be rendered more frugal, so that the loss of money may be compensated by the improvement of their morals. Add to this Arnisaeus, <note>Henning Arnisaeus, a German political theorist</note> Politics book 2, chapter 5, page 561. Let the goods which the People need to sustain life be sold with only a modest tax imposed: what is taken away from those things should be made up from curious goods, without which human life can be led, and which rather have a great power to soften bodies and weaken minds. For in this way, the poor will be provided for, whose number is great, and a limit will be placed on the luxury of powerful men: but if they refuse to be cured, it will be fair that some benefit returns to the Republic from their madness, etc. And Bornitius <note>Jacob Bornitz, a writer on economics and law</note> says this has been accepted in Belgium, in *The Treasury*, book 4, chapter 2: <note>original German: "Daß niemand guldin Stück/ Posament/ Perlen und dergleichen trage/ wa er nicht Acciß davon gegeben."</note> That no one should wear gold pieces, lace, pearls, and the like, unless they have paid an excise tax on them. Keckermann, <note>Bartholomäus Keckermann, a German writer on politics and logic</note> Politics book 1, chapter 22, page 363, and Practical Disputations 34, question 14, page 724. # Concerning the Public Treasury. Chapter IV.

The Roman people used to employ contractors (a practice that was also common among other nations. *Bulenger, chapter 6, at the beginning*). But for the most part, they demanded payments beyond the legal limit: *Law 16, Digest on the Signification of Words.* Hence their name was hateful and infamous. This is discussed extensively and beautifully by *Engelhard, On Taxes, thesis 31, letter r, folio 81, etc.* Thus they are commonly called "public dogs"; robbers stealing by day and night: who in peace, just as soldiers do in time of war, strip the merchants bare—men hated by God and men alike: *Klock, On Taxes, thesis 46, b.* So also says *John of Salisbury, in the Policraticus, book 6, chapter 2.* What, he asks, is a Publican <note>original: "Publicanus"; a tax farmer or collector</note>? Is he not the head of ruin and violence? What is a Publican? A plunderer without shame, a physician of destruction. Is not the tax collector more monstrous than thieves? For a thief steals while fearing; this man, however, commits his crimes with confidence. The thief fears the snares of the Law; this man considers whatever he does to be the Law. The Law deters the thief from illicit acts; this man drags the Law into the wicked profit of his own malice. *Bulenger* has more to say in this vein in *On Taxes, chapter 3.* Therefore, in the opinion of others, the leasing out of taxes is not in the interest of the subjects. *Klock, On Taxes, thesis 46, c. and see thesis 47.* And to this pertains what *Leunclavius* writes in the *Pandects of Turkish History, number 246*: The *Sultan of the Ottomans* <note>original: "Sultanus Osmanidarum"</note> sells all the Custom Houses <note>term: Telonia; offices where tolls or duties are collected</note> throughout his Empire for the highest price, for either a few or many years; and therefore, if any promise him larger sums of money in the name of taxes than they can actually deliver afterward, they are cast into prison as people who are insolvent and who wished to defraud the Sultan. This is called the "Prison of the Publicans" in Constantinople. And in the entire Kingdom of the *Ottomans*, the tax collectors are almost all Jews, a race devoted to exactions and usury far beyond all other mortals: since even the Turks or Muslims themselves, being men of a slightly more sincere conscience, do not wish to be called Publicans: just as if it were a sin for a good man to be addressed by a name joined with infamy because of the wickedness of others, even if he himself does nothing beyond his duty.

# On the Public Treasury, Chapter IV. 111

Regarding the tolls within <note>original: "Herin Zöll innen"</note>, they must acknowledge that these have been entrusted to them as a fief; they cannot rightfully claim that the tolls belong to them absolutely. Nevertheless, prescription <note>legal ownership through long-term use</note> or custom is, even here, considered equal to a grant from the Supreme Prince. *Engelhard on Customs, theorem 7, at the end.* Thus, in former times, when Emperor Louis IV heard the complaints of all the Bavarian <note>original: "Bojorum"</note> Bishops, Prelates, Nobles, Leaders, and Citizens—who lamented that villages, cities, and farmers were being emptied and plundered by the greed of tax collectors and the magnitude of customs duties—he commanded Aribo, Duke of the Austrian border, Theodomar, Archbishop of Salzburg, and others, to diligently inquire of the elders how the customs were granted in the time of Louis and Carloman. These men compelled more than forty Nobles to swear an oath. *Johannes Aventinus, Annals of the Bavarians, book 4, page 372;* see also *Heinrich Klock on Customs, theorem 22 and following.*

Furthermore, tolls are called "new" when they are introduced under the color and pretext of some new name or right. For the increasing of old tolls and the establishment of new ones are judged to walk with an equal pace <note>i.e., they are legally equivalent</note>. *Imperial Recess of the year [15]76, paragraph:* "Furthermore, we are..." <note>original: "Weiters seynd auch Wir"</note> where it says: "partly to establish new tolls by water and by land, and partly to begin raising old tolls, and this also partly under the name of Excise <note>term: Ungelt; a tax on consumption, usually drink</note>, Surcharge, Bridge-money, or Road-money, and whatever other appearances there may be." And mandates are given without a restitution clause when old tolls are increased or new ones established without the permission of the Imperial Majesty. *Chamber Court Precedents, under the word "Toll."*

Thus, in this matter, every innovation is regarded as a new customs duty: *Heinrich Klock, theorem 8, and Engelhard, theorem 7, folio 15.* Unlawful customs duties are created in two ways: by their institution and by their collection, or "flogging" <note>extortionate enforcement</note>. *Hænon, Political Disputations 5, theorem 88, folio 285.* Indeed, some believe that new customs duties are easily granted by the Emperor when the domestic treasury is narrow <note>impoverished</note>, and especially if the place for which the grant is sought is not burdened by other tolls <note>term: pedagiis; specifically tolls paid by travelers</note>. *See Mynsinger, century 5, observation 31.*

However, *Heinrich Klock on Customs, theorem 4,* requires a most just cause and urgent necessity. Thus, when a Prince is approached for the sake of this privilege, all circumstances of the business must be included in the petition—even those that might move the Emperor to a contrary opinion. If the matter so requires, commissioners should be requested to come to the actual site and diligently inspect all locations with their own eyes. If these commissioners neglect to summon the opposing party, it is consistent with the law that they have performed their assigned duty invalidly. *Klock, paragraph 16.* One might, however, not undeservedly wonder here why the Estates of the Empire <note>term: Imperii Status; the princes and authorities who had a seat in the Imperial Diet</note> are able to impose a Collection, a Land Tax <note>original: "ein Landstewr"</note>, upon their subjects...

### XVII.
Sometimes Magistrates and others who earn a public Salary in some way, are made Taxable to the Republic. Thus the Venetians, in the war against Bayezid, the Emperor of the Turks, enacted a law—beyond other exactions—that all Magistrates should return half of their stipends for one year to the Republic. *Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse, book 3, chapter 6, number 40 and following. Thus, it is also more humane to impose a certain portion of the harvests; <insert>than when one must pay a fixed amount annually regardless of hail and wind.</insert> <note>The author switches briefly to German to emphasize the practical risk of fixed taxes during bad weather.</note> Hence Appian writes in *Book 5*: "We have not imposed a tax upon you based on a fixed assessment so that we might collect a tribute free from risk; rather, we have established that you should contribute portions of your harvests, so that we may share in your misfortunes." Arnisæus also believes that all inequity regarding tributes is avoided if everyone is assessed equally; and if the contribution is made equally from the census, according to the ratio, portion, and quantity of the goods which each person possesses. <note>See Arnisæus, *Political Doctrine*, Book 1, Chapter 16, folio 390, and Book 2, Chapter 5, folio 558.</note> In this regard, Florus, in *Book 1, Chapter 6*, commends the census of Servius <note>Servius Tullius, the sixth King of Rome, credited with establishing the census to distribute tax burdens by wealth.</note>; because, when he recorded the distinctions of estates in the ledgers, he commanded fixed tributes from individuals: whereas previously everyone contributed equally. Hence Diocletian and Maximian <note>Roman Emperors</note> in *Law 3 of the Code on Annual and Tribute Declarations* forbid anyone to be burdened beyond the measure of the things they possess. One person, or one part—for instance the Commoners, a City, or a certain Province—ought not to be burdened above the rest; but everyone, Nobles and ignobles, Rich and poor, ought to be burdened equally according to the measure of their means: if the benefit is to be common, the burden should also be common. <margin>Maullius, *On Homage*, Chapter 9, number 128, etc.; and the things I shall say below in number 20, verse 1, where I deal with immunity, pertain to this.</margin>

...they have gathered the greatest force, it is not right for them to be immune from **Tributes** <note>Latin: *Tributis*; general taxes or levies paid to the state</note>; provided that this is done moderately against the poor, or even below moderation, lest war seem to be declared against good skills and industry. Likewise, slaves younger than twenty years, who since the last five-year period had been sold for ten thousand pieces of copper or more; so that they might be valued at ten times more than what they were worth. To that end, and so that contributions may be imposed equally, **Valuation** <note>Latin: *Adæratio*; the process of converting goods or services into a monetary value for tax purposes</note> was invented, which is also a necessary requirement of a contribution. This contribution is also called "by copper and scale" <note>original: *per æs & libram*; a Roman legal term referring to formal transactions of weight and balance, here meaning taxation according to wealth</note>. Lipsius discusses the fairness of this tribute in *Wonders of Rome*, book 2, chapter 3; he considers it almost unjust if it is imposed uniformly upon all heads. Indeed, before King Servius, it was the custom for tribute to be conferred upon heads: so much so, that when the King needed money, the poor were pressed by the burden equally with the rich. Tarquin likewise brought back the ancient institution and exacted ten denarii from the head of each person, as the same author relates in that place; this institution destroyed many among the common people. Truly, Dionysius deals with the poll tax of the Romans and when the tribute was instituted at greater length in that same place. There was another "provisioning poll tax" <note>original: *annonaria capitatio*</note> imposed on landowners according to the number of acres and the "heads" <note>referring to laborers or livestock</note> by which they are cultivated and plowed: Law 1 of the Theodosian Code on imposing lucrative taxes, which seems to almost coincide with the "acreage tax" <note>original: *jugatio*</note>. See also another method of poll tax, taking account of income, in Froissart, volume 1, chapter 155. However, a tax is considered more common and more equitable if it is commanded "by copper and scale," or according to the capacity of one's inheritance, rather than those imposed by "smokes" <note>hearths</note>, or houses, or even that which is imposed upon the head. The authorities can compel the wealthy to contribute. Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), a leading Renaissance humanist</note> rightly advises in *The Education of a Christian Prince* that if necessity demands that something be exacted from the People, then it is the duty of good Princes to act in such a way that the smallest possible burden falls upon the weak. For it is perhaps expedient to call the wealthy to frugality. But to drive the poor to hunger and the noose is both inhuman and unsafe. Indeed, the wealthier Subjects can be compelled to pay on behalf of the poor. <note>original: "pro pauperibus solvant"</note> *Sebastian Medices, final consultation, Volume 3, among the Illustrious Jurists, 1603 Frankfurt edition in quarto.* It also seems advisable that when the Subjects of Vassals and other Mediators are taxed, that contribution should be exacted immediately by the Lord of the territory himself, and not by the Nobles. For unless this is done, the Collectors often perceive more profit from the exaction than they themselves pass on. *Johannes Althusius, Politics, under number 10.* <note>Althusius was a legal scholar known for his theories on federalism and popular sovereignty.</note>

A most equitable Law was that which the Venetians once decreed to sustain the expenses of the war waged with Emperor Maximilian: that all tenants should bring into the treasury a fair portion of the income derived from the leasing of houses; with the exception of those who, having been driven from their homes by the enemies of the Republic in this war, had betaken themselves to the City; and those whose income did not exceed a tenth part of an ounce. <note>original: "decimam unciæ partem"</note> *History of Venetian Affairs, book 12, page 503.* Among the Romans also, the poor were exempt from the taxes that used to be paid under the Kings: they were [not] compelled to contribute Tribute for war subsidies; it was thought sufficient if the poorer citizens raised children and offered their bodies to danger for the safety of the Republic. *Bulenger, chapter 11.* Also in the past, those in Rome who were the thinnest and poorest, and did not report more than one thousand five hundred copper coins in the Census, were called *Proletarians* <term>Proletarii: those whose only contribution to the state was their offspring (proles)</term>; while those who were assessed with no money, or very little, were called *the head-counted*. <term>Capite censiti: citizens ranked by their physical presence rather than property</term> *Aulus Gellius, book 16, chapter 10.*

### On the Public Treasury, Chapter IV.

Even a tax is more easily borne when it is implemented gradually and in parts, at distinct and different times: *see the penultimate law of the Code on the collection of patrimonial estates, book 11* <note>original: "l. penult. Cod. d. collat. fundor. patrimonial. lib. II." — likely referring to the Justinian Code</note>, a practice which greatly relieves the poorer citizens. Likewise, a tax is considered light when it is demanded by kind, humane, and fair Collectors <note>term: Exactoribus — officials responsible for enforcing the payment of taxes</note>. *According to law 33 on interest; Althusius, Politics 11 at the end; Keckermann, book 3, chapter 1, page 334; see also Caspar Klock on contributions, thesis 62.* And finally, that Tax <note>term: Collecta — a general contribution or assessment levied on the people</note> is borne with a fairer mind from which no one is exempt. *Tholosanus, book 3 on the Republic, last number at the end; Keckermann, practical disputation 34, question 11; Chokier, aphorism 2, chapter 10, number 6, page 90.* It is both just and equitable that no one—neither a private man nor a People—be immune; since the utility of those things which are spent returns equally to all. *Dionysius, book 52; Cicero, On Duties, book 2.* Where there is inequality, there malice and envy creep in: so much so that Subjects measure the advantages of others with the same pain as they measure their own injuries:
