Often the extraction is less hated than the extractor. *Boccalini, report 2, page 34.* This pertains to what I said above in this chapter, number 16, verse 1, regarding the hatred toward Tax-Farmers <note>term: Publicanorum — private contractors who collected taxes for the state, often notorious for extortion</note>. Thus, the hatred under which the Tax-Farmers labored was increased by the fact that they mostly employed base men in their service, through whom they exacted public monies; these men acted more harshly with the poor and a little more mildly with the rich. *Bulenger, chapter 3.* Bodin relates somewhere that he was present at the Assembly among the Tectosages <note>note: A Celtic people of Gallia Narbonensis, centered around Toulouse</note> in the year 1556, in which a petition was made to Henry II, King of France, to remove those leeches and plunderers of the Treasury from that Province. For they promised with bound faith that they would pay the Taxes <note>term: Vectigalia — revenues or customs duties</note> by the prescribed day, and would deliver them at their own expense to whatever part of the Kingdom the Royal Majesty designated, with complete integrity and not a single penny <note>original: "obolo" — a small coin</note> missing. They argued that in this way, the King would be spared greater expenses, would receive the gold owed to him, and would exempt the Tectosages from that annoyance and misery which they sustained from so many collectors and treasury officials. The plan seemed fair and consistent with reason to the King, yet it was not admitted or approved; this was due to certain vain arguments brought forward by those whose robberies would have been harmed by such a concession, and by certain of the King's intimates who supported them.

-># Political Discourses<-

If the King had obeyed the advice of his Counselors, it is wonderful how much he would have consulted the interests of himself and the Republic. For in that way, he would have obtained <note>original: "consequu[tus]"</note> a great deal of advantage and would have removed the insatiable greed of the Tax Collectors <note>term: Quæstors; originally Roman treasury officials, here referring to any state financial officers</note>. The wiser men have always <note>original: "Sem[per]"</note> judged that excessive rigor in demanding <note>original: "exigen[dis]"</note> public payments has something of injustice about it. *Ayrault, On Adjudicated Matters, book 2, title 11, chapter 4.* The highest Law is the highest injury <note>note: A famous legal maxim (Summum Jus summa injuria) suggesting that law applied without mercy becomes injustice</note>: what of that matter which, for no other reason, is law derived from injury, than because it consists of necessity? Of this kind are Tributes, which if they are demanded too harshly, if with bitter and stubborn investigation: where is there not finally an injury? Or, just as *Verres* <note>note: Gaius Verres, a Roman magistrate infamous for his corruption and tyranny in Sicily</note> used to oppose the name of a "good General" against charges of greed: is it worth the effort to object to the poverty of the treasury as an excuse for extreme persecution? And yet the Treasury ought not to abound on the condition that while the Republic grows in money, it fails in the loyalty and goodwill of its citizens and allies. For this reason at Rome, it was resolved that *Fabius*, the Pro-praetor in Spain, should be rebuked in the Senate; he had applied such great diligence to demanding grain from the allies that he alone had brought a greater supply into the City than many Praetors had brought together. For it is necessary that a great injury be inflicted when neither property nor money is settled except from the unwilling, except from those caught unaware, or except by holding an auction. Therefore, also at the persuasion of *C. Gracchus*, Tribune of the people, it was decreed that this commanded grain should be sold publicly, and the money restored to the allies. What kind of Tax Collector one ought to be, the same *Cicero* shows by his own example in the Oration for *Plancius*: courteous to businessmen, just to merchants, generous to townsmen, abstinent toward allies, and most diligent in every duty. But truly, the Prince will easily heal the frauds and deceptions of the collectors if he cuts back their number. For if the People ought to pay twenty, on account of costs and expenses 40 or 60 will be demanded: and not without the greatest tears and complaints of many. *Chokier, book 2, chapter 10, page 96.* *I know well,* says *Pierre Matthieu* <note>note: A French historian and advisor to Henry IV</note>, *in the history of the recent troubles, page 88, that there is no crown <note>term: escu/écu; a gold or silver coin</note> leaving the hand of the peasant which is worth a teston <note>term: a coin of lesser value</note> by the time it enters the King's coffers: so much is it gnawed away by the many hands through which it passes.*

# On the Public Treasury, Chapter IV

It is not at all surprising why Title 25 of Book 10 of the Code <note>The *Codex Justinianus*, a fundamental work of Roman law</note> is inscribed: *concerning immunity to be granted to no one*. Citizens hate those among them who are exempt. A benefit given to a few becomes an injury to the Common People. There ought to be an equal inspection of all persons in public functions, lest while the expenses of some are lightened, the accounts of others are burdened. *Guillaume Fornerius, Selected Works, book 1, chapter 20; Peregrinus, On the Law of the Fisc, book 6, title 5, number 18; Sixtinus, On Regalian Rights, book 2, chapter 6, number 98, etc.* Hence some believe that the Prince cannot grant anyone immunity from ordinary collections <note>term: *collectis* — direct taxes or levies gathered for the state</note>: *Ægidius Thomatus, Treatise on Offices, section: Nobility through investiture, number 17 and following, folio 647, etc.* Others concede this only if the Prince wishes to take the tax remitted to someone out of his own Treasury, rather than thrusting the burden onto other subjects. *Following Cacheranus, Rolandus a Valle, and others; Bocer, chapter 11, number 5.* For immunity is most unjust if it tends toward the prejudice of the poorer classes. *Theodorus Reinkingk, Treatise on Secular Government, book 1, class 3, chapter 12, number 64, etc.; see also Moditius, section: plebiscite, questions 17 through 22; Gilkenius on the Authentic "Quas Actiones," chapter 11 of the Code on the Most Holy Churches, where they treat immunity at length.* Salvian <note>Salvian of Marseille, a 5th-century Christian writer who critiqued social injustice</note> writes gravely in *book 4, folio 104*:

> Behold the remedies formerly given to several Cities; what else did they achieve but to render all the rich immune, while piling up the tributes of the wretched? From this we perceive that nothing can be more wicked than the rich, who destroy the poor with their own "remedies"; and nothing more unhappy than the Poor, whom even those things given as a remedy for all, actually kill.

And the same author in *book 5*:

> It is all the more unworthy and deserving of punishment that not everyone sustains the burden of all; rather, the tributes of the rich oppress the poor little men, and the weaker carry the bundles of the stronger. What I am about to say is much more: the Rich themselves sometimes create the tax additions for which the Poor pay. The powerful decree what the Poor must pay; the favor of the Rich decrees what shall ruin the multitude of the wretched. For they themselves feel nothing of what they decree.

*And other things which can be read there; see also Bulenger, chapter 3.* Aeneas Piccolomini <note>Pope Pius II</note> reports in his *Commentaries, chapter 151*, that among the Florentines in the time of Cosimo de' Medici, civil wars arose because of the exactions of money, which pressed upon the poorer citizens more than the wealthy; and by the counsel and command of Cosimo, everyone reported their resources for the census <note>term: *censum* — an assessment of property for taxation</note>: and by that deed, it was brought about that equality was thereafter preserved everywhere. Bodin also has much against irrational immunity, *in the said chapter 2, book 6 of The Republic, number 660; Servin, volume 1, plea 8, folio 390.* And concerning the granting and prescription of immunity, Maulius has more in his treatise on Ho—

# Political Discourses

*See the works of Homag, chapter 9, number 69; and Bocer on collections, chapter 11; Winceler, observation 17; and Klock, thesis 26; Engelhard, thesis 14. Regarding exemption, Molina also treats this in dispute 673.* Nobles were long ago made immune from collections, taxes, and other burdens in almost all places. *See Waremund, chapter 4, number 66; Bocer on collections, chapter 11, number 32; Winceler, observation 14; Klock on taxes, thesis 31.* However, Maullius disputes this in *chapter 9, number 67*, where he says it is especially wrong for those goods which Nobles buy from subjects <note>Commoners or peasants</note> to be possessed freely by the Nobles; he argues that in this way, the burdens of the other subjects are increased against equity. The Equestrian Order <note>The knightly or noble class</note> acquired this immunity because in the past, they alone bore the burdens of war; no one performed military service except the Nobles. And so it is decreed in the **Laws of the Swedes**, *book 2, chapter 10*: <note>original Latin: "Quicunque vult habere suas possessiones..."</note> **"Whoever wishes to have his possessions and estates free from the payment of tribute, whether he be a knight or a soldier, with no one excepted; he is bound to have a horse of the value of 40 marks, and preferably better rather than worse, a saddle fit for the use of arms, a spear, and armor fit for the remaining parts of the body, with nothing lacking by which one can defend oneself. If a taxpayer desires to become free, then let him appear as prescribed, equipped with horse and arms; so that those who are to perform the inspection on behalf of the King may inspect the person and his reputation, as well as the horse, arms, and the estates for the maintenance of his status. All those free from tribute are bound to present themselves when the inspection of arms occurs, whether knight or soldier, and personally put on the armor and sit upon their own horse, provided with horse and arms as expressed above, etc."**

And for this reason, the Nobles of Portugal replied to King Sebastian (as noted in *Conestaggio, book 1, page 43*) that it was not honorable that they, whose ancestors had helped the Kings in acquiring the Kingdom, should be subject to the assessments and tributes which are collected for war. Now, however, the burden of waging war has fallen from the Nobles to the common people, yet the burdens do not cease, but increase daily.

The Learned <note>Scholars and academics</note> also enjoy this liberty in part, *see Heigius, part 1, question 17, number 18, etc.* But these are those who are exiles for the love of knowledge and despisers of wealth: not those who scrape together great riches. Truly learned men are always poor. *Richter, Ecclesiastical Axioms 237; Boccalini, report 45 and 2, report 9.* **"Because they do not know how to lie, nor deceive, nor practice usury, and much less despoil their neighbor."** *Guicciardini, book 1 of "Hours of Recreation," title: "Why money accompanies the wicked rather than the good."* The Clergy also have a privilege here...

# Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter IV.

<margin>Q 2</margin>
<meta>catchword: CHAPTER</meta>

<note>The author is discussing whether clergy or certain classes should be taxed.</note> They hold this position: there is an extensive dispute as to whether and when they can be collected from. This is debated by Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse in *The Republic*, book 3, chapter 7; Molina in *On Justice and Law*, dispute 672; Winckler in *Decisions on Collections*, decision 8; Waremundus in *On Subsidies*, chapter 12; Maullius, chapter 9, number 52, and others. But such exemptions were earned by their poverty and the purity of the primitive Church. Let us therefore conclude with Justinian <note>Byzantine Emperor and legal reformer</note> in his *Novels* 43, section 3: "If taxes are distributed in small amounts and equally among everyone, not only will the amount paid be very little, but the contribution will also be more moderate, light, tolerable, and easy to bear, the more people it is collected from."

To this end, there were formerly "equalizers" and "inspectors" who would amend the records after inspecting and balancing the estates against one another; thus, those who had been assigned too heavy a burden were relieved, and those who had been assessed too lightly were increased. <note>Citing the Code of Justinian, books 10 and 11, regarding censors and tributes.</note> See also Bulenger, chapter 11; Wesenbeck, counsel 103; Busius, *Subtleties*, book 3, chapter 3; and Caspar Klock, *On Contributions*, thesis 51.

Furthermore, people should be freed from the burden of payment if their assets are diminished. Salvian <note>A 5th-century Christian writer</note> complains in his fifth book that this was not done in his own age: "Many of the poor and wretched," he says, "having been despoiled of their small belongings and driven from their little fields, still suffer the taxes of the things they have lost, even though the property is gone." Taxes and other burdens should also be reduced or waived due to infertility of the land (see Bulenger, chapter 14, and as I have mentioned elsewhere above) or if the taxpayer's inheritance is diminished by some other misfortune. Caspar Klock, *On Contributions*, thesis 53. Regarding the reasons for the moderation of collections—**concerning the proceedings for reduction** <note>original: "von den Ringerungs Handlungen"</note>—see Lord Bocer, *On Collections*, chapter 12, number 6, etc.

3. Finally, I add this: in cases of extreme necessity, all <term>immunities</term> <note>Exemptions from taxes or public service</note> cease to apply. Klock, thesis 27. Hence, even a Count who is invested with his own county is not immune from Imperial collections, even if his title is **free, jurisdictional, and without tax.** <note>original: "frey/ gerihiglich/ vnd ohne Steuer"</note> Bocer, book 2, *On Collections*, at the end. Nor is any privileged estate considered exempt from the "Turkish taxes" <note>Special taxes raised by the Holy Roman Empire to fund wars against the Ottoman Empire</note>. See the Imperial Recess **at Speyer in the year 1544, sections "Namely shall," "That also such help," and "And in particular," etc.** <note>original: "zu Speyr d. A. 1544. §. Nämlich sollen... §. Das auch solche Hilff... & §. Vnd insonderheit"</note> Mynsinger, decade 15, Response 1, numbers 9, 10, and 14. Generally, immunity is not extended to burdens imposed for a public war or other evident necessity. Mynsinger, observation 70. Pierre Ayrault, in *Judged Matters*, book 10, title 14, supports with several precedents the rule that immunities cease when the matter concerns "altars and hearths" <note>original: "pro aris atque focis" — a Latin idiom meaning the defense of one's home and most sacred values</note>, and that words regarding the excuse from duties must be interpreted strictly.

## CHAPTER V.

Now it is pleasing to wander into the fields of Law <note>original: "campos Juridicos"</note>, and to examine one or two questions from the subject of tax collections <note>original: "collectarum"; referring to the gathering of public funds or tributes</note>. And first, a most controversial question presents itself to us here: Whether a Prince can burden the subjects of his Vassal, who live within a Feudal territory, with Provincial taxes? *James of St. George in his treatise on homages, no. 36* as well as *Chasseneuz, in the Customs of Burgundy, rubric 1, section 4, verse on High Justice* seem to deny this. *Rudinger, Feudal Controversies 2, chapter 28, throughout; and Thomatus, on tax collections, folio 398, number 8* feel otherwise. I would separate Feudal Estates which belong to the Prince's Territory from those which are not simultaneously bound to the Prince by the Right of Sovereignty <note>original: "Jure Superioritatis"; the legal standing of a supreme ruler over a territory</note>. *See also Mr. Bocer, on collections 4, no. 22.*

II. But can the Prince demand from the Vassal himself those extraordinary contributions publicly decreed by the Emperor and the States of the Empire; or even those which we commonly call *Land-taxes* <note>original: "Landstewren"; a German term for territorial taxes paid to a sovereign</note>? So thinks *Hartman Pistor, question 46, number 33; Modestinus Pistoris, counsel 5, no. 5; and Gylhausen, in the tree of civil judgment, part 1, on Jurisdiction, chapter 1, no. 4; Heigius, 1, question 18, number 23, and many following.* Let there be added also *James of St. George, treatise on homages, gloss 1, number 36; Wesenbeck, treatise on feuds, chapter 10, number 18.* But the opinion of those who disagree is more pleasing to our mind. *Clarus, section on feuds, question 29, number 2; Knichen, on invested pacts 2, chapter 5, number 26; Schrader on feuds, part 10, section 5, no. 115; and Rosenthal, chapter 5, conclusion 78, number 2; and Cothman, counsel 11, number 32; Caspar Klock in the Basel disputation on collections, thesis 37; Mynsinger, decade 15, Response 1; Bocer, said chapter 4, number 12; and Winceler, observation 23.* This opinion is certainly confirmed by evident reason; for since the Vassal is obligated to perform personal services <note>original: "servitia personalia"; the traditional military or courtly duties owed by a knight to his lord</note> for his Lord, he cannot be further burdened with taxes or other weights

III. Collections, which we call <term>Landsteuren</term> <note>Provincial or territorial taxes</note>, are partly personal and partly patrimonial, and thus are mixed burdens; they are imposed on persons principally on account of things and possessions, and in proportion to them: and they do not have a fixed and determined payment; but are varied according to the will of the Superior, due to an emerging necessity. *Gail, book 2, observation 52, number 9 and following; Heigius, part 1, question 17, number 28, etc.; Althusius, Politics, chapter 13, from the beginning.* Therefore, they can hardly be imposed upon Foreigners <note>original: "Forensibus," meaning those residing outside the jurisdiction</note> and non-Subjects: even if they possess immovable property in that place where the Collection is to be paid. *Natta, counsel 160, number 7; Gravæus, 2nd conclusion 52, number 13, etc.; Rosenthal, On Fiefs, chapter 5, conclusion 80; Maullius, On Homage 9, number 40, etc.; Bocer, On Collections, chapter 9, number 8 and following.* Indeed, it is not even free for the Lord of the territory to impose whatever Collection he wishes—namely on the soil or the possession—such that Foreigners would also be bound to pay it. *Following Castro; Mynsinger, decade 7, Response 64, number 50; Bocer, in the cited chapter, number 10, etc.; through the Law "ne in potestate" in the Digest on Arbitrations, and law 2, paragraph "sed si" in the Digest on Judgments.*

In certain cases, however, Foreigners can be taxed in that place for goods situated within the territory: for instance, for the repair of Bridges, or for the guarding and security of the place; provided, of course, that such guarding and repair also concerns the utility of the possessions themselves. *Gail, Rosenthal, and Gravæus in the places cited above.* Thus, a Collection which is imposed for the marriage of the Lord's daughter can only be imposed on Subjects: but that which is required because of an incursion of enemies—because it immediately concerns the benefit of the soil—binds Foreigners as well. Hence, the effort of those Estates is not to be disapproved of, who strive to make the rents and goods of outsiders liable to impositions in their own way.

# On the Public Treasury, Chapter V.

### QUESTION I.

1. Regarding the first of the questions now proposed, it might indeed be argued with some plausibility: Considering that the Lords Margraves <note>original: "MGraffen"</note> of B. specified certain particular cases in the feudal grant <term>feudal grant (concessione feudali): the legal document by which a lord grants land or rights to a vassal</term> in which they reserved the Princely High Sovereignty for their Princely Graces—namely: Escort Rights <term>Escort Rights (Glait/Geleit): the right to provide armed protection to travelers for a fee</term>, Hunting Rights <term>Hunting Rights (Wildtbann): the exclusive right to hunt high game</term>, High Justice <term>High Justice (Hohegericht): jurisdiction over capital crimes punishable by death</term>, Appeals, and whatever belongs to those aforementioned acts (that is, to the acts specifically named above)—that therefore, His Princely Grace has completely waived all other rights flowing from the High Territorial Sovereignty and those which are considered properly annexed to the superiority or territorial jurisdiction. For indeed, the inclusion of one is the exclusion of all others <note>original Latin: "unius inclusio, sit exclusio omnium cæterorum"</note>, according to the law *eum prætor* in the Digest on judgments, and the notes therein by Schrader, counsel 1, number 314, and counsel 14, number 19.

2. Furthermore, regarding the fact that in this reservation clause <note>original: "clausula reservatoria"</note>, mention is made at the very beginning of the Princely High Sovereignty—namely, that the same shall be reserved to the feudal lord—it might be answered: that such generality is limited and restricted by the immediately following specification of certain acts pertaining to the sublime right of the territory. This is because a preceding general clause is restricted to the things specified, as our Doctors of Law deduce from Law 3 of the Code on transactions. In this manner, the late Doctor R. G. of blessed memory—for the reasons just cited—concludes in the counsel provided to us that the High Territorial Sovereignty is reserved to the Lords Margraves only in these specifically determined cases.

3. Notwithstanding this, however, and other reasons which we have considered with due diligence: we hold it as certain that, in general and without distinction, the High Princely Sovereignty in all cases where a Territorial Prince is entitled by law and equity to exercise the same, is reserved to the aforementioned feudal lord; and that His Princely Grace remains entirely free to exercise such sovereignty (yet without prejudice to those rights specifically given to the noble vassals <note>original: "Vasallis"</note> in this our case by virtue of the investiture <term>investiture (investituræ): the formal ceremony or document transferring a fief to a vassal</term>).

4. For firstly, the Lords Margraves reserved to themselves the Princely High Sovereignty in express words and generally. Which generality of words must surely be understood generally.

And this will have even more place in the matter of Jurisdiction; for the reason that jurisdiction regards a universality which is one in itself, even though it may be exercised in many ways. Ludovicus Romanus, consultation 271, number 4, and consultation 262, number 1, volume 2. Because things omitted can be supplied by interpretation from the many things expressed. <note>Citing various legal doctors and Alciatus on the interpretation of omitted qualities in law.</note>

<margin>9.</margin> Therefore, and because these rights of superiority <note>original: "Jura superioritatis"; the supreme legal authority held by a sovereign</note> do not belong to the vassal: they must—not only by virtue of the reservation clause, but also by the law itself—remain and reside at all times with the Lord of the fief <note>original: "Domino feudi"</note>, as the one to whom the territory still belongs and to whom those rights undoubtedly pertained before the granting of the fief.

Reichs-Ritterschafft</term>, and furthermore, "Landed Residency" <term>Landsässerey</term> refers only to those who are settled, housed, and established under a Prince's authority. *Indeed, because he who possesses a plot of land or some fief in a certain place cannot be said to be an inhabitant of that place, nor be considered to have a domicile in that place: <note>Latin: "l. libertus. 17. §. sola. 5. ff. ad municip. l. cùm neque. Cod. de incol. lib. 10."</note> and by reason of the possession of goods alone, one cannot rightfully be called a Subject. <note>Latin: "per l. rescripto. 6. §. ult. ff. de muner. & honor."</note> Castrens. book 2. consultation 89. Matthaeus de Afflictis in chapter 1, "In what manner a vassal owes an oath." Rolandus a Valle, counsel 1, volume 3, number 30. See also Gail in the treatise On Arrests, chapter 61, number 8. And a Vassal, insofar as he is a Vassal—even if he holds feudal property situated in the territory of a Prince but does not have a domicile in the same place—is not subjected to the ordinary jurisdiction of the Prince: as Paurmeister shows with many examples in On Jurisdiction, book 2, chapter 8, number 42. Rosenthal, On Fiefs, chapter 5, conclusion 78, numbers 5 and 6. And this is proved by many points from the proceedings between the Duke of Bavaria and the Count of Ortenburg held in the Imperial Chamber Court, as Wehner demonstrates in the place cited above.*

17. Furthermore, the custom—which originates in Bavaria and other places—that no one may possess or hold a noble estate without the burdensome quality of subjection <note>original: "sine onerosâ qualitate subjectionis"</note> (that is, Landed Residency), is entirely unknown in the Land of S. *Which is also supported by the traditions of Matthias Stephani, On Jurisdiction, part 1, chapter 7, section 2, number 128.*

18. According to all of this, we hold entirely that the well-mentioned K. von D. are by no means to be considered Landed Residents <term>Landsässen</term> of the Margraviate, nor are they obligated to the Lord Margrave regarding their persons in any way other than as **Vassals** <note>original: "Vasalli"</note>. They are certainly exempted from the aforementioned **burdens of personal subjection**, such as being considered a member of the Estates of the Margraviate, being required to seek or give justice there, performing hereditary or territorial homage, and the like. *For a Vassal and a Subject differ in their entire nature.* <note>original: "Etenim Vasallus & Subditus, toto genere differunt."</note> *Rosenthal, chapter 5, conclusion 75. 26. A territorial Prince <note>original: *Lands-Fürst*</note> is permitted to garrison the fortresses located within his land with soldiers. *Petra, on the Rights of Princes, question 12, number 402; Raudensis, response 28, number 30, book 1.*

27. No less important is the "right of opening" <note>The *ius aperturae*, a feudal right allowing a lord access to a vassal's castle</note>—namely, that such cities and fortresses must be open to a Prince against anyone whomsoever for his wars and necessities, and no one may be detained therein against his will. *Following Wesembecius and others, Johann Rudinger, century 3, observation 95.* Which species of supreme jurisdiction the Lord of the fief, in this our case, reserved for himself in the letters of investiture with the most ample words, and which necessarily imply sovereignty <note>original: *superioritatem*</note>.

28. To this must also be reckoned the security of the public roads, which pertains specifically to the Prince. *Alciatus on the law "how much," 157, after number 9, on the significance of words.* Likewise, the granting of safe conduct, whether in person or in writing, upon the country highways: which is a part of the jurisdiction or territory; and belongs to the Lord of the territory by ordinary right. *Gail, book 2, observation 64, number 3. From Alexander and Schürpf, Wesembecius, counsel 33, numbers 3 and 10.* And in this case, it is also expressly reserved to the Lord of the fief.

29. But truly, as pertains to those acts by which the right of sovereignty or territory is exercised in peace: these concern either the sanctioning of laws and political ordinances, or the collection of the fruits <note>revenue or benefits</note> of this supreme jurisdiction.

30. Thus, the places situated under a Prince’s territorial authority must observe the common provincial laws <note>original: *Landrecht*</note> and territorial ordinances of that same territory. *From Gail, Knichen, on the right of sovereignty, chapter 3, number 276.* For our Doctors <note>legal scholars</note> maintain that the right of decreeing and ordaining, or the power of making laws, pertains to the "pure" or—as Bartolus calls it—the "greatest" command <note>original: *merum... maximum Imperium*, referring to the highest level of judicial and legislative power</note>. *Menochius, on retaining possession, remedy 3, number 585; Rolandus a Valle, counsel 42, beginning "the donation having been seen," number 12, volume 2; Cephalus, counsel 458, "most serene," numbers 44 and 48; Natta, counsel 672, beginning "turning," number 7; Gylman in the Symphorema, part 1, title 2, on counterclaims, volume 1, in the case of Mainz against the City of Erfurt, number 129; Bidembach in Noble Questions, 7, toward "pure command."*

31. So can a territorial Prince hold all those settled under his authority to the use of uniform measures and weights. Because no one can establish a norm or standard unless fortified by jurisdiction; he who is an inferior must take the form and weight from the archetype <note>the original standard</note>.

# Political Discourse

The Prince is bound to select [standard measures]. <note>This refers to the legal principle that the sovereign sets the standards for weights and measures.</note> This is argued in the Code regarding tax collectors and book 10. 32. Although it is commonly held that "Forestry Authority" <note>original: "Forstliche Obrigkeit"</note>—as an integral whole—comprises both the forestry right and the hunting right; and that these two together, but not separately, constitute the Forestry Jurisdiction: as Wehner proves from Meichsner, Friedrich Mindanus, and others under the words "Forestry Right / Forest / Hunting Right." This is supported by Thomas Michael, discourse on jurisdiction, thesis 51; and agreed upon by Demba, question 15; and Rudinger, century 2, observation 42. Thus, it might be argued that the Lords Margraves intended to reserve for themselves only the hunting right <note>original: "Bannum ferinum"</note> and not the forestry right and the entire Forestry Authority. <margin>The text here is partially lost in the binding.</margin>

33. However, it would seem in every way that the Lords Margraves are to seek full Forestry Authority over these estates. For this difference is observed between the hunting right and the forestry right or Forestry Authority, where by ordinary law, all-encompassing jurisdiction belongs to the lord of the territory. Knichen, book 2 on investiture pacts, chapter 2, number 10. Regarding this, we can conclude nothing specific at this time, as it depends more on what has been customary and traditional in each place from of old; rather than what is disputed by legal scholars; and therefore Custom <note>original: "Consuetudo"</note> is what usually rules in such servitudes <term>servitutibus: legal obligations or burdens on a property for the benefit of another</term>, as has been handed down in these terms by Schurff, counsel 1, "when huntings," number 46, century 3; and Gail, book 2, observation 68, numbers 1 and 2. <margin>Text lost in binding.</margin>

34. However, it has now—by the custom of almost all places and our own modern practices—come to this: that both pure and mixed command are considered to be contained within the single term "Jurisdiction." Thus, he who has the greatest jurisdiction, that is, the High Authority or High Court... <margin>Text lost in binding.</margin>

# Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter V.

[The judge] should possess both pure and mixed authority <note>original: "merum & mixtum Imperium." In Roman law, "merum" (pure) referred to the power of the sword/capital punishment, while "mixtum" (mixed) referred to civil administration.</note>. Thus, likewise in our modern customs, the lower jurisdiction—that is, the **lower authority** or **lower court**—not only encompasses those matters which are commonly referred to as simple jurisdiction, but also contains several of those which belong to mixed authority. *Speckhan, century 1, question 90; Coler, on Procedure, part 2, chapter 1, number 105; Modestinus Pistor, on Illustrious Questions, 61, number 3; Schneidewin, on Fiefs, part 2, number 85; Matthias Stephanus, book 1, on Jurisdiction, chapter 3, number 70 and following; Andreas Knich, on the Privileges of the Duke of Saxony, page 124; Daniel Moller, book 4, Semestria, chapter 45, number 1; Wehner, under the terms "Court" and "High Court."* Consequently, the difference between pure and mixed authority seems to be almost abolished in our Republic today.

35. Now, when the Lords Margraves <note>The sovereign rulers of the territory.</note> have specifically reserved for themselves the **High Court**—or pure authority—and have granted or loaned in fief to the noble **Vassals** only the **lower court** (as indicated in question 7, though still retaining the right to hear appeals): Therefore, the Margraves have the right to adjudicate all **misdeeds and crimes** on these feudal lands that concern **skin and hair, body and life** <note>A legal idiom for corporal and capital punishment.</note>. *For he who has superior jurisdiction*—the **High and Neck-Court** <note>original: "Ober- und Halsgericht." The power to sentence a defendant to beheading or other capital penalties.</note>—*possesses the power of the sword* <note>original: "potestatem gladii."</note>, *and thus the right to punish wicked men; so that he can investigate and judge all crimes, both public and private; such as the crime of Homicide, Adultery, Forgery, Incest, Debauchery, Arson, Theft, etc. Coler, on Executive Procedure, part 2, chapter 1, number 124; Schneidewin, in the Epitome of Fiefs, part 2, number 85; Rudinger, century 2, observation 70, number 2. Many other such crimes and offenses, which are claimed by pure authority, are enumerated individually by Chasseneuz in the Customs of Burgundy, rubric 1, verse* "And the rights of these," *etc., as well as by Matthias Wehner under the terms* **Zent** <note>A regional administrative and judicial district.</note> and **Fraiß** <note>A term for high criminal jurisdiction or the terror of the law.</note>. From this it follows that even the investigation of an **atrocious physical injury** <note>original: "injuriæ realis atrocis." A serious physical assault as opposed to a verbal insult.</note> belongs to him who holds the High Court, specifically when one desires that the offender be looked upon with a punishment by the authorities.

36. It is also held that whoever is responsible for the **lower court** may not banish anyone from a town or village, or confine them therein. *Law "nulli," joined with the gloss on the word "faculty," Code on the Sentences and Interlocutories of all Judges; Alexander de Imola on the law "magistratibus," Digest on Jurisdiction; Schneidewin on Fiefs, chapter 2, number 89; Gylman, Symphorema, Volume 2, part 3, title 10, vote 2, folio 235.* Of a similar condition is the condemnation to the **mines** <note>original: "metalla." A form of forced labor.</note>, the deprivation of liberty, etc. *Bolognetus on the law "Imperium," Digest on Jurisdiction, numbers 39 and 71; there also Cagnolus, number 204 and following.*

37. Likewise, condemnation to life imprisonment <note>original: "ad perpetuos carceres"</note>—*Bologn. num. 1; Cagnol. num. 218, 220, 221*—and indeed even imprisonment for a set time for the purpose of punishing a specific crime, is a matter of Pure Authority <term>Imperium Merum: the highest level of legal power, including the right to inflict capital punishment or severe physical penalties</term>. *Bologn. num. 1; Caccialup. num. 29; Valasc. num. 167.*

38. Similarly, only he who possesses Pure Authority may brand a criminal, or punish them with rods or whips <note>original: "virgis aut flagellis castigare"</note>, **to beat with rods** <note>original German: "mit Rutten aufhawen"</note>, or cut off the ears. *Jacob. de S. Georg. in his Invest. gl. cum mero & mixto num. 4; Andr. Knichen. in the treatise on sublime and royal territorial rights num. 391; Emer. à Rosb. in civil practice cap. 2. num. 9.* To this also belong the **branding iron**, the **shame-stone** <note>A heavy stone carried by offenders as a public humiliation</note>, and other such judicial compulsions. *Mynsing. response 16. num. 29; Zasius, num. 23. on the law of Authority regarding jurisdiction; Bologn. ibid. note 4. num. 43; Gylman. Vol. 2. part 3. tit. 10. fol. 236.*

39. Likewise, **imprisonment** <note>original German: "die Gefängnus"</note>, or the detention of a person in criminal cases or on account of some grave offense, is also a matter of Pure Authority. *Prosperin. in his criminal practice book 1. tit. 4. quest. 27. num. 6. & seq; Emer. à Rosb. in judicial process tit. 2. num. 13; Hartm. practical observations tit. 50. obs. 4.*

40. Likewise, the **power to apply the criminal interrogation or torture** <note>original German: "Peinliche Frag oder Folterung"</note>. *Emeric. à Rosb. tit. 2. num. 14. in civil practice; Gail. book 2. on public peace num. 16; Bidemb. quest. 7. fol. 46.*

41. Only those enjoying Pure Authority can take **Oaths of Renunciation** <note>original German: "Urphets-Verschreibungen"; a legal document where a released prisoner swore not to take revenge for their imprisonment</note>, sworn obligations, and testimonies of non-retaliation from offenders (specifically those who, because of the crime committed, could have been punished in body or life). *Bidemb. quest. 7. fol. 48.*

42. And the noble vassals cannot, in our opinion, claim for themselves the custody and incarceration, the banishment of criminal men, etc., or the investigation of crimes, etc., unless it has been established otherwise by long-standing custom. For although in several places in the Empire the **High Authority** <note>original German: "Hohen Obrigkeit"</note> is arranged such that one lordship has the investigation of criminal cases <note>original: "cognitio causarum criminalium"</note> while the other has the **Execution of the Sword** <note>The right to carry out the death penalty</note>, nevertheless, the **High Court** <note>original German: "Hochgericht"</note> according to common law—and especially in these lands according to the custom of the region and in the German language—comprises the whole of Pure Authority and also a great part of Mixed Authority. As Schneidewin teaches and testifies, *part 2. quest. 6. num. 85. in the feudal summary*; and likewise Bologn., following the Doctors of Law, writes on the law of Authority regarding jurisdiction, num. 10 and following: When justice is administered regarding the prosecution...

# On the Public Treasury, Chapter V.

...in criminal matters, because in such cases jurisdiction constitutes **pure authority** <note>original: *merum Imperium*; a technical term for the highest level of legal power, including the power of life and death</note>. This is confirmed by the following argument: that pure authority is a complete and integral whole, of which criminal jurisdiction is a part. Therefore, on account of that part, the whole itself is judged to be of the same nature as the part. *Law 3, section "incertum," Digest on acquiring possession; and Law "locus," with the notes there, in the same title.* That this must also be observed in feudal matters is shown by *Baldus in chapter 1, section "cum enim," column 2, on contentions between Lord and Vassal, number 2.* Since even the Jurisconsult <note>a legal expert or scholar</note> himself defines pure authority in no other way than as the **right of the sword** <note>original: *jus gladii*</note> and the power of punishing the wicked. This right, by law, is commonly thought to encompass not only capital punishment, but all more severe coercion whatsoever, and all the degrees of pure authority designated by *Bartolus*. *Law "si quid erit," on the office of the Proconsul.* To these views *Zasius* subscribes in his frequent interpretation of the law "Imperium," numbers 2, 3, 7, and 8, where he teaches: pure authority is the power of blood and public vengeance, or jurisdiction equipped with the sword; by which, for the public utility, the wicked are punished. Under the "power of the sword," one understands the power of corporal punishment, which consists of physical penalties: namely, in inflicting the penalty of natural or civil death, in driving someone into exile, in condemning them to the mines, deporting them, or interdicting them from fire and water <note>a form of banishment</note>; and it also includes pecuniary fines which are imposed because of crimes, where it is in the interest of the public utility that they be punished. *Caspar Valascus* holds the same in the same place, number 157 and the two following; as does *Sebastian Sapia*, who teaches that every criminal cause belongs to pure authority, number 17.

# Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter V.

The highest Jurisdiction is rightly called the power of establishing a ruling in either a criminal or civil matter; or, as Gaeddaeus <note>Johannes Gaeddaeus (1539–1639), a prominent German legal scholar.</note> argues in his *Disputations on Jurisdiction*, it may be defined as the power of hearing and judging any matter whatsoever. Similarly, Wesenbeck <note>Matthaeus Wesenbeck (1531–1586), a Belgian jurist influential in the Holy Roman Empire.</note> in his *Paratitla* defines Jurisdiction, taken in its general sense, as the public power of hearing legal cases. From this, Princes claim for themselves in their territories by right of Sovereignty <note>original: "Superioritatis jure"</note> not only the "Greater Regalia" <note>The highest sovereign rights, such as coining money or declaring war.</note> and "Lesser Regalia," nor only those rights expressed in the chapter *What are the regalia* in the *Books of Feuds*, but also jurisdictional rights, including "pure and mixed command" <note>original: "merum & mixtum Imperium" — the power to inflict capital punishment (pure) and the power to administer civil justice (mixed).</note>, which today are considered Regalia by accepted custom. *Thomas Michael, in his Disputations on Jurisdiction, thesis 46, following many others he cites.* This holds unless the general right of Sovereignty is restricted by an express and specific grant. *Knichen, chapter 5, On Territorial Law, number 133 and following.*

### QUESTION III.

<margin>49.</margin> The Imperial Tax <note>original: "Reichssteuer"</note>—which is the subject of the present Question—is the name given to that which is indicated or imposed upon the common Estates <note>The princes, bishops, and cities that held a seat in the Imperial Diet.</note> by the Emperor, based on the decrees of the Empire and the will and consent of the Estates, for the promotion, maintenance, and rescue of the common good, as necessity demands, and for the preservation of public utility, peace, and tranquility in the Empire. This is done with the modest requirement that they collect or demand such taxes from their subjects and subsequently deliver them to a certain designated place; however, they shall not exact anything beyond the sum designated for each in the Imperial Register <note>original: "matricula Imperii" — the official list of the Empire's members and their required financial/military contributions.</note>, nor shall they apply it to their own use. *Imperial Recesses of the years 1547 at Speyer, 1548 at Augsburg, 1557 at Regensburg, 1566 at Augsburg. Gail, book 2, observation 53. Matthaeus Wehner in Practical Observations, under the word "Taxation" (Schatzung).* Thus, the announcement of this kind of general Collection is not imposed by the Estates upon their subjects by their own right by virtue of their Regalia; rather, that sub-collection occurs more as a form of execution of the Emperor's decree. *Johann Rudinger, century 4, observation 29, following Sixtinus on Regalia, book 2, chapter 14, number 31.* And so, between this and the Provincial Collection (which will be dealt with in the resolution of the following question), there is no small discrepancy, not only regarding authority but also regarding effect. *Caspar Klock, Disputation on Contributions, Basel, thesis 9.*

# Political Discourses

The question of whether the Margraviate <note>original: "MGraffschafft"</note> has the right to demand taxes from the sub-tenants <note>term: Hindersässen (dependent tenants or residents on noble estates who were not full citizens)</note> must be considered and concluded based on the following reasons <note>original: "rationibus"</note>. First, it is notorious and known to everyone in the Empire that the Free Noble Knighthood in the Land of S. has been, for time immemorial, through well-established privileges or freedoms—both for themselves and for their subjects—altogether exempted and freed from all taxation and similar burdens. This applies especially to those collections <note>original: "Collectis"</note> which are granted and approved by the Estates of the Empire to His Imperial Majesty. *Bidembach approves this through many Recesses of the Empire, question 18 and last.* And the Free Knighthood in the Swabian, Franconian, and Rhenish Circles <note>term: Circles (administrative groupings of states within the Holy Roman Empire)</note> are not called to share in these burdens <note>original: "in partem onerum vocirt"</note>. For this very reason, and by a singular privilege <note>original: "ex singulari Privilegio"</note>, they are not drawn among the Estates of the Empire <note>term: Status Imperii (the princes and authorities who had a seat and vote in the Imperial Diet)</note> at this time, so that the aforementioned Noble Knighthood may be spared from the common Imperial burdens. *Acts of Brunswick, in folio, part 2, page 36.* Therefore, the Knighthood—who are not summoned to the Imperial Diets and do not consent to the Imperial tax—stands in a much different condition than the Estates of the Holy Roman Empire, upon whom a certain assessment <note>term: Anschlag (a fixed tax quota or valuation)</note> is imposed. For this reason, until now, His Imperial Majesty has almost always requested a "compassionate aid" <note>term: mitleidige Hülff (a voluntary contribution rather than a mandatory tax)</note> from the Knighthood in times of Imperial necessity, without any fixed assessment. This is emphasized everywhere in the Imperial Recesses <note>term: Recess (the official resolutions or minutes of an Imperial Diet)</note>, especially the Imperial Recess of the year 1500, in the section "We or the," etc.

51. Now, according to the law, it is the duty of all laudable provincial princes and authorities to protect and allow the exempted persons—especially the nobility—to remain undisturbed and unhindered in their freedoms. *As handed down by Bartolomeo Cipolla in the treatise on Military Command, regarding the cause of Nobility, number 39. "All good men," says Cicero, "always favor the Nobility: both because it is useful to the Republic that there be Noble men worthy of their ancestors; and because the memory of famous men who served the Republic well should prevail among us, even after they are dead."* <note>original Latin: "Omnes boni... pro semper Nobilitati favemus..."</note>

52. Secondly, it appears that all of this holds even more weight in the present case <note>original: "casu"</note>, because for many years—and as we shall mention—before the year 1550, no demand for this tax was ever made by the Lords Margraves. Rather, every time the laudable Knighthood, in the manner previously indicated...

For such contributions are only then delivered into the Knightly Chests when they are collected from free noble estates and from subjects subordinated to no one else. For indeed, the privileges of the Swedish nobility <note>original: "Svecica nobilitatis"</note> ought to or can be extended only to noble and free estates; but by no means to those which are mediately subject to the Empire, and immediately subject to the territory and jurisdiction of another Estate. This is the doctrine delivered by Lord Bidembach, question 1, number 7. And consequently, the contribution ought to be brought into the Chest of the Knightly Circle only from free estates that are immediately subject to the Empire. Gylman in *Summary of Supplications*, Volume 1, title 4, folio 299; and here may be referred all those things which Lord Doctor Bidembach discusses in questions 18 and 19. # On the Public Treasury, Chapter V.

It follows clearly from this that the subjects living on these aforementioned estates have nothing to do with the assessments of the Knighthood <note>The "Knighthood" refers to the local organized nobility as a political estate</note>, nor may they be taxed by them, or be compelled to pay anything into the knightly chest.

63. Thirdly, it is particularly important to note here that these fiefs, before the noble family of K. was invested or enfeoffed with them, were held within and of the territory of the Margraviate of B. Thus, the subjects living there, together with other residents of the Margraviate, were obligated to bear the assigned portion of the Imperial taxes at all times; and the total burden resting upon the entire Margraviate was thereby somewhat distributed and lessened by them. Now, it is commonly concluded by legal scholars that a Prince can in no way let a part of his land out of his hands, or dismember it, in such a way that the burdens thereby fall upon and are increased for the remaining subjects alone. <note>original Latin: "Ac quamvis Princeps verbis usus fuerit amplissimis..."</note> **And although a Prince may have used the most ample words, he is nevertheless never deemed to have abdicated from himself, or transferred to another, those powers and rights by which either the Princely Dignity or Sovereignty is diminished, or by which the common burdens are increased.** <term>This argument is handed down by Molina in his commentary on the Customs of Paris, title 1, section 1, gloss 5, on the word "the fief," number 49.</term> <term>Surdus agrees in his legal opinions, opinion 275, throughout volume 2.</term> <term>Peregrinus in "On the Rights of the Treasury," book 1, chapter on those who have fiscal rights, number 98.</term> <term>The collectors of the "Symphorema" of Imperial Chamber Court petitions, Volume 1, part 1, title 2, on counterclaims, vote 1, number 176, etc., folio 125, column 1, etc.</term> For it is chiefly considered unlawful and not permitted for a Prince to alienate his cities or subjects because, by such a separation, the burdens of the rest who remain under the alienating Prince are increased; and this tends toward the detriment of the entire Commonwealth, both because of the collections <note>taxes</note> and because of other inconveniences. <term>Pruckmann in his treatise "On Regalian Rights," section on absolute power, effect 6, folio 457, numbers 23 and 76.</term> And hence the investiture of a fief, granted by a Prince to a Nobleman, does not enjoy immunity to the prejudice of the Community as a third party; and a Nobleman cannot acquire for himself or his people immunity from a duty against public law, not even through a Privilege of the Prince. <term>Ægidius Thomatus, treatise "On Collections," folio 321, numbers 19, 35, and following, and folio 632, throughout the discourse.</term>

The question is: are they able to do so? And it seems it must be said: no. For it is not enough (says Chassanæus) that they are subject in High Justice, but it is required that they be *their* men. Because when an act is required with a specific quality, it is necessary that they be their men *and* subject in High Justice: it is not enough therefore for the quality to exist in essence, unless the act is also present. But the men of a Vassal are not called the men of the [Over]lords, but are the men of the Vassal; and the Vassal, by reason of his fief, is bound to provide services to the Lord; thus far Chassanæus.

# Political Discourses

81. If, therefore, the <term>Superiority</term> <note>Latin: *Superioritas*; the supreme territorial power</note>, together with the <term>High and Low Justice</term> <note>Latin: *merum & mixtum Imperium*; the full power of the law, including capital punishment</note>, has been reserved for the Lords of the Fief upon these estates, and it has been expressly stipulated to the vassals that they shall impose no new burdens upon the subjects at V. <note>Likely an abbreviation for a specific village or district</note>: then we can conclude nothing else from what has been deduced thus far—as well as from several reasons for decision introduced in the preceding question—than that the Lord Margrave alone should and can tax his own subjects with such extraordinary collections and provincial taxes. This is because His Princely Grace has, in the manner often indicated, reserved all High Princely Authority for himself, and the noble vassals have no such right.

82. For indeed, because the imposition of collections <note>Latin: *impositio Collectarum*; the levying of taxes</note> is, according to the common opinion of the learned doctors, among the <term>Regalia</term> <note>Latin: *Regalibus*; royal or sovereign rights belonging to the prince</note>, it is therefore said to belong to the Prince alone. This is so much the case that not even vassals, when they hold high and low justice and all-encompassing jurisdiction in a place, are able to impose a tax on their men and subjects. <note>Citing: Chapter 1, "What are Regalia," Book 2 of the Feudorum; and there Baldus on the word "extraordinary." Jacobus de Sancto Georgio in the law of investiture, gloss on "with high and low justice," number 16, and in the gloss "those indeed invested," number 75. Schurpff, century 1, counsel 59, number 26. Schneidewin on Fiefs, part 2, number 119.</note> Rudingerus embellishes this at great length in *Feudal Controversies*, book 2, chapter 28, throughout. How much more, therefore, must it be judged that the exaction of taxes is taken away from these vassals, who do not have all-encompassing jurisdiction, but only "low" jurisdiction <note>Latin: *bassam jurisdictionem*; minor legal authority over civil matters, excluding capital crimes</note>, as they say.

83. Furthermore, it strongly favors the Lord Margrave that—as the records demonstrate—he has for a long time and on various occasions requested the provincial tax from the subjects in Visch <note>Likely the name of the specific territory or family in question</note>. Such Margravial rights have been renewed and rooted in all renewals of investitures <note>The formal ceremony of granting a fief</note> under that general reservation of High Princely Authority.

84. Against this, the introduced reasons for doubt can achieve nothing. For although the "subject and vassal of a vassal" is not held to be the "subject and vassal of the Lord" <note>A reference to the feudal principle *Vassallus vassi mei non est vassallus meus* (The vassal of my vassal is not my vassal)</note>, this only takes place in view of and regarding those rights which were granted to the vassal by the Lord. However, in respect of the rights and jurisdiction reserved by the Lord for himself, the subjects of the vassal are indeed, and remain, subject to the Lord of the fief. Nor is it inconsistent that someone is, and can be, the subject of two Lords, though in different respects. <note>Citing: Everhardus in the law...</note>

And as for the saying that "the vassal of my vassal is not my vassal," this is not true if the vassal of my vassal, or the subject of my subject, is a vassal or subject by reason of a <term>fief</term><note>A landed estate held on condition of feudal service</note> or territory in respect of which he is my vassal or subject to me. This is specifically declared by Guy de la Pape, *Decision 551, number 7*; Decio on the law *Consilii*, section *socius*, number 1, *Digest on the rules of law*; Br. on the law *concerning accessions*, at the beginning, *Digest on various and temporary prescriptions*; and the same on the law *Claudius*, number 2, *Digest on who can hold a pledge*; Baldus on law 1, number 9, *Code on common legacies and trusts*; based on the argument in chapter 1, section *illud*, *On the prohibition of feudal alienation by Frederick.*

85. Secondly, what was argued above to the contrary from Jacobinus de Sancto Georgio and Chassanæus should not lead us into error. For as far as Jacobinus is concerned, although he relates the authorities of several <term>Doctors</term><note>Learned legal scholars</note> who maintain that a Prince cannot impose a <term>tax</term><note>original: "Collectam"; a gathered assessment or tribute</note> upon the men of his vassals, he immediately adds: "I have defended in a question of fact that this ought to be limited, unless it concerns the necessary defense of the Prince's own fatherland, etc." Furthermore, the reason why the power to tax the vassals of subjects is taken away from Lords or Princes is recounted by Jacobinus as follows: He says that although the Emperor can impose a <term>super-tax</term><note>original: "superindictum"; an extraordinary tax levied above the standard rate</note> upon his subjects when a public necessity exists (*Law 1, Code on super-taxes, book 10*), yet since the subjects are bound to provide a <term>standard tax</term><note>original: "Indictum"</note> to their own Lords in a similar case, the Emperor certainly cannot demand a super-tax from the subjects of those Lords, lest the men themselves be burdened with a double load. Therefore, this reasoning fails entirely in our proposed case, where the vassals—by an added pact of <term>investiture</term><note>The formal act of handing over land or office</note>—cannot demand a super-tax. To all of this may be added those points which Thomatus brings against this very opinion of Jacobinus, *folio 398, number 8.*

Regarding Chassanæus, he speaks of the *Customs of Burgundy*; he strengthens his opinion not by the authority of the Laws or the Doctors, but by authority drawn from Burgundian law. And finally, he adds that it must be considered that by reason of <term>jurisdiction</term><note>The legal power to exercise authority and administer justice</note>, someone can say a certain land is his own. (*Felino Sandeo on the chapter "examinata," outside the section on oaths; supported by what Panormitanus says in the chapter "pro illorum," outside the section on prebends; and Aretinus in his 30th Counsel; Felino in chapter 2 on oaths.*) Thus, it can be said that someone is the "man" of another; or one can say that such a man is "his," because he holds jurisdiction over him. From the aforesaid, therefore, the Lords of Uchon can say that because they have jurisdiction...

->QUESTION V.<-

<margin>86.</margin> Regarding this fifth question—namely, whether the Co-Counts <note>term: Mitgraffen; refers to lords who share jurisdiction over a territory</note> may tax the estates of the noble vassals—it is first to be noted that a distinction must always be made between those estates which are feudal <note>original: "feudalia"</note> and those which do not belong to the fief, yet are located within the feudal district and may have come to the said vassals from private individuals under any title whatsoever. For as far as such estates are concerned, they are held no differently than if they were still possessed by their former owners. This is illustrated by Peregrinus and by Johann Bidembach in questions 18 and 19. Natta affirms that if nobles buy the lands of peasants <note>original: "bona Rusticorum"</note>, those lands remain subject to services and burdens, since even the Church is bound to do this when it is the purchaser. For nobles cannot buy and acknowledge such "pagan" lands <note>gloss: peasant estates</note> to the prejudice and ruin of others. In this case, one is not looked upon as the Lord of the place or as a Noble, but as the possessor and purchaser of peasant goods; therefore, as he desires the benefits, he should not flee the consequences. Knichen decides extensively on this point: that nobles purchasing peasant lands with money are subject to the burdens and services thereof.

<margin>87.</margin> However, whether these fiefs and the estates specified in the letter of investiture <note>the legal document granting the fief</note> may be burdened by the Co-Counts with Imperial or Territorial taxes <note>term: Reichs- oder Landsteuren; taxes owed to the Holy Roman Empire or the local sovereign</note> is quite difficult to discern, owing to the varying opinions of our interpreters regarding this question and the many Daedalian <note>labyrinthine or complex</note> twists of distinctions and limitations. Nevertheless, highly respectable arguments and significant reasons are to be brought forward which seem to incline entirely toward the view that the vassals are obliged to give and contribute their share of both Imperial and Territorial taxes.

In the year 1548, page 16, paragraph "Wiewol nun" <note>German: "Although now"</note>. In these words: **Whether they are exempt or not exempt, privileged or not privileged, they are to be assessed for taxes, etc.** Thus, one who has been invested with a certain County, **freely and peacefully without tax**, although he may be free from the Provincial Tax <term>Landsteuer: a tax paid to the local territorial prince rather than the Emperor</term>, this in no way exempts him from the burdens of the Empire. 89. This is also the opinion of Modestinus Pistoris in the said counsel 5, number 5 and following. This opinion is greatly strengthened by this argument: because a Vassal is similar to a Usufructuary <term>Usufructuary: someone who has the right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</term>; according to the text in title 23, final paragraph, there: "The usufruct of that property indeed passes to the recipient," book 2 of the *Feuds*. 90. Thirdly, it is no less concluded by many distinguished legal scholars: **that in a case of public necessity, a Vassal may be collected upon or assessed with Provincial Taxes.** Jacobus de Sancto Georgio in the treatise *On Homage*, glossary 1, number 36. And also Wesenbeck, chapter 10, *On Feuds*, number 18, says that four cases have been accepted by custom in which, in this regard, the Vassal is held to provide aid. And especially it is argued by Lord Petrus Heigius, book 1, question 46, number 23 and many following, with many respectable arguments sought from the reasons of law and equity; **on account of imminent and unforeseen extreme necessity, Vassals ought to be burdened along with others:** for example, if for the defense of his province, the Lord has need not only of auxiliary soldiers, but also of salaried soldiers, and not only the Citizens themselves, but also the Vassals are compelled to go forth into the battle line. Where the burden affects the whole province generally, the same reasoning of the common utility of the Subjects concurs. To such an extent, that not even by custom or prescription can the Nobles protect themselves in this cause, so as to be less bound even for a feudal estate to the duties of the patrimony when public necessity urges; namely of war, the ransom of the person of the Prince, and the endangerment of his State.

**100.** Thirdly, it is specifically provided for in law that, as far as the land tax is concerned, the **Noble Vassals** (insofar as they are such) are not obligated to pay taxes on, or give tax from, their feudal estates, which they are bound to earn through their physical service. *And so it is held without distinction—unless a different custom has been accepted—by Clarus in the section on fiefs, question 29; Knichen on vested pacts; Schrader on fiefs; Rosenthal on fiefs; and Cothman in counsel 11. This is because that immunity was granted to the Vassal not for free, but on account of the inconvenience, or as a remuneration for the burdensome personal services which the Vassal is bound to perform for the Lord by reason of the fief. Mynsinger illustrates with many reasons that this opinion is common, equitable, and to be followed in judging; and Modestinus Pistor defends it no less elegantly than broadly in his 9th counsel, beginning: *Such questions.*

103. For collections of this kind (the provincial taxes) are partly personal and partly real, and thus mixed duties: which are imposed on persons principally on account of their things and possessions. And these do not have a fixed or determined payment, but vary according to the will of the superior due to emerging necessity; and therefore they are commonly called **extraordinary duties**. *Gail, book 2, observation 52, numbers 9 and 10.* Consequently, they cannot be imposed upon vassals, insofar as they are <term>foreigners</term> <note>original: "Forensibus"; meaning those residing outside the specific jurisdiction</note> and not subjects: *Gail, in the cited place, number 13.* This holds even if they possess movable or immovable property in the place where the tax is imposed. *Law 'rescripto', final paragraph; Law 'praeterea', paragraph 'patrimoniorum' of the Digest on duties; Law 'libertis' 17, paragraph 'sola' 13 of the Digest on Municipalities; Law 'cum nec' of the Code on inhabitants.* This is because, firstly, a tax is imposed by reason of **jurisdiction** over the person, which is primarily obligated by reason of their property; however, an act of jurisdiction cannot be exercised over a foreigner and a non-subject. *Cravetta, counsel 195, number 1; Pacianus, counsel 5, number 8.* Secondly, because foreigners perceive neither the honors nor the conveniences of the place. Therefore, they ought not to be burdened with taxes: a natural reasoning which uniquely pleases Natta, *counsel 160, numbers 7 and 8.* Bernhard Graeve disputes this question at length in *book 2, conclusion 52, number 13 and following; and Rosenthal, chapter 5, conclusion 80.*

104. Furthermore, Paulus Castrensis denies that it is free for the Lord of a territory to impose whatever tax he wishes, namely on the soil or the possession alone, so that even foreigners are bound to pay it. *On Law 'si ex toto' 8, at the beginning, number 5 of the Digest on legacies 1; followed by Mynsinger, Response 64, number 51, decade 7; through Law 'ne in potestate' of the Digest on arbitration; and Law 2, paragraph 'sed si agnat' of the Digest on judgments.*

105. And although some wish that in certain cases foreigners can be taxed for goods situated in a territory; for instance, for the **repair of bridges**, for the **guarding and security of the place**, etc.; provided, of course, that such guarding and repair also concerned the utility of the possessions themselves. *Gail, cited place, number 15; Rosenthal, cited chapter, conclusion 81; Graeve, number 15.*

<summary>This page discusses the legal distinction between a subject and a foreign vassal, arguing that those who do not reside in a jurisdiction (foreigners) are generally exempt from extraordinary provincial taxes unless the funds are used for local infrastructure that directly benefits their property.</summary>

Furthermore, the situation is far different for a non-resident <term>forensis; a landowner living outside the jurisdiction</term> who is also a <term>vassal; one who holds land from a superior lord in exchange for service</term> and who, by that title and in view of his feudal properties, must already perform his <term>feudal services; duties such as military aid or counsel owed to a lord</term>. 106. Fifthly, to decide controversies in the matter of payments or the levying of taxes <note>original: "collectandi"</note>, the ancient custom of the region and the place where such taxes are imposed must be considered and observed above all else. And if, according to established custom, even non-residents have been accustomed to being taxed by reason of their possessions, that custom must be maintained. One must not depart from it: for the true interpretation of the law is derived from practice, and one should deviate from ancient practice as little as possible.

<margin>Gail, observation 12, number 18 and following. Caspar Klock, Disputation on Contributions, thesis 8. Gravia, book 2, conclusion 52, number 16 and following.</margin>

Through this, even if these vassals were not exempt by the law itself <note>original: "ipso jure immunes"</note>, they would nonetheless have acquired immunity from taxes through legitimate <term>prescription; the acquisition of a right through long-continued use or the passage of time</term>. For it is beyond all doubt that immunity from taxes can be acquired through prescription of that length of time for which no memory to the contrary exists.

And it carries the power of a privilege and a most special grant.

111. **Secondly**, it is nowhere to be found in the Imperial Recesses <term>Reichs-Abschieden: the official resolutions passed at the conclusion of an Imperial Diet</term>, nor is it mentioned in them, that the nobility should **contribute** anything toward the Turkish Taxes <note>special taxes levied across the Empire to fund wars against the Ottoman Empire</note>, or other Imperial and Circle levies, or even territorial taxes, from their fiefs <note>Lehengütern</note> which they are bound to earn through personal service. 112. Furthermore, the Imperial Recesses speak only of exempt **persons**, but not of exempt estates. It is not mentioned in any Recess that the authorities shall be free or permitted to burden exempt estates with taxes. Therefore, it cannot be **inferred** from those same Imperial Recesses that the authorities are authorized to burden exempt estates with taxes, even in the cases mentioned in said Recesses. Rather, it follows instead that no authority is empowered to tax exempt estates in any case. This is confirmed with many other arguments **by Lord Mynsinger in the frequently cited first counsel, fifteenth decade, first question, almost throughout.** <note>Joachim Mynsinger von Frundeck (1514–1588), a prominent jurist of the Imperial Chamber Court.</note>

Since indeed the law of vassalage does not make anyone a subject, but subjection must properly be measured by whether one has a domicile in the territory of the Lord; as stated above in this chapter, question 5 and question 69 in the final gloss, and chapter 6, question 81, and chapter 9, question 14, or derives their origin from there. proceeds. Nor is the question here whether the **Vassals** <note>feudal tenants holding land from a superior lord</note> are immune; but rather, it is debated whether they ought to be burdened with the double weight of feudal services and extraordinary contributions.

118. For truly, *non-existent things have no qualities.* Thus, the question now is not: whether the **Lord of the Fief** <note>Latin: *Dominus Feudi*</note> reserved the **Right of Superiority** <note>Latin: *jus Superioritatis*</note> to himself in these estates, but only this is said: that Superiority, as well as that supreme power which is exempt from the laws, does not extend so far that someone may be burdened with a double load against the principle of natural equity. For a Prince cannot do what is unjust; and there is no power that can lawfully attempt anything against right reason and the law of contract and integrity.

### QUESTION VI.

119. Because, according to the preceding decision, the **Vassals**—with respect to their feudal estates—may not by law be taxed or burdened with Imperial and other levies: therefore, His Princely Grace the **Margrave** <note>German: *MGraff*</note> is not authorized to seek any arrears from them. However, as was argued in the third and fourth Questions, the subjects residing within this feudal district are not to be burdened with Imperial and territorial taxes by the **Knighthood** <note>the organized body of local nobles</note> or these noble Vassals at all. Instead, they are to be burdened with territorial taxes solely by His Princely Grace the Margrave, as the **Territorial Prince** <note>German: *Lands-Fürst*</note> and the one in whose territory they are; also, the Imperial levies raised from these subjects shall be applied to the quota which is at all times imposed upon the Margraviate. Accordingly, it could not be said without a particularly great reason that these taxes should either still be raised from the subjects, or that the Vassals are bound by law and equity to return what they have turned to their own use or have improperly allowed to be delivered to the Honorable Knighthood. # Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter V.

121. From this *narrative of the facts* <note>original: "narratione facti"</note> it is not only to be learned that before the year [15]68, the then-outstanding tax was completely waived; but it is also further well and sufficiently understood that His Princely Grace, Lord Margrave E. F., by omitting such taxation (which followed the humble petition of the Junkers <note>A "Junker" was a member of the landed nobility or minor aristocracy</note> of K.), intended to *altogether bestow some Princely benefit* <note>original: "omninò Principali aliquo beneficio afficiren"</note> upon both the K. family and their feudal subjects. He did not wish to *burden* <note>original: "graviren"</note> them in such a way that they would, in time, be troubled to their greatest hardship—especially with the arrears of many years of fallen levies—or that the Junkers of K. should be forced to make good out of their own *patrimony* <note>private family inheritance</note> that which was delivered into the Knights' Chests (*and indeed, not without the Lord Margrave's knowledge* <note>original: "& quidem non nescio Domino Marchione"</note>). *For we ought to interpret the benefits of Princes as fully as possible* <note>original: "Beneficia quippè Principum, quàm plenissimè interpretari debemus"</note> according to Law 3, *On the Constitutions of Princes*. Nor should those things granted in someone's favor ever be interpreted in such a way that they produce hatred or a burden for them. In these gracious and precarious indulgences, that which is said ought deservedly to take place: namely, that all causes and all fruits ought only then to be provided by him who possesses a thing by prayerful request <note>referring to "precarium," a legal right held by permission of another</note> when he has caused a delay, or from the day of the injunction—that is, after the lawsuit has been contested. See Law *quæsitum est* 8, paragraph *Et hoc interdicto* 4, and paragraph 6, in the Digest *on precarious holdings*. And likewise Wesenbeck in the *Paratitla*, number 6.

122. *Secondly*, these *extraordinary collections* <note>special taxes raised for emergencies</note> have a very different nature than *ordinary tributes* <note>regular taxes</note>, or other annual interest and fixed revenues, *which have a certain and perpetual cause*. These latter, if they have not been paid for several years, should subsequently be reimbursed for the sake of equity. However, such *collections* are levied *on account of a supervening necessity* <note>an unexpected emergency</note>; and it is also necessary that the *communities* <note>original: "Universitates"</note> who are *burdened* with them be *summoned* to the levy, or otherwise be properly dealt with at all times. *As noted from Mynsinger by Wehner under the word* Tax <note>original: "Schatzung"</note>, *folios 293 and 294.* Because this did not happen in this place, and these subjects—since the *suspensive indulgence* <note>a temporary stay or grace period</note> of His Princely Grace, Lord Margrave E.—have not been *summoned*, assessed, or had any tax demanded of them, it follows from this that nothing can be rightfully demanded of them regarding such a tax. This is because not only the *right of collecting* <note>original: "jus collectandi"</note> is required, but especially the proper assessment of a contribution.

It distinguishes between regular taxes and extraordinary levies, noting that the latter cannot be collected retroactively if the subjects were not properly summoned at the time of the emergency.</summary>
