# Political Discourses

...causes an obligation. As is said elsewhere and for the same reason: services do not exist in the nature of things unless they have been formally declared <note>original Latin: "operas non esse in rerum natura, nisi quando sunt indictæ"</note>. This is supported by the traditions of Surdus in *Counsel 262, number 32*, where he teaches that an obligation for collections is not contracted from the beginning at the time of registration for the future, but only when the collection is actually imposed.

123. One should not be misled to the contrary by what was introduced from Thomatus; for the reasons supporting his opinion <note>original Latin: "rationes ipsius opinionem fulcientes"</note> are to be understood as referring to a very different case. Namely, where an entire Corporation <term>Universitas: a legal body or collective community</term> is burdened with a certain land tax, which is thereafter distributed among the cities and villages; and if one or another person wished to withdraw themselves from it, the deficient portion would be carried and, as it were, advanced by the others. In such a case, it is fair that when the misconduct of the one seeking exemption comes to light, he should not only be taxed henceforth, but also be held to the restitution of that which the others paid on his behalf. We are not dealing with such a case here <note>original Latin: "Quo in casu nos non versamur"</note>: because here, by the gracious command of the Prince, the imposition has been omitted until now, and it is not the Margraviate's provincial estate, but the Lord Margrave himself who demands this arrears. Other arguments of the aforementioned Thomatus are to be understood as applying to ordinary tributes, which have a perpetual cause <note>original Latin: "tributa ordinaria, quæ perpetuam causam habent"</note>, and are not applicable here.

### Q U E S T I O N VII.

124. We now proceed to detail the principal rights which have been granted to these noble Vassals. It is found, firstly, in the feudal deed <term>Lehenbrief: a formal document granting a fief</term> that they were invested by the Lord Margrave with the Castle of Egg, the village of U., together with the "people" <note>original German: "Leute"</note>. Now, regarding this word "people": although in former times it was used generally for the subjects of a Prince <note>original Latin: "pro Subditis Principis"</note>, understanding those who were devoted to a lord with all sovereignty and lordship (see Hotoman in the *Feudal Lexicon* under the word *Leodes* or *Leudes*). From this, "Man" <note>Latin: "Homo"</note> was commonly used for a full subject, and "Homage" <note>Latin: "Homagium"</note> for the oath by which residents or subjects bind themselves to their territorial Prince. However, nowadays, especially in feudal grants, this word "people" is used for "own-men" <note>Latin: "propriis hominibus"</note>, whom we commonly call bondservants or serfs <note>original German: "Leibeigne Leut"</note>. See Knichen, *Book 2 on Investiture Agreements, chapter 3, numbers 13 and 14*. Nor are such servants considered as subjects, because they can...

Thessaurus, decision 254, number 1 and following. 128. It is further argued here that these noble vassals cannot presume to collect Imperial taxes, much less demand a provincial tax. Therefore, we hold in every way that in this feudal contract, the words "Tax" and "Prayer-Grant" <note>original: *Steur vnd Beth*. *Beth* or *Precaria* was originally a voluntary grant requested by the lord, later becoming a fixed tax</note> are used *as synonyms*. And even if, by the *singular custom of the place*, there might be a distinction between them, nonetheless nothing else is understood by them than the annual, customary *tributes* <note>original: *Tributa*</note> and common burdens brought down from antiquity, which are not to be changed and *are considered to have a perpetual cause*. We must infer this from these words of the feudal contract: (nonetheless, they shall leave the poor people to their customary prayer-grants, taxes, and services, and not oppress them beyond that, *etc.*).

129. And even if the word "Tax" were not to be understood as these annual, customary, long-established taxes—*which can neither be increased, nor ever cease or be diminished*—it could by no means be taken to refer to the *public right of collection* regarding Imperial or provincial taxes, but only to *private collections*. These are granted by law even to every simple *community* <note>original: *Commun*</note> that otherwise has no high authority <note>original: *Obrigkeit*</note>, *for the necessity and administration of their own affairs*. <note>Citing Wesenbeck and Stephanus Bertrandus</note> For sovereign rights are not understood to be granted through any *general words*. <note>Citing Jacobinus de Sancto Georgio and Claude de Seyssel</note> Where it is said: *Sovereign rights, and those reserved to the Prince as a sign of supreme power, are not understood to be granted through any general words.*

# On the Public Treasury, Chapter V.

130. **Furthermore, the Noblemen of K. are also enfeoffed with courts; however, this should be understood to refer only to the lower courts.** <note>original: "nidern Gerichten"</note> For the learned Doctors rightly conclude that, in cases of doubt, it is assumed only the inferior or "low" jurisdiction has been granted. **Chasseneuz** <note>Barthélemy de Chasseneuz (1480–1541), a French jurist</note> in *Customs of Burgundy*, first rubric, title on justices and their rights, on the word "justices," number 19, following the gloss on **Clement I**, on the word "all-encompassing," regarding competent forums. **Jason** <note>Jason de Mayno (1435–1519), an influential Italian legal scholar</note> follows this in his commentary on the law *Imperium* 3, number 11, regarding jurisdiction; he does not believe that "pure sovereignty" <note>original: "merum Imperium," referring to the power of life and death or high justice</note> is granted unless it is specifically designated. See also the first law on the office of the same. Furthermore, the ancient custom has proven that the aforementioned agreements of investiture are of a very strict nature: for all investitures where it is stated **"with courts"** confer nothing except the inferior jurisdiction (**the hereditary courts**). <note>original: "die Erbgericht"</note> This is pursued by **Knich** in book 2 of *Agreements of Investiture*, chapter 1. And this is what our **Doctors of Law** commonly say: one enfeoffed with a Castle, along with jurisdiction, is not understood to be enfeoffed with pure sovereignty. **Chasseneuz** in the cited place, following **Jason of Bologna**, who treats this question most extensively over several columns in his notes on the law *Imperium*. And **Covarrubias** <note>Diego de Covarrubias (1512–1577), a Spanish canonist</note> in *Practical Questions*, chapter 6, number 10, who testifies that this is the common opinion. This appears to be entirely beyond controversy in our present case, where the Prince, having granted the Castle with jurisdiction, reserved the pure sovereignty (**the High Court**) <note>original: "das Hohe Gericht"</note> for himself.

131. Moreover, he to whom only simple jurisdiction belongs (**the lower and hereditary courts**) has only the recognition of civil and financial cases: **concerning what involves rents, debts, landed estates, standing, movable, and immovable goods,** even if they exceed the sum of three hundred gold pieces. **Schneidewein**, part 2, number 88. **Coler**, part 2, chapter 1, number 105 to the end, and part 4, chapter 1, number 68. Likewise, such a judge may take cognizance of lesser crimes: such as verbal injuries, and also physical ones, provided they are not atrocious. **As when one person scuffles with another, pushes, strikes them black and blue, draws a knife, etc. Likewise, causing a "bloody rush" <note>original: "Blutrüssig machen," a legal term for a wound that draws blood, often marking the boundary of lower jurisdiction</note>. Such small breaches, which are atoned for only by fines and are not to be punished more seriously by law, belong to these courts. Schneidewein & Coler** in the cited places.

From this, it should be observed as a Rule, that use and custom <margin>tradition; namely, what acts each person has exercised</margin> regarding jurisdictional matters are to be looked at first and foremost, and are thus to be preferred entirely over written law. (Ibid, Question 7, number 5).

## QUESTION VIII AND LAST.

138. Finally, it would also be asked: what is the difference between these words (*Services* <note>Dienste</note> and *Socage* or *Compulsory Labor* <note>Frondiensten</note>)? And indeed, Valentin Forster <note>A German jurist (1530–1608) specializing in Roman and feudal law.</note> writes thus in *On Jurisdiction*, part 2, folio 467: It must be observed that these works are generally called *Frondienste* from the old Saxon *Fron*, which according to Saxon Law is called "Holy." <gloss>Gloss on the Saxon State Law (Landrecht), book 1, article 53.</gloss> From this comes *Fronvest* <note>a public prison</note> and *Fronbotte* <note>a court beadle or messenger</note>; concerning which see the Saxon State Law, book 1, article 8, who testifies for two, book 1, article 15. 

However, Wehner <note>Matthias Wehner, author of "Practica juris civilis."</note> in the entries for *Dingnotull*, *Dienst*, etc., folio 86; likewise Gail in *On Arrests*, 10, number 4; as also Knichen in *On the Agreement of Investiture*, chapter 3, number 29, etc., seem to hold these two terms as synonyms. 

But because the word *Fron* does not mean "holy," but rather "common" or "public": as for example, *Fronveste* (a common prison), *Fronteichnamb* <note>Corpus Christi; literally "the body given for the many"</note> which is handed over for the many, *Fronfaste* (a common fast), etc. Thus, *Frondienst* are properly those works which concern the public utility of some territory, or City, or Village, and must be performed by all subjects of that same territory, City, or Village. Of this kind are those things done for the repair of bridges, public roads, and dikes so that the breaking in of waters may be prevented, and similar things. *Services* <note>Dienste</note>, however, specifically so-called, are works owed by individual subjects which they must provide to their Lords, according as it was either agreed upon or observed from antiquity.

# Political Discourses

139. Since, however, Lords must take care that they do not demand more than is customary from their subjects, nor burden them with a desire for innovation—as *Sixtinus* <note>Regnoldus Sixtinus (1543–1604), a renowned German jurist</note> warns at length and with gravity in *On Regalian Rights, book 2, chapter 13, number 48, etc.*—and since the Letter of Investiture <note>original: "Lehenbrieff"; the formal deed granting a fief</note> expressly stipulates that the subjects shall be left to their customary services: therefore, ancient tradition must be respected. One must look to what these subjects performed during the time they were still under the Margrave, and the duty of said subjects must not be determined through a scrupulous catching at words <note>original: "ex scrupulosa verborum captione"; a warning against overly literal or pedantic legal interpretations</note>.

140. The words "to possess and to dispossess" <note>original: "zubesißen vnd zuentseßen"</note> we cannot understand otherwise than that power is hereby given to the vassals <term>Vassal: a person granted the use of land in return for homage and service</term> not only to possess these feudal holdings, but also to defend them in court, or to legally evict those who might hold any of these pieces of land. For the word "dispossess" is mostly taken to mean "to deprive of possession," but at times it is also used for "defense." For not only does a vassal have possession and a certain "quasi-ownership" of the Fief <term>Fief: an estate of land held on condition of feudal service</term>, but therefore, as a Lord, he can claim the feudal property for which he has been duly invested from any possessor; and this is done through a "useful action for recovery" <note>original: "utilem rei vindicationem"; a legal procedure to reclaim property</note>. *See the section "of the thing" and the gloss there on the word "claim," Book 2 of the Fiefs, titles 8 and 43.* From this same quasi-ownership, it also follows that a vassal, when sued by another, can protect himself through a legal exception and offer a defense. *See said titles 8 and 43.* Because it is a rule of both laws <note>Civil and Canon law</note> that to whomever we give a right of action, the right to an exception is even more applicable. And in the name of possession, "Interdicts" <note>court orders to stop an action or restore a state of affairs</note> are also granted to the same vassal. *Menochius <note>Giacomo Menochio (1532–1607), an Italian jurist famous for his work on legal presumptions</note>, remedy 4 on obtaining possession, number 375, and remedy 1 on retaining possession, number 81, etc.*

141. In the event, however, that the original document of investiture does not read "to possess and to dispossess" <note>original: "zubesißen vnd zuentseßen"</note> but rather "to occupy and to remove" <note>original: "zubeseßen vnd zuentseßen"; a subtle shift in German spelling/meaning implying administrative control</note>, these words would be understood to mean that the vassals may lease the mentioned feudal holdings, grant the right to collect fruits <note>the right to income or produce from the land</note> to another during their lifetime, sub-enfeoff <term>Sub-enfeoff: to grant a portion of one's own fief to a subordinate</term> something from it, and may pull all such things back to themselves again in due time and in due measure.

# ANOTHER LEGAL RESPONSE; WHETHER UNREGISTERED
->assets should fall to the Treasury?<-

In the Principality of B., the situation regarding taxes and other similar contributions <note>original: "Contributionibus," referring to various forms of public levies or emergency taxes</note> is such that every administrative district <term>Ampt: a local administrative and judicial district</term> of said lordship is responsible for a specific named sum which it must deliver annually. This sum is distributed, divided, and collected among the inhabitants and residents of the districts by the appointed collectors <note>original: "Exactores"</note> according to the nature of each person's wealth, based on the landed taxable property and monetary rents <note>original: "Geltgülten," income derived from land or investments</note> they possess.

In this Principality of B., a certain district E. is required to contribute 5000 florins <note>fl. or "Gulden," a standard gold or silver coin of the period</note> per year, which has indeed been correctly delivered every time.

In this same district, there was a resident named A. H. who, after he had passed away, was found—following the completion of the inventory and description of his estate—to have reported and declared himself in the tax register as being worth 1000 florins too little. Because of this, the Lordship <note>the ruling authority or government</note> stepped in, seized a property from the deceased's surviving heirs worth approximately 1000 florins, sold it, and confiscated the money.

However, as mentioned above, the Lordship did not lose a single penny <note>original: "Häller," a small copper coin of very low value</note> in taxes, but rather received the required 5000 florins correctly every year <note>because the district as a whole made up the shortfall</note>.

Thus, the question is asked, firstly: whether this Lordship has a legal cause of action <note>original: "Action"</note> against the surviving heirs by which it is entitled to this confiscation? And, whether the Lordship is not obligated to return the seized 1000 florins, and if such a claim for return would be upheld in a court of law?

# On the Public Treasury, Chapter V.

These matters are in many respects considered equal, so that they appear to have the same nature: for they are demanded by the one to whom the **regalian rights** <note>Latin: *regalia*; these are the exclusive rights and privileges belonging to a sovereign or monarch.</note> belong. This is taught regarding **Tolls** <note>Latin: *Vectigalibus*; taxes on the transport of goods.</note> by Friedrich Mindanus (Book 2, Chapter 43, Conclusion 5), Knichen (On the Saxon Law of Non-Appeal, Chapter 5, numbers 60 and 66), and before him, Rolandus à Valle (On the Profit of Dowries, Question 3, number 8). This is also confirmed by the **Imperial Recess of the year 1576** <note>A formal resolution or decree from the Imperial Diet of the Holy Roman Empire.</note> in the sections "Furthermore they are" and "through which then," etc. The same is established regarding **collections** <note>Latin: *collectis*; a form of direct taxation or assessment.</note>; as appears from Johannes Köpen (Question 32, numbers 4 and 8) and Regnerus Sixtinus (Treatise on Regalian Rights, Book 2, Chapter 14, number 16 and following). Similarly, not only collections but also tolls are imposed for a just cause and an urgent, just necessity. This is especially true since collections are demanded not only for the construction of roads and bridges, but also for the defense of the fatherland: Rolandus à Valle (Consultation 91, numbers 25 and 27, Book 2). Likewise, the exacting of collections and the right to demand tolls are granted if the poverty of the Province necessitates it (Law 1, Code, *Where new tolls cannot be instituted*; Baldus, Consultation 340, number 3, at the verse "and when the fatherland," volume 5; Mynsinger, Observation 31, number 3, century 5).

3. **Secondly**, it might be considered not a little prejudicial to the heirs that the Emperor Antoninus, in Law 1 of the Code *If a sale was celebrated on account of public payments*, etc., taught in these words: <note>original: "Venditionem ob tributorum cessationem factam, revocari non oportet; neque priore domino pretium offerente, neque creditore ejus, jura hypothecæ, sivè pignoris prætendente."</note> **"A sale made on account of the failure to pay taxes ought not to be revoked; neither by the former owner offering the price, nor by his creditor claiming rights of mortgage or pledge."** Other legal texts agree with this constitution (Laws 2 and 3 of the said title; Laws 1 and 2, Code, *On seizing and selling pledges for the cause of tribute*; Law "When the possessor," 5, final paragraph, Digest, *On the census*; Law "On estates," 36, Digest, *On the law of the treasury*). This is also confirmed by Felicius <note>OCR: Feltasius</note>, following Innocentius, in the *Treatise on Assessment and Collections* (Part 2, Chapter 3, numbers 10 and 13; also Part 3, Chapter 1, number 11), Rolandus à Valle (Consultation 32, numbers 3, 4, and 8, Book 1), and Wesenbeck (Consultation 103, number 9, at the end). From which it can be concluded, not without reason, that a Lord—on account of the failure to provide owed taxes and collections—may make use of a **confiscation** of those goods from which the taxes were not provided. And thus, against one who does not declare goods subject to public collections and exactions, an **action of forfeiture** <note>Latin: *actio commissi*; a legal proceeding to seize property due to a breach of obligation.</note> may be exercised, as taught by Thomas Maul in the *Treatise on Homage* (Title 9, On Collections, number 136 and following), where he cites Fachs (Consultation 41), which is included in Volume 2 of the *Consultations of Illustrious Jurists and Academies of Our Time*, etc.

5. Notwithstanding the reasons introduced above, however, I am entirely of the opinion that those goods which were omitted in the tax declaration should not be confiscated or seized by right of law; this is understood only of those places in which a contrary rule has not been introduced through a lawful **Statute** <term>Statutum: a local law or municipal ordinance</term>, long-standing use, or custom. For it is well known that in matters of collection, custom prevails most strongly. *Wesembeck, Consultation 181, number 118.* <note>Matthaeus Wesenbeck was a prominent 16th-century jurist.</note>

6. I am initially moved to this because, although in many different titles of **our law** <note>original: "Juris nostri," referring to Roman Civil Law</note> concerning **tributes** <term>Tributis: regular taxes</term>, **indictions** <term>Indictionibus: extraordinary tax assessments</term>, and other exactions, it is treated; yet it is nowhere to be found that those who declare themselves unequally in the tax, profit themselves too little, and fail to fully disclose their total assets to the collectors, should be punished with the confiscation of the withheld goods. From this it is rightly inferred that a Lord who is protected neither by Law, nor by Custom, nor by an old Statute (established before the case occurred), cannot induce the publication of goods: since it is the same thing for something to be done without the Law as against the Law. According to **Baldus** <note>Baldus de Ubaldis, a famous 14th-century jurist</note> in the chapter "In Genesis" near the end, on elections. Hence the saying of the same Baldus is tossed about: "What is not provided for by Law is not held in practice." # Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter V.

<margin>Punishments and hateful dispositions are to be restricted.</margin>
...punishment. <note>original: "c. in poenis. d. Reg. jur. in 6." refers to the Rules of Law in the Sixth Book of Decretals.</note> And hateful dispositions <note>In legal terms, "hateful" (odiosae) refers to laws that impose burdens, penalties, or restrictions on liberty.</note> ought to be restricted rather than extended. <note>original: "c. odia. d. t."</note> Furthermore, we ought to be more inclined toward mercy than toward severity. <note>original: "l. respiciendum. ff. de poen." referring to the Digest of Justinian on penalties.</note>

8. Therefore, the Jurisconsult <term>Modestinus|A famous Roman jurist from the 3rd century</term> rightly said: I do not think that a person commits a fault who, in doubtful questions, readily answers against the <term>fiscus|The private or imperial treasury of the state</term>. And not without merit did Capitolinus praise the Emperor Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher, when he said that in cases involving financial gain for the state, he never judged in favor of the treasury. This is also confirmed by Hart. Pistor. And specifically, that in cases of doubt, the interpretation ought to be made against the tax collection, as it is something "hateful" or burdensome. This is evident from Corneus, Panormitanus, Cravetta, and Wesenbeck; the same is taught regarding <term>gabelle|A term for taxes or duties, often specifically salt taxes</term> by Bartolus, Socinus, and Garcia Mastrillo.

9. Which then—secondly—is also principally strengthened by this: that in clear law, the penalty of deprivation of goods <note>The seizure of private property by the state.</note> should never take place unless it is expressly imposed either by Law or by Statute. <note>Citing Panormitanus and Felinus.</note> It is certain, moreover, that today, according to the most recent law, the goods of offenders are by no means subject to confiscation, but are to be left to the next of kin. <note>original: "auth. bona damnatorum. C. de bon. proscript."</note> Prosper Farinacci <note>A prominent 16th-century Italian jurist known for criminal law.</note> says that whatever the law may be, everyone nevertheless observes the contrary: namely, that goods are not confiscated in any case, except for the crime of heresy or <term>lese-majesty|Treason or an offense against the dignity of the sovereign</term>; unless it has been otherwise arranged by Statute or Custom.

10. Hence, a sentence in which a Judge imposes the penalty of confiscation or deprivation of goods suffers from the vice of nullity, and is overturned even without a formal appeal; even if it was delivered by a Judge possessing broad and general discretion. <note>Citing Baldus, Decianus, and Peregrinus on the rights of the fiscus.</note>

Rather, I consider that if such delinquents were compared against each other, it would be found that he makes himself more liable to a greater punishment who—in a highly urgent levy for the help and rescue of the Christian name, the Imperial-German Nation, our common Fatherland, and indeed all of Christendom against tyrannical, overwhelming Turkish power—disobediently opposes the Roman Imperial Majesty, the common good of the Holy Empire, and his own territorial Prince and Magistrate. By doing so, as much as lies within him, he invites the Turkish yoke and servitude upon his own neck and those of others. Likewise, just as he who uses force is worthy of a greater penalty than he who commits something secretly to the prejudice of another, etc. <note>original: "Pariter, ut is, qui vim adhibet, majori poena dignus est, quam qui in alterius praejudicium, clam aliquid committit"</note>. According to the Imperial Recess of the year 1544, section "yet shall etc.," it is nonetheless presumed that if one of the subjects should falsely declare his assets, he should be punished without remission according to the size or smallness of his concealment and the nature of the same; but even there, mention is made of the double penalty, and less so of confiscation.

# Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter V.

13. Fourthly, this opinion is approved in these terms by Caspar Klocke <note>A prominent 17th-century legal scholar on taxation</note> in his *Disputation on Contributions*, 65. Nor is Thomatus distant from this view in *On Collections*, page 579 and following, where he teaches that he who exercises the right of collecting taxes may seek those collections through a personal action <note>A legal claim against a specific person</note> if the goods are described in the assessment. But if they were omitted, he argues that a mortgage action <note>A claim against the property itself</note> is available for the unpaid taxes. Indeed, Bartolus himself confirms our opinion in his commentary on the law *commissa* at the end of the Digest *on publicans and taxes*, where he says it is introduced and accepted by statutes that goods not assigned in the tax register (cadastre) are to be held as confiscated. From this it appears clearly that, according to Bartolus’s opinion, in places where such statutes do not exist, there is no place for confiscation simply because goods were not declared to the tax collectors.

14. In the same way, fifthly, the Lord to whom the taxes are due in the present case has even less reason to complain about this minor assessment and declaration. Considering that in the narrative of the facts, report, and indication, it was stated that 5,000 florins are due annually to Office E. (to which the disputed contribution belongs), which sum has been correctly delivered every year; and therefore, the Lordship has lost nothing at all of the taxes owed.

15. In consideration of all this, I conclude once more on this first question: that the mentioned 1,000 florins, which were not indicated in the ordinary assessment for the usual tax, have by no means fallen into forfeiture <note>original: "in commissum"</note>, nor should they by right have been confiscated or seized. Indeed, I have no doubt that this confiscation and deprivation of goods was undertaken solely based on an unfair report by the officials; therefore, it can be undone again through proper means without offense to the Lordship. Just as it is decreed regarding undue taxes (in which cases, however, the law usually proceeds more strictly than in the present case): that an undue tax, paid through error, must be restored (as the Divine Severus and Antoninus <note>Roman Emperors known for legal reforms</note> wrote in a rescript). See the final law at the end of the Digest *on publicans, taxes, and forfeitures*.

<meta>This page continues the legal discourse regarding the collection of taxes and the rights of the state treasury (Fiscus) over private property when payments are overdue.</meta>

-># Political Discourses<-

Regarding the argument presented, one must remember that among the methods used against those who show themselves slow in the payment of taxes <note>original: "Raichung der Steuren"</note>, it is understood that the property subjected to the tax <term>Collecta: a specific type of tax or assessment levied on property</term>, and the fruits grown upon it, may be publicly sold and liquidated. However, this must not be extended beyond the specific amount of the debt. Thus, in such a case, the goods are sold solely for the purpose that the Lordship <note>The ruling authority or government</note> may satisfy the outstanding taxes from the proceeds of the sale. For it is established that the thing for which the tax is owed should be sold only for the amount of the burden; following Cravetta, Roland, and Tileman de Benignis, Regnerus Sixtinus teaches this in *On Regalian Rights*, book 2, chapter 14, number 169. And the reason is manifest enough: although goods are obligated to the Treasury <term>Fiscus: the public treasury or state's financial interests</term> due to the cessation of tribute payments, and are bound by legal pledge <note>original: "pignore nexa"</note> according to the Code *if on account of tribute cessation*, and Festas *on valuations*, part 2, number 10; therefore, if the Treasury, having initiated a mortgage action <term>hypothecaria actio: a legal claim to seize property used as collateral for a debt</term>, should occupy them and subject them to the spear <note>original: "subjiciat hastæ" – a Roman metaphor for a public auction</note>, it is consistent that it should only satisfy itself from that portion of the price for which the goods were obligated, and return the remainder to the owner of the land. For it is foreign to the simplicity of our law that one should act through a mortgage action beyond what is owed, since the creditor has no further interest. See Oldendorp *on actions*, action 10.

22. Nor should the tradition of Thomas Maullius lead anyone away from the path of truth; for he, being destitute of legal texts, relies on the authority of Ludwig Fachs; who, although in the previously cited counsel found in volume 2 of *Illustrious and Celebrated Counsels of Jurists*, etc., seems to extend the "action of forfeiture" <term>actionem commissi: a legal penalty where property is forfeited entirely due to a breach of duty</term>—which has a place in customs duties <note>original: "Vectigalibus"</note>—to taxes as well; nevertheless, it is clearly evident from the facts of the case that in the situation proposed to him, the forfeiture was introduced by a singular local statute. Furthermore, Fachs himself did not give a definitive counsel, but (as he says himself) only wished to propose certain things for the sake of thinking more deeply on the matter.

23. Regarding the third point, concerning the reasoning of public utility, it is in no way denied that taxes <note>original: "Collectæ"</note> serve the preservation of the land and people, and should be properly allocated and not remitted for anyone. However, this is by no means to be understood as meaning that the presiding officials should immediately seize and sell non-profitable goods, taking not only the arrears but the entire property...

It critiques legal scholars like Maullius and Fachs who argued for harsher forfeiture rules, emphasizing that such penalties usually require specific local statutes.</summary>

## QUESTION II.

<margin>24.</margin> Concerning the second *Question* proposed above: Namely, whether—on account of the withholding of owed taxes—the heirs of the deceased (in cases where *Confiscation* does not apply) can be burdened with other penalties? The *opinion of those in the affirmative* might be supported by the following *Reasons*. *First, for the heir is considered to have the same legal standing as the deceased:* <note>original: "heres censetur ejusdem juris, cujus fuit defunctus"</note> *Law: 'the heir', in the Digest on the Rules of Law; and he is bound to fulfill the acts of the deceased. Rick, Treatise on the Union of Offspring, chapter 7, number 65. And he (according to the Canonists) must clear the conscience of the deceased. Antonius de Butrio, in the chapter 'if delegates', number 13, on competent jurisdiction; arguing from the final chapter on the violation of sepulchers. And Butrio adds that this cannot be done otherwise, unless he restores what his predecessor unjustly obtained. Through the text in the chapter 'sin', on the rules of law in the 6th book. Furthermore, shameful gains are to be extorted from the heirs.* <note>original: "turpia lucra ab heredibus sunt extorquenda"</note> *Law: 'against the heir', in the Digest on false accusations; and the law 'let us see', in the Digest on things done through fear. And of things badly acquired, the treasury is the heir. See the law 'Lucius Titius' at the end of the section on the rights of the treasury. Baldus in chapter 1, in the title 'what are regalian rights'.*

<margin>25.</margin> *Secondly, the same has been specifically accepted in the crime of defrauded Customs-tax.* <note>original: "fraudati Vectigalis"</note> *Law: 'of defrauded customs', 8, in the Digest on public taxes and customs; where the Jurisconsult Papinian says: the crime of defrauded Customs-tax is transmitted to the heir of the one who committed the fraud, by reason of the forfeit. And Ulpian, in law 14 of the said title, says: forfeits in the name of Customs-taxes are also transmitted to the heirs, etc.*

<margin>26.</margin> Now, it is indeed placed beyond all doubt that the aforementioned heirs are bound to compensate—unwaveringly and without distinction—the arrears and the taxes lacking to the Office <note>likely the Tax Office or Treasury</note> due to the incomplete declaration of profitable goods held. *Because, namely, whether they have been made wealthier or not, the goods of citizens are bound by the bond of a mortgage by the law itself, with every cause and interest, according to the measure of the imposed Taxes.* <note>original: "hypothecæ nexu, ipso jure sunt devincta"</note> *Law 1, and the gloss there, in the Code: 'if for public payments', etc. And therefore, heirs are summoned to court not merely by reason of the inherited estate, but by reason of the possession they have taken up.*

27. In the same manner, it cannot be denied that A. H. (in the event that he had **deceitfully** <note>original: *dolosè*</note> concealed anything) might have been faced with a fitting and moderate punishment were he still alive. **For the Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, in a case not far dissimilar, wrote in reply: if anyone, in order to evade the loyalty of the tax assessments, craftily feigns a state of poverty, once detected, he shall be subjected to competent indignation.** <note>original: *Cùm Impp. Gratian. Valent. & Theodosius...*</note> This text is found in the law *quisquis*, 2. of the Code on tax assessments and registered taxpayers, book 11. <term>Code (C.): The Codex Justinianus, a collection of Roman laws.</term>

28. However, when the aforementioned A. H. has passed away, and a complaint regarding the low tax payment is only made after his death, it is concluded—not without cause—that such an alleged forfeited penalty cannot be transmitted to his heirs. **For it is of undoubted law that punishments should not extend beyond their authors, as we know.** <note>original: *Juris etenim est indubitati, quòd pœnæ non egrediantur auctores*</note> From the Code on punishments; and that **actions arising from crimes do not pass against the heirs, unless the legal contest was joined with the deceased while living.** <note>original: *actiones, ex delictis non transeant adversùs heredes...*</note> See law *sicut pœna*: 38. on the rules of law; and law *pupillû*. 111. section *in heredem*. In that same title, the Jurist Gaius says that **actions which are penal arising from a wrongdoing are not accustomed to pass to the heir; such as for theft, damage to property, goods taken by force, and injuries, etc.** <note>original: *in heredem non solere actiones transire...*</note> There is also a text on this same matter in the single law of the Code on how far heirs are liable for the crimes of the deceased.

29. **Hence, although no one doubts that in the matter of Customs Duties** <note>original: *Vectigalibus*</note>**, a penalty for forfeiture has a place due to a failure to declare goods;** nevertheless, Sixtinus reports, in his *Treatise on Regalian Rights*, book 2, chapter 6, number 166, and **expressly** teaches, **that the aforesaid penalty of forfeiture only passes to the heirs of him who committed the crime of customs fraud if the investigation was initiated while the one who offended was still alive.** <note>original: *quòd prædicta commissi pœna...*</note> And he supports this opinion of his through the text of the final law, section 13 on punishments, in the Digest on public taxes and customs. There, the Jurist Marcian says: **penalties cannot be sought from heirs if the investigation was not moved while the offender was living. And this is the case in Customs Duties just as it is in other penalties.** <note>original: *pœnæ ab heredibus peti non possunt...*</note>

30. Beyond all of which, it is to be learned that the **arguments** introduced above to the contrary are considered entirely irrelevant (as far as the first **reason for doubt** is concerned). The rule contained therein is **limited** so that it does not take place **in penalties descending from the crime and wrongdoing of the deceased: as was shown above.** <note>original: *in pœnis, ex defuncti crimine & maleficio descendentibus*</note>

31. But as for the further claim made: **that heirs must be compelled to the restitution of things unjustly acquired by their predecessor, and that shameful gains** <note>original: *lucra turpia*</note> **are to be extorted from the heirs, etc.** This is partly to be understood as applying **if the heir has been made wealthier thereby.** <note>original: *si heres exindè locupletior fit factus*</note>

35. Whether the said law *Bene a Zenone* (Code: *On the four-year prescription*) has a place not only regarding the Emperor, but also other States of the Empire, is to be inferred from this: that the same are provided with all Royal Prerogatives <term>Regalia: rights and privileges belonging exclusively to a sovereign</term>. Hence it is said, that Princes, Dukes, and Free Cities exercise an almost majestic jurisdiction in their territories, as per Schrader, *On Fiefs*, part 10, section 1, number 33; and they use the clause of "fullness of power" <note>original: "clausulâ plenitudinis potestatis" - a legal term for absolute sovereign authority</note>; Natta, consultation 179, number 14. They exercise in their territories those things which are reserved for the Emperor as a sign of the Imperial Crown. Just as Peregrinus, *On the Law of the Treasury*, book 6, title 4, number 17, extends the cited law, *Bene a Zenone*, to others who also possess Superiority <note>original: "Superiores habentes" - referring to those with territorial lordship</note>, where he cites Baldus, Felinus, Socinus Junior, Alvetta, and others, etc.

36. For firstly, granted that the penalty of forfeiture <term>Commissum: a legal penalty where property is confiscated for a breach of law or contract</term> should also take place regarding the taxes <note>original: "Collectis" - specific imperial or territorial taxes</note>, and therefore the ownership of the withheld goods would have fallen to the Lordship by the law itself: nevertheless, at the very least, a declaratory sentence of forfeiture would be required. For although it is certain that in matters of customs duties, because of the failure to declare merchandise, the thing falls into forfeiture (Legal College of Leipzig, among the consultations of Modestinus Pistoris, consultation 48, number 17, book 2), yet in taking it away, a human act and a declaratory sentence are necessary. Gail, *Observations*, 51, number 5, book 2; Josephus Ludovicus, conclusion 15, number 75. And Grammaticus testifies concerning the common opinion in decision 15, number 8, whom Magnerus Sixtinus follows and cites, *On the Regalia*, 2, chapter 6, number 171. For even if confiscation or another penalty is incurred by the law itself, the Judge must nevertheless [hear] the accused of the crime...

### CHAPTER VI.

Furthermore, besides the methods narrated above (concerning which one may likewise consult Johann von Chokier <note>A 17th-century political theorist</note>, *Treasury of Political Aphorisms*, chapter 2, aphorism 10), there are also other methods by which a Prince restrains the abundance of money; nor does he entreat the substances of his subjects (thereby bringing some loss upon them). Namely, from the alteration of coinage, Princes sometimes reap great utility. Thus Hippias <note>A tyrant of Athens</note> ordered the coin which was then used in Athens to be declared "wicked" <note>original: "improbum"; meaning debased or invalid</note>, and commanded that all money be brought to him at a certain fixed rate. And when those who wished to strike coins with a different mark came together, he hired out that same silver. See Aristotle, *Economics*, Book 2. Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note>, being in need of money, imitated Hippias in changing the money, but more cautiously. For he proclaimed (as Polyaenus says in *Stratagems*, Book 6) that he would strike a different currency, and that everyone should bring their coins here so that they might be struck in another form. # Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter VI.

...impressed a mark upon it, and ordered each single coin to be worth double its previous price: by which means he gained half of those funds which he had collected, and affected none of the citizens with loss. <note>The author is likely referring to a historical anecdote of a ruler devaluing currency to pay debts.</note> The Romans, during the Punic War, when the Republic was not sufficient for its expenses, made a profit of five parts and dissolved their debt by diminishing the weight of the bronze pound <term>libra: a Roman unit of weight</term>. Later, under the pressure of Hannibal, the *asses* <term>as: a bronze Roman coin</term> were made to weigh only one ounce (which previously were three ounces) and it was decided that a *denarius* should be exchanged for 16 *asses*: thus the Republic gained half. Soon, by the Papirian Law, the *asses* were made half-ounce. See also Bornitius, book 6, chapter 6 and following. And Plautus touches upon this in the Prologue of *Casina*:

> ->For now the new comedies that come out<-
> ->Are much more worthless than the new coins...<-

Likewise under the Emperors, and even more so, the weight and price were frequently tossed about and changed: as Balduinus proves in *On the Laws of Constantine*, book 2, regarding the law "We command," on the sum of silver, page 118. And furthermore, certain people, when the value of money has been increased but the intrinsic goodness <note>The "intrinsic goodness" refers to the actual precious metal content of the coin.</note> has been corrupted, persuade the Great Lords <margin>that they should have their customs duties and income paid back to them in the old currency.</margin> See Heinrich Klock on taxes, theorem 69, and I have made mention of this matter somewhere above. This truly requires a prudent and pious judgment.

But the changing of money is hardly ever done without the inconvenience and injury of the subjects. See especially Bornitius *On Coins*, last chapter. Whence among the people of Navarre, when the King is inaugurated, he swears among other things that he will not change the coinage more than once. <note>original: "se non nisi unâ vice Numum mutaturum"</note> See *Duplicate of the advice sent to King Philip III*, at the beginning of the *History of Navarre*. And all the wisest men judge that this unusual change (or rather depravation) and augmentation of money which is noticed today are omens of great mutations in Republics. See Keckermann, *Politics*, book 1, chapter 21, page 330; and I advised the same in my *Politics*, book 1, chapter 4, number 51, verse 2. Nicolaus Oresmius and Gabriel...

-># Political Discourses<-

Gabriel <note>original: "Gabriel etiam Biel"</note> Biel also wrote unique treatises on the origin and power, as well as the alteration of money; these were annexed by Marquard Freher to his discourse on Monetary Law. In these works, a specific doubt is proposed: **Whether a Prince can derive profit from money by establishing its value as greater than the material is actually worth?** They respond that in only one case can a Prince seek profit from money: namely, when he requires a subsidy for the defense of the State <note>original: "Reipublicae"</note>. For that case and others, Hænon cites his political disputation 5, thesis 84.

And as if from an oracle, the opinion of Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and political philosopher</note> came forth in *The Republic*, book 6, chapter 3, at the beginning: **Not only can money not be corrupted, but it cannot even be changed without inconvenience to the State.** This is because a change in the price and material of coins brings doubt to the census and to the goods of every person. As a result, no one can determine how much they actually possess in assets; agreements and contracts become uncertain—those involving partnerships, guardianships, trusts, mandates, as well as buying, selling, hiring, and leasing, by which the fellowship of life is maintained. Revenues, taxes, and tributes become uncertain; finally, even the penalties and rewards imposed by laws and judges will be uncertain in the future. Lastly, the resources of the treasury and many things in both public and private operations must necessarily remain doubtful and suspended. And a little later: by which it is understood, when coins are corrupted by the Prince himself through law and public authority, how much destruction will come to the State.

On this matter, Juan de Mariana <note>A Spanish Jesuit theologian and historian</note> also disputes weightily and laboriously in *The King's Institution*, chapter 8, where among other things, on page 269, he proposes the following: "Indeed, I will not deny (for how could I?) that money was often debased by our ancestors; and that sometimes such straits can occur in which one must necessarily recur to that remedy. But I contend, first, that not everything done by our ancestors is free from vice. Second, that under the name and appearance of ready utility, fraud lies hidden; it is a mere mockery, and greater inconveniences arise publicly and privately from that fabrication; nor should one ever descend to it if we wish our affairs to be safe. And furthermore, I establish this: **it is not within the Prince's right to take the goods of his subjects, whether movable or landed, so that he can at his whim either take them for himself or transfer them rashly to others.** They are babblers and flatterers—of whom many live in the courts of Princes—who argue otherwise; but from those principles, it is nevertheless concluded that he cannot command new tributes upon the people without their consent. For he should demand by entreaty, not drain his subjects, nor pluck away anything daily according to his will." From these points...

# On the Public Treasury, Chapter VI.

...and those who were wealthy a short time before are reduced to poverty. For that would be to act as a tyrant, who always measures everything by his own desires and claims everything for himself; not as a King, who tempers the power received from a willing people with law and reason, and does not extend it immeasurably. From these two points, it follows that a King cannot, at his own whim and without consulting the people, debase the currency; for that is a type of tribute <note>A form of hidden taxation</note> by which something is taken away from the goods of the Subjects. Who would allow the exchange of gold for an equal weight of silver, or silver for iron? What then, if one gives silver coinage for the most part instead of gold, or copper instead of silver? This is what happens whenever money is adulterated <note>The practice of "clipping" or mixing precious metals with base metals to devalue currency</note>. A King will indeed be permitted to change the form of the coinage, since among those things contained within royal right by Imperial law, the minting of money is numbered; however, the value must be sanctioned according to the quality of the money and prior laws.

And indeed, the value of money is twofold: one is *natural*, taken from the quality and weight of the metal, which can also be called *intrinsic*; the other is *Legal* and *extrinsic*, which the Prince defines by law; just as with the prices of other goods, so that they are not sold for more than what the law has actually decreed. He is a fool who would separate these values in such a way that the latter—namely the *Legal*—does not cling to the natural: he is unjust who commands that what is commonly valued among men at five should be sold for ten; nor will he achieve this through any diligence or severity. For men are led by common estimation, which is born from the quality of things, their abundance, or their scarcity: in vain would a Prince strive to tear up these foundations of commerce, which would stand better if left unmoved; to deviate from common consent is to bring a kind of violence upon the mind.

What happens in other goods should be extended to money: the Prince, in taxing the value by law, ought to consider the legitimate price and weight of the metal, and not strive beyond it, except that a small amount may be added to the value of the metal for the labor of minting, etc. Relevant here is what François Baudouin <note>original: "Fr. Balduinus," a 16th-century French jurist</note> writes in *Book 2 of the Laws of Constantine the Great, page 124 in my edition, etc.* It would perhaps be desirable for coins to be minted at public expense with such weight that the raw metal was worth no less than the stamped metal. For in this way it would more easily happen that (as our Gaius <note>A celebrated Roman jurist</note> said it ought to be) the power of money would be one and the same everywhere; *Law 3, Digest, on that which is in a certain place* <note>original: "l. ideò. 3. D. de eo, quod cert loc." referring to the Corpus Juris Civilis</note>; and with the hope of profit removed, every occasion for private individuals to secretly mint money would be taken away. But since that which we wish for—and which certain ancient Jurists not only wished for but even demanded—has no hope of ever being obtained, the next best thing is...

->Dross, and not silver.<-

->This is known everywhere.<-
<note>These introductory verses lament the corruption of the coinage, using the metaphor of "dross" or "scoria" (the waste matter separated from metal during smelting) to describe debased money.</note>

Wicked merchants—or rather, I should call them embezzlers—according to Albert Krantz <note>original: "Crantzio"; a 15th-century German historian</note> in book 12 of his *History of the Vandals*, chapter 38, have made a mere commodity out of the coinage. They export it to places where they can make their own private profits in the smelting furnace to the detriment of the public. This is undoubtedly a matter of great importance, if it is well considered. For it is incredible to recall how much better that solid coin was a hundred years ago than it is now. This is so that those who hold annual incomes—whether Princes in their taxes or private citizens in their rents—may understand what they have lost. Affairs are always so arranged that as the coinage fails, all trade and the success of individuals in their gain likewise decrease, with those things which were previously held vanishing invisibly from the hand. It is undoubtedly a great task to establish the coinage successfully; it was a matter that exhausted even the Romans, the masters of the world.

However, Marquard Freher <note>A prominent German jurist and historian (1565–1614)</note> reveals the cause of this fluctuating monetary system and simultaneously offers a suitable remedy in his *On Monetary Affairs*, book 2, chapter 5, page 56. He says: "The value of gold and silver coinage does not remain at its first valuation, but has long since exceeded it, and is stretched further and further every day. This happens for no other reason than the debasement of the common currency; it is necessary that it happens, and I would wonder if it did not. For since the larger and solid coins receive their estimation and valuation only through the smaller ones—the *solidus* through the *denarii*, the *denarius* through the *as*, the Thaler and Florin through the Batzen, Groschen, Schillings, and Albus <note>These are various historical European coins of varying silver content</note>—and entirely (as the jurist Volusius Maetianus writes in his book *On the As*) every silver coin receives its power from the number of copper pieces; so much so, that as Ausonius truly said:

->Gold has great honor, yet the price of gold is the copper coin.<-

<margin>Dross</margin>
It is necessary, if the valuation of money is to remain stable, that there be a certain proportion of that copper to the gold and silver. This is not only for the price of the metal—which, being base and more corruptible in itself, ought to be mixed with silver only most sparingly—but also for the use and purpose of each. For those smaller coins were prepared not for the amassing of wealth (for what Euclio <note>A reference to the stingy protagonist of Plautus's play *Aulularia*</note> would wish to heap up and guard such things as a treasure?) but only for buying things of immediate necessity, and minor things at that, and they are exchangeable in only one region; therefore, the Commonwealth has need of a smaller number of them. To this point, money taken on loan under <term>Usury and Interest</term> <note>original: "Usura & Fœnore"</note> ought to be referred: which can serve as a protection in sudden dangers. # On the Public Treasury, Chapter VI.

Those who accept money under interest <note>original: "sub Usuris"</note> in the name of the Republic, are engineering the destruction of the Treasury and the State; I understand this to apply to cases where extreme necessity does not demand it. (In this respect, the same author says in *number 670*: Nothing is more pernicious or more absurd than for Princes to launch a war based on high-interest loans or borrowed money. King Charles VIII of France experienced this to his great disadvantage during the Neapolitan expedition, as Comines recorded in *Book 7, chapter 5*. But a pious and prudent statesman will judge all these matters wisely.)

There are several Republics overwhelmed by great debt. In Venice, there are three "Mountains" <note>The "Monti" were public debt funds in Italian city-states where citizens "piled up" their money for the state to use in exchange for interest.</note> (this is what they call the burdens of borrowed money), and there, in times of war, the payment of interest is suspended. Donato Giannotti, in the treatise *On the Glory of the Venetians* <note>original: "Von der Venediger Herrligkeit"</note> translated into our vernacular by Hieronymus Megiser, *folios 256 and 258, etc.*; and Bembo, in *Book 12 of the History of Venice, folio 505 at the end and the following folio*. Even the Patrimony of Saint Peter <note>The land and territories under the direct temporal rule of the Pope.</note> is burdened by a manifold weight of mortgages (*the Pope does not have much income from his States, and what he used to have is all pledged or obligated*) <note>original Italian: "de suoi Stati, il Papa, non ha molta entrata, & quello che soleva havere, sono tutte impegnate, ò obligate"</note> although it is commonly said of the Pope: *That he never lacks money, as long as he does not lack a hand and a pen.* <note>original Italian: "Che non lui mancano mai danari, quando non manca la mano, & la penna." This refers to the Pope's power to raise funds through administrative decrees and signatures.</note> *Political Treasure, part 1, report on Rome, folio 31.* Henry II, King of France, owed more at his death than his ancestors had collected from their subjects in forty years. Emperor Charles V and his son Philip contracted much heavier debts. Bodin reports that all of this happened due to the vice of high interest <note>original: "vitio Usurarum"</note>, *chapter 2, number 667.* Therefore, a loan at extraordinary interest must never be taken unless extreme necessity urges it. See Bornitius, *this book, chapter 7, section 2*, and *The Touchstone, final chapter*; both of whom should certainly be consulted.

<margin>Mountains of Piety.</margin>
To this topic belong the "Mountains" of the Supreme Pontiffs, which are accused of impiety even by Catholics themselves. Many people everywhere are invited to deposit money into these, not only by the very certain hope of profit, but also by many additional privileges. From this it happens that anyone of the lowest lot who can scrape together money from anywhere, whether justly or unjustly, flees to those "Mountains" and secures an income for himself, so that he may spend the rest of his life without labor. Even many prostitutes shine and are adorned from this source; the fruits of Church Benefices <note>Income-generating church offices.</note> are transferred there with impunity and spent on illegitimate sons according to privilege—a fact which not even the Catho- <insert>lics themselves can deny.</insert>

The merchants, with ready minds, lent the money. Having led them into the court, he confessed the enemies' plot and exhorted them to be the guards of his person. For, he said, they would only recover their money if they kept him safe and sound. Thus it happened that for the sake of their money, the merchants took up arms; some surrounded Leucon’s person, while others guarded the palace. Leucon, with the help of these men and the most loyal friends he had around him, seized and slaughtered the participants of the conspiracy; and once the empire was restored to security, he returned the money.

# Concerning the Public Treasury, Chapter VI.

This practice has also been very frequently observed in the Kingdoms of Spain, as taught by *Vasquius* and *Caspar Klock* in *On Contributions, thesis 48*: namely, that while wars were raging, gold and silver were accepted as loans from the citizens of Seville and others arriving from the Kingdoms of the Indies <note>referring to the Spanish colonies in the Americas</note>. Add to this *Conrad Summenhart* in his *Treatise on Contracts, question 44 and following*, where he discusses this type of borrowing and its requirements at greater length.

However, Vitellius <note>Roman Emperor, 69 AD</note> acted wickedly and unjustly: for after he had attained the Principate while heavily burdened by debt, he sought out his creditors and told them that he had given them their "safety" in exchange for their money, and he demanded the return of the contract tablets <note>effectively canceling his debts by threat of force</note>. *Dio, Roman History, book 65.*

It can also be enjoined upon the wealthier subjects that they should always have a certain sum of money ready at hand, with which sudden dangers may be met. This can serve as the safest kind of Treasury, and it does not burden the Republic with interest. In this way, individual Athenians set aside a tenth part of their property or patrimony for war expenses. *Diogenes Laertius in his life of Solon; Petrus Perrenon, 2 Observations, chapter 28.*

Dionysius, the Tyrant of Syracuse, when in want of money, ordered that a declaration be made to him of all the funds belonging to families of orphans. Once this was done, he used that money himself until the individuals reached the age of legal guardianship. *Aristotle, Economics, book 2.* Following his example, some Princes claim the money of wards for themselves as a kind of Royal right <note>term: Regale; a sovereign prerogative or right belonging to the crown</note> until they reach the years of puberty, *as I said in Politics, book 1, chapter 4, number 40.*

The Ephesians, when they lacked money, passed a law stating that it was not permitted for women to wear gold; whatever gold they possessed at that time, they were to lend to the State. *Aristotle, ibid.* So too Chabrias the Athenian persuaded Tachos, King of the Egyptians, to command that whatever silver or uncoined gold anyone possessed should be brought to him. When it was brought, he persuaded the King to use it and to recommend those who had lent it to the Admirals <note>original: Navarchis</note>, who would repay the debts out of the tributes. *Aristotle, said book 2 of the Economics.*

When Hannibal was shaking Italy and besieging the City [Rome] itself, the Fathers in the Senate spoke thus: "Let us carry all silver, gold, and coined copper to the Triple-Commissioners of the Exchange <note>original: Triumviros Mensarios; public bankers appointed in times of crisis to manage state funds</note>, without any prior decree of the Senate; so that this voluntary offering and the competition to help the Republic may excite the minds of the Equestrian Order first, and then the rest of the Commoners, to emulation." But once victory was gained and the Carthaginians broken, the Senate decreed that the borrowed money must be repaid to each person in good faith. *Bodin, said chapter 2, number 654; Bornitius, this book 2, chapter 8, and book 6, chapter 5.* Indeed, unless this is done, I know not what more unjust thing could be devised. Pietro Bembo <note>A Venetian cardinal and historian (1470–1547)</note> reports in *Book 7 of the History of Venice* that the Republic labored under a severe lack of money due to the massive expenses incurred in war. Therefore, when the Senate was assembled, Doge Loredan promised that he would lend ten pounds of gold to the Republic; he then exhorted the remaining citizens, whom he knew did not lack the means, to each do the same for their part. Thus, on that day and the next, many pounds of gold were brought into the Treasury <note>original: "Ærarium"</note> as loans, freeing the City from its fear.

And in *Book 10*, the same author narrates that when they were in the war against Pope Julius II and needed money, the Senate decreed that within 25 days, those who possessed carved silver or gold should bring it to the Overseers of the Mint <note>original: "Duumviros"</note> for the coining of money. That gold or silver was to be credited to them with a profit of a tenth part; as for those who did not bring it, their goods were to be sold.

*And a little later:* Because it was evident to the Fathers <note>The Senators</note> that many of those citizens who possessed ample wealth could still not be induced to contribute to the treasury—held as they were by no charity for their fatherland and no love for the Republic—the Council of Ten <note>original: "Decemviri," the high governing body of Venice</note> commanded their ministers to first warn them of the matter. If after eight days they had contributed nothing, they were to be seized and thrust into prison; if they hid themselves, the ministers were to snatch the household property from their homes and hand it over to the magistrates to be sold off. That these two measures should be publicly ordered had never happened before that time. But these things are to be understood as regarding Fiscal debtors (as I think), as I advised above in *Chapter 2, final number, verse 3.*

III. In cases of extreme necessity, one may even resort to the selling off <term>Distraction: the legal selling or dividing of assets to pay debts</term> of some portion of the territory. Since in such a case it is even permitted to secularize Sacred things, as Jacob Bornitius <note>A 17th-century jurist and political theorist</note> teaches with several examples in *Book 2, final chapter; see also Lord Lather, Book 1 on the Census, Chapter 17.* And yet, if any part of the Territory is to be alienated, the greatest effort must be made to attach a "covenant of resale" <note>A clause allowing the state to buy the land back later</note>; or other methods should be employed which prevent a firm and perpetual alienation, ensuring that the sold goods can eventually be recovered. *The Author of the Counsel (whom they say was Lord Georg Obrecht) titled: "In what manner a State of the Empire may improve its revenues and income."* <note>original German: "Welcher maſſen ein Stand des Reichs / ſein Gefäll vnd Einkommen verbeſſern möge."</note>

of such estates, nor is it rightly undertaken even by an absolute Prince without the consent of the Estates <note>The "Estates" refers to the representative assemblies or social orders of a realm, such as a Parliament or Diet.</note>; since this pertains to the "Real Majesty" <note>original: *realem Majestatem*; a legal concept where sovereignty resides in the state/body politic rather than the person of the ruler.</note>; *Hotman, Illustrious Questions, 1; Mr. Dr. Harpprecht at the title of the proem of the Institutes, number 45, etc.; Clapmarius, book 5, chapter 12; Arnisaeus, book 3 on the Right of Majesty, chapter 1; Bornitius here, book 2, chapter 9; Lather on the Census, book 1, chapter 16; and as I said in the treatise on Appeals, chapter 2, section 16, as well as in the Politics, book 1, chapter 2, number 6, and book 2, final chapter, number 27 and following;* and it would be done to the prejudice of those who are thus separated from the state. *Heigius, part 1, question 19; Pruckmann, treatise on Regalian Rights, section on "unfettered power," member 2, fourth chapter, effect 6, page 457, etc.* 

It is upon this foundation that the donations of Constantine the Great, of Louis, and of other Emperors are challenged. <note>The "Donation of Constantine" was a forged decree claiming the Emperor gave vast territories to the Pope; the author notes it is legally contested because a ruler cannot give away the state's substance.</note> *Girard, book 4, page 391; Wolff, Memorable Readings, century 4, page 103; Bronchorst, Contradictions, 4, assertion 87.* By these same tunnels <note>A metaphor for legal undermining or strategic arguments.</note>, the Will of Lady Matilda was attacked by Otto IV. She was the daughter of the late Roger, Prince of Sicily, and wife of King Conrad, son of Emperor Henry IV; in this will, she bequeathed the March and Apulia to the Roman Church. *From Hotman, in the cited place, at the beginning.* 

And so, for this reason, the Treaty of Madrid between Charles V and Francis I was broken; because, contrary to the common law of all Nations and against the Laws of the Gallic Empire <note>France</note>, Charles had compelled the King to cede the lordship of Burgundy and Belgium without the consent of the Senate and the French People. *Martin du Bellay, book 3 of the Memoirs, page 223 and following.* For this same reason, many provinces in France were taken back from the English, which John, King of France, had given to them while he was a captive in England. *Froissart, Volume 1, chapters 201, 214, 246, and see chapter 310 at the end; Girard, book 15, page 217, book 16, page 282, etc., Volume 2.* 

And hence the people of La Rochelle <note>original: *Rupellenses*</note> did not wish to be reunited with the French Empire except expressly on this condition: <gloss>that the city of La Rochelle, and all the country of the Rochellais, should remain forever within the jurisdiction and domain of the King of France: and should never be removed from it, nor separated by marriage, by peace, nor by any adventure that might ever happen to the Kingdom of France, by whatever condition it might be.</gloss> Also in *Guillaume Paradin, book 2 of the History of Lyon, chapter 62,* Philip, King of France, promises: <gloss>that he could not alienate, in whole or in part, the rights which he has in the city of Lyon, nor release them from his hand and crown. And where that might be done, he declares by a principal edict that all such acts are of no value.</gloss> 

Nor do other peoples employ any different law: *Bodin, book 6 of the Republic, chapter 2, number 640;* namely, it is clearly provided for, mostly by the Fundamental Laws, that the state should not be diminished by alienation or mortgage without the counsel or consent of the Estates...

Thus, in the chapter *Intellecto* <note>original: "cap. intellect. extr. de jurejur." referring to a specific section of Canon Law regarding oaths</note>, the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope</note> enjoins the King of Hungary not to carry out alienations <note><term>alienations</term>: the transfer of ownership of property or rights to another party</note> made to the disgrace of the Hungarian Crown, notwithstanding the oath by which he had previously bound himself to ratify such alienations. This is especially true since he is bound, even in his coronation, to preserve the rights of his Kingdom and the honor of the Crown undiminished. And it is not only Princes who are so bound, but also in Republics—whether Popular or Aristocratic—the Senate, the People, and especially the Magistrates themselves are accustomed to swear to the same effect. Under this pretext, the people of Lucerne excused themselves when King Henry II of France requested through ambassadors that they should step down on his behalf. *Bodin, in the place just cited.* And it is specifically provided in the *Laws of Lübeck, book 2, title 5, paragraph 4*: *that a Council shall not borrow, lend, or act as a guarantor for Princes or Lords, whether Spiritual or Secular, from the common property in any measure or manner.* <note>original: "daß ein Rhat vom gemeinen Gut / für Fürsten oder Herren / Geistlich oder Weltlich / ettwas borgen / leyhen / oder aber auch vor Bürgen sich einstellen solle; in keinerley Maaß noch Weise."</note>

2. Regarding the Kings of France, *Bodin* writes (*chapter 2, number 641*) that there were those who urged Princes toward the sale of estates and other public places, as if they would make a more fruitful profit; a sentiment that brings about Tyranny and the ruin of the Republic (*namely, if richer assets are sold at a cheaper price without the most pressing necessity; for otherwise, these things would be contrary to what we shall soon say from number 654.*) But this is even more unjust, he says: because the money which unskilled Princes collect from these sales is not invested for the sake of public utility, but is usually bestowed upon the most foul and base men. Above all, those Goods and rights which are destined for the protection and preservation of the Republic must never be sold at any time: likewise the pastures of the Cities and of the Peasants, by which the poor are sustained. For all these things ought to be sold under no reasoning, because the sellers destroy the Republic and the Subjects. *Lord Obrecht, in the cited place.* This could be applied more cautiously: that estates or rights belonging to the Republic should rather be granted as a Fief <note><term>Fief</term>: land held on condition of feudal service</note> in exchange for money (with Sovereignty retained, <insert>with reservation of the Territorial Authority</insert> <note>original: "mit Vorbehalt der Landes Obrigkeit"</note>), rather than being utterly alienated. *Bornitius, book 2, chapter 7.* (For it happens very rarely that Fiefs do not revert to the Lord within the span of a hundred years: as *Latherus* observes, *book 3, chapter 1, at the end.*) And likewise, they should not be sold to any others than Subjects, lest they be simultaneously withdrawn from the jurisdiction and Command of the Prince. Let the regular nature of Fiefs <note>Feudal land holdings</note> be changed upon payment of a pension or an honorary fee: *One should allow—by means of a substantial sum of money—that vassals, in the event of a lack of feudal heirs, may appoint their daughters or others as heirs, etc.* <note>original German: "Man gestatte / vermittelst einer stattlichen summen Gelts / daß die Vasallen / in casu deficientium Feudalium heredum, jhre Töchtern oder andere / zu Erben einsetzen mögen / &c."</note> And in this way also the Byzantines, in a scarcity of money, sold public groves and Sacred places. These were indeed fruitful for a certain time, but unproductive as perpetual property. Likewise, those things which Fellowships <note>Sodalitates; guilds or religious fraternities</note> possessed, and those which pertained to ancestral rites; both others and those situated in private fields. But the most convenient method of raising money and fulfilling credit, Bodin <note>Jean Bodin, influential political philosopher</note> thinks (*said chapter 2, number 654*), is found in the words of Livy, who says: Many people, to whom a third payment was owed from the money they had loaned during the consulship of Marcus Valerius and Claudius, approached the Senate. Since the private citizens demanded what was fair, and the Republic was not solvent <note>unable to pay its debts</note>, they decreed a middle ground between equity and utility: that since a large part of them said there were lands for sale and they had a need to buy, an abundance of public land should be made available to them. The Consuls would value the land, and impose a tax of one *as* <note>a small Roman coin</note> per acre as a token to testify that it was Public land; so that if anyone, when the state was able to pay, preferred to have the money rather than the land, he could restore the land to the People, etc. Maecenas <note>advisor to Augustus Caesar</note> agrees, in his oration to Augustus in *Dio Cassius, Book 52*: I feel, he says, that you should sell the possessions brought into the treasury (of which I see many have been acquired through wars), excepting only a very few that are absolutely useful and necessary to you, and lend the price of them to others at a moderate interest. By this reasoning, the land will be more fertile when cultivated by the owners' own efforts; and these men, when they become wealthier by that opportunity, will contribute more to the public, and the republic will have sufficient and perennial revenues. # Political Discourses

Just as the Republic of Venice used this remedy at one time, and by a decree of the Fathers <note>The Venetian Senate</note>, published this Edict: That whoever among the People assisted either the fleet or the military forces with money, provisions, or soldiers, it would be so that when the war with the enemy was concluded, thirty from their number who were believed to be the best deserving would be promoted to the Patrician order. And furthermore, in the same place, Grégoire adds: That there was a similar method of collecting money in France and elsewhere, from the creation of nobles; a certain price being established by which commoners might redeem nobility, and a certain contribution being imposed on property owners—for instance, a third or another portion—for the sake of obtaining immunity in the future, after the manner of other nobles. The wealthy especially solicit this nobility, and therefore a Prince or Republic could reap a not insignificant golden harvest from it. But here a danger looms, lest the sordid and those ignoble by nature, raised to this privilege of nobility through money, should defile the rank of nobles itself to the disgrace of the entire order; and that honor, which is owed to virtue alone, should become cheapened through such filth. The Venetians also, as *Bembo* <note>Pietro Bembo, a Venetian cardinal and historian</note> records in his *History of Venice, book 7, page 308*, recalled from exile those who had fled because of an accidental death, provided they served the Republic's military for four months at their own expense along with four men fit for war.

### IV.
Beyond the ordinary course, Princes also occasionally sell **Magistracies**, and offices, dignities, and Privileges; which is not to be approved except under the most urgent necessity. *Bodin, book 6, chapter 2, number 651; Bornitius, book 2, chapter 6; after Molina; Nicolaus Betsius, Treatise on Family Pacts, last chapter, page 740; and Latherus on Census, book 3, chapter 16 and following.*

The Emperor **Justinian** disputes heavily against the merchants of Power <note>Those who buy and sell government offices</note>, when he says in *Novel 8, at the beginning*: We must provide for this entirely, that the Governors of nations, whoever hold the Civil administrations of the Provinces, should use clean hands; and abstain from every acceptance of bribes; content for those things alone which are given by the Treasury. Which will not happen otherwise, unless they themselves receive their individual posts without payment; [giving] nothing at all...
