# On the Public Treasury, Chapter VI.

<margin>The Emperor Justinian's decree on judicial integrity.</margin>
...giving nothing, neither on the occasion of voting, nor to those who wear the official belts <note>original: "cingula habent" — referring to those holding military or administrative office</note>, nor to any other person at all. For we have considered that although immoderate profit to the Empire may be diminished, nevertheless our subjects will perceive the greatest growth if they are preserved from harm by the Judges; and both the Empire and the Treasury <term>Fiscus: the Emperor's personal or state treasury</term> will abound by employing wealthy subjects, etc. And in the *New Constitutions <note>Novellae</note> 86, chapter 3*, it says: "For this reason, we appoint Judges without charge, and we command them to take an oath; so that they may preserve Justice for every petitioner according to our Laws."

So also the Emperor Alexander Severus never allowed honors involving the "right of the sword" <note>juris gladii: the power of life and death, or high criminal jurisdiction</note> to be sold, as if to say: "It is necessary that he who buys, must sell. I will not tolerate merchants of power; if I tolerate them, I cannot condemn them. For I blush to punish a man who buys and sells." — *Lampridius*.

And so Seneca says in *On Benefits, book 1, chapter 9*: It is no wonder that provinces are despoiled, and the Tribunal becomes a matter of money, knocked down to one party after a bidding war has been heard from both sides: since it is the law of nations that you may sell what you have bought.

Cicero, in his *Fourth Oration against Verres*: "But while you were Praetor, who would fear the Censor or the Law? He is not bound by it, since he was not appointed by law: or would he fear your reproach, when he had sold that which he had bought from you?"

The same thing is said to have been observed by Louis XII, King of the French: saying that merchants of this kind sell piece by piece what they had bought in bulk. Certainly, against him who buys an office, there is a presumption that he will afterwards act perversely in all things. *Paris de Puteo, Treatise on Syndicates... and Michael Piccart, Historical-Political Observations...* and I myself touched upon this in *Politics, book 2, chapter 3, number 12*.

By this reasoning also, offices are exposed as prey for the wealthier, and the poor are excluded from all dignity, contrary to Christian piety. And yet, administrators of Republics have sometimes fled to this remedy. The Venetian Senate, in order to have funds for waging war against the Emperor Maximilian, decreed: that if any citizen from the common people held a perpetual office from the Republic, and if he saw to it that ten times the annual salary (or if there be no salary, the sum of profit established before the Magistrate) was given to the Republic within fifteen days; then upon his death, either his son, grandson, brother, or whomever he had appointed as heir to that office, would succeed him. Furthermore, for those whose offices were temporary, if they brought eight times the salary to the Treasury, those offices could not be taken from them while they lived; however, by the liberality of the Fathers <note>the Senators</note>, that sum of eight times the salary was shortly after reduced by law to five times.

## CHAPTER VII.

Those who preside over the Treasury are to be appointed as <term>Quæstors</term> <note>Ancient Roman officials responsible for the administration of the treasury and public records.</note>; so named because they are created for the sake of inquiring into, preserving, and spending public money. *Aristotle, Politics book 1; Law 2, section 22, On the Origin of Law.* Today we call these Treasurers *Chamber-masters or Revenue-masters; Chamber-Councilors.* <note>original: "Cammer- oder Rentmeister; Cammer-Rhät"</note> Every Republic whatsoever seems to stand in need of this office. Their origin among the Romans was most ancient, and existed before almost all other Magistrates: *Sole law, in the beginning, Digest on the office of Quæstor.* These men, of course, collected the taxes and tributes of the Roman People in the Provinces, provided pay for the soldiers, and likewise received those payments which were weighed out by Kings and nations; they entered every single receipt and expense into the accounts. They exacted monetary penalties, both in Rome and in the Provinces, and recorded them in the public ledgers; they sold confiscated goods and returned the proceeds to the public treasury. Finally, they provided clear and distinguished accounts of all matters and monies, and once these were completed and consolidated, they deposited them into the Treasury <note>original: "Ærarium"</note> through their scribas <note>professional clerks or secretaries</note>. Indeed, the Quæstorship <term>Quæstura: an ancient Roman office responsible for the treasury and financial audits</term> was formerly held in such high honor that even men of consular rank, having already performed great honors, did not deem it unbecoming to hold the office. <margin>See Alexander ab Alexandro, *Genial Days*, book 2, chapter 2, and the commentary there by Tiraquellus; and add Lancellottus Conradus in *The Temple of Judges*, book 1, chapter 1, section 4, folio 355.</margin> This matter was handled in various ways under the Emperors <note>original: "Augustis"</note> and was frequently changed: <margin>Justus Lipsius on book 13 of the *Annals* of Tacitus, note 89.</margin> under them, the Imperial Procurators <note>original: "Procuratores Cæsaris"</note>, or Accountants <note>original: "Rationales"</note>, sustained the duties of the Quæstors. To this also pertains the entire title of the Code regarding the Office of the Count of the Sacred Largesses <note>The official in charge of the imperial treasury and mines</note>; on the Office of the Count of Private Affairs; and on the Office of the Count of the Sacred Patrimony; see also Henricus Scotanus in his *Summaries*, folio 140, etc. As for what defines a Collector, a Chief Collector, a Tax Assessor, a Leveler, an Inspector, or an Estimator; Paulus Busius teaches this in *Subtleties*, book 3, chapter 3, and I have touched upon it above.

The duty of a good Quæstor was expressed by Marcus Cato of Utica <note>Cato the Younger, famous for his integrity and strictness in financial oversight</note>, regarding whom see Plutarch in his *Life of Cato*, and above in chapter 2, final number, verse 3. Happy is the King who has a man knowing how to organize revenues and expenses. Conestagius writes that such happiness never befell the Kings of Portugal. Since the Quæstors there were always chosen from the number of the Nobility, for whom courtly favor rather than expertise had opened the way to that Office; hence he says they only gave effort to maintaining their dignity and rank by other means, while remaining little concerned for the revenues of the Kingdom. <margin>Book 1 of *The Union of Portugal and Castile*, folio 42 in my edition.</margin> More fortunate in this regard was Henry the Great, King of France <note>Henry IV</note>, who in this area utilized the faithful service of the Marquis de Rosny <note>Better known as the Duke of Sully, Henry IV's chief minister</note>. Although Waremundus may criticize him: <margin>On Subsidies, chapter 6, number 19.</margin> nevertheless, Pierre Matthieu extols him with great praise. <margin>Book 1 of the *History of France*, at the end.</margin> *He did not care,* he says, *about all the lesser gods, so long as he pleased Jupiter.* <note>original: "Il ne se soucioit... de tous les menus Dieux, pour plaire à Jupiter." A metaphor suggesting Sully ignored the complaints of minor nobles to serve the King's interests.</note>

# On the Public Treasury, Chapter VI.

Many have conducted their own business to the detriment of the King and his people; this man, however, like Craterus <note>A loyal general and confidant of Alexander the Great.</note> near Alexander, considers only the service and the profit of the King. The Emperors of the Turks deprive those whom they place in charge of their Treasury of a necessary part of the body <note>A reference to the use of eunuchs in Ottoman administration.</note>: whether this is done rightly is disputed by Kirchner against Bodin <note>Hermann Kirchner (1562–1620) and Jean Bodin (1530–1596), influential political theorists.</note> in his *Discourse on the Republic, 16, corollary 1.* It seems also that he whom Statius extols with much praise was a Prefect of the Treasury, in *Book 3 of the Silvae: The Tears of Etruscus.* <note>Publius Papinius Statius (c. 45–96 AD); the poem "The Tears of Etruscus" honors the father of Claudius Etruscus, a high-ranking financial official.</note>

> Through all peoples, and the expenses of the great world.

Regarding a certain Romeo, Mariana writes thus in *Book 3 of the Instruction of a King, chapter 7, page 263 in my copy:* <note>Juan de Mariana (1536–1624), a Spanish Jesuit historian.</note> Romeo, although a foreign man, was accepted into the favor of Raymond, Count of Provence. When he had rendered the taxes three times greater than they were before through honest means, he was finally attacked by accusations and called to account. Offended by such injury, he departed with the staff and scrip <note>A small bag or satchel carried by pilgrims.</note> with which he had come to Compostela; nor could it ever be known from where he had come, or where he went. Truly, if we had a few Romeos in our time, we would by no means be pressed by such great poverty in the treasury.

Just as faithful and prudent <term>Quaestors</term> <note>Treasury officials or financial administrators.</note> are to be praised, so on the contrary, the <term>Exactors</term> <note>Tax collectors, often used here in a pejorative sense for those who extort.</note> and the architects of unlawful exactions (**forgers of taxes, schemers**) are not to be listened to by the Prince: although the whole world now almost abounds with, and is oppressed by, a multitude of them. We have everywhere as many masters of "making a treasury" as possible (says Bodin in *Book 6 of the Republic, chapter 2, at the beginning*) who are accustomed to exhaust the resources of the citizens and urge Princes toward unusual types of taxes. Indeed, of those who so craftily devise these things, I have seen no one who would take account of dignity and honesty in that category. These Exactors are for the most part foreigners, and by this means, to great digni—

They accommodate themselves to the temperament of the King, partly by investigating ways of finding money, and partly by removing obstacles which seem able to cast any delay upon the King's counsels and purpose. *Conestaggio, On the Union of the Kingdoms of Portugal and Castile, page 36 in my copy.* These men imitate the agents of Trajan <note>Roman Emperor, 98–117 AD</note>; of whom it is said that each one used to meet with wealthy men and ask: "What do you have? When he had learned this, he added a third: "Lay down what you have." *Erasmus, in the Apothegms, book 8, page 629 in my copy.* Such men in former times in France were certain Italians. And such new burdens will turn out this way: those advisors do not consult for the Prince, but for themselves: **they cost more than they create in profit.** Whence Bernard de Girard, *book 2 of the History of France, page 126,* says of Protadius, the advisor of Brunhilda: "He advised his master to make exactions, the profit of which he himself drew; which is a customary thing for those who, by such villainous and foul means, have gained the favor of Princes." It is the custom of almost all such men to cloak the ruin of the State with their own robberies; and under this pretext, to behave so impudently that if anyone opposes their rapacity, they dare to cry out that an injury is being done to themselves and to the State. And therefore **Saint Luke** most excellently attributes the word <term>συκοφαντεῖν</term> <note>sykophantein: to extort by false charges or "to play the sycophant"</note> to the person of the Master of the Tax Collectors. **Malan**, *in the larger annotations on Luke chapter 19, verse 8.* Salvian also, in *book 4 of the Government of God,* describes those vultures who turn their minds to rapacity, and by various and exquisite calumnies and auctions...

# Concerning the Public Treasury. Chapter VII.

He condemns those who plunder through a singular kind of greed with these words:

> It is a more serious matter that the many are proscribed by the few, for whom the public tax collection is their private prey, and who turn the titles of fiscal debt into private gain. And this is done not only by the highest officials, but by almost the lowest; not only by the Judges, but even by those serving the Judges. For what cities are there—not to mention the towns and villages—where there are not as many Tyrants as there are Court officials? <note>original: "Curiales." These were members of the municipal councils in the Roman Empire, often burdened with the unpopular task of tax collection.</note>

These are the "Palatine dogs," devouring all the best men. *Boethius, On the Consolation of Philosophy, Book 1, prose 4, page 9 in my edition.* <note>Boethius (c. 477–524 AD) was a philosopher and statesman; "Palatine dogs" refers to corrupt palace officials.</note> Today, says Waremundus ab Erenberg, *On Subsidies, chapter 6, number 13, and throughout the discourse, and after him, Keckermann, Practical Disputation 34, problem 14,* there are found Masters who, with great diligence and labor, devise new ways of collecting and raising money and sell these schemes to Princes. It is their custom to persuade Princes that taxes can be established without injury or loss to the Subjects, and that there will be no Subject who will not pay the imposed Tribute with a cheerful face and the greatest joy.

The most prudent Landgrave <note>A German noble title, specifically the Count of a large territory.</note> of Hesse, Philip, judged those who urge such "Sweet Tributes" to be worthy of the noose. Such men are worthy not of reward, but most worthy of the noose, the rod, and the sword. They also fall into the crime of Bribery <note>original: "Ambitus," referring to unlawful striving for office or favor.</note> if they act with this end in view: that by pleasing the Prince, they might extort dignities for themselves, or by enriching the Treasury in this way, they might capture the Prince's favor. *Deciani, Criminal Practice 8, chapter 22, number 17, and chapter 23, number 5.* Likewise, those who advise taxes that are not supported by legitimate custom—by which the subjects are oppressed and burdened—are branded with infamy by the public Law of Equestrian Games <note>original: "Turnier," referring to the rules of knightly tournaments where dishonorable men were excluded.</note>. *Tournament Articles 9 and 11.*

To this also pertains an anecdote related by Caspar Ens, *Epidorpides, volume 2, page 187*: A certain Cardinal was labored under a heavy hatred by everyone, because he was commonly believed to be the author of new Contributions for the Pope. When, however, methods for raising money were being discussed before the Pope and certain more secret Advisors, one man who was not very favorable to the Cardinal said:

> Indeed, Most Holy Father, I know of no better way of collecting money without any complaint from the Subjects—nay, even with their very joy—than if the skin were stripped from Armellino (for that was the Cardinal's name) and carried around your domain, as is otherwise done with the skins of wolves. For I do not doubt that all your Subjects would voluntarily contribute a coin just for the sake of inspecting it.

For it is often the case (as I have cited elsewhere from Boccalini, *Parnassus, century 2, report 6, page 34*) that the collector is more hated than the tax itself.

# Political Discourses

than the collection itself. And therefore, the punishment of these same men <note>the corrupt tax collectors</note> best pacifies the indignant minds of the people. *Boccalini, 2nd Advertisement, 82.* A Prince is bound to resist these Scoundrels with every effort, and to consider this: that he should count it as the greatest benefit given to his People, that he has freed them from such collectors. *Hippolytus a Collibus, in The Prince, chapter 33.* According to Cassiodorus, *Variae, Book 5, Epistle 39,* King Theodoric was very reluctant to allow the fortunes of the Provincials to be subject to the will of the collectors; he adds: "It is a type of evident plunder to give according to the will of one who hastens to increase his own advantage further." These Collectors may call "good and easy" that which is the worst thing in the Kingdom: to whom a pious Prince should in no way give ear. 

Hence Darius, the son of Xerxes <note>The author likely means Darius I, father of Xerxes, or is citing Plutarch's account of Darius's moderation</note>, is praised; when he had proclaimed a tribute for his Subjects, he summoned the Governors of the Provinces and asked them whether that Tribute was heavy for the People. And when they replied that it was moderate, he ordered that they should collect only half of that part. *Plutarch, in Apophthegms.* And generally, no thing so exterminates the good as simulated good. For a manifest evil is fled from and avoided as an evil; but an evil hidden under the appearance of Good, while it is not recognized, is not avoided, but is looked up to as if it were Good, and being thus joined, it exterminates the Good. 

A prudent Prince also ought not to lend an ear immediately to those "Inventors" <note>referring to 'projectors' or people who invent new schemes for taxation</note>; but he ought first to examine diligently those things which they propose. To be sure, those inventions are sometimes beautiful in theory; but more often they presuppose many things of a sort that are found to be entirely false. *See the documents of this matter in Bodin, Book 6, chapter 2, number 663 and following.* Likewise, not every Region can bear heavier Tributes and Taxes <term>Vectigalia: taxes on goods or customs duties</term>. Hence *Juan de Mariana, in Book 3 of The Kingly Institution,* writes prudently: let it be persuaded that it is not fitting for Spain to be burdened with great Taxes. First, because a great part of it consists of places with squalid dryness, horrid cliffs, and rocks. Often, on account of the dryness of the air, we labor under a penury of provisions, so that the yield does not respond to the labor and the expenses: in which case it becomes a grave thing to increase the calamity of the time with new and great Tributes. 

Next, by the Plowmen in Spain, and the Shepherds, and all other farmers, the tithes <term>decuma fructuum: the tenth part of the produce</term> of all fruits are paid with complete faith to the Temples <note>the Church</note>. If as much again is forced to be paid to the Lords of the estates—certainly by those who do not have their own fields—how much will be left for the wretched ones, both for themselves to live on, and for what may be contributed into the Treasury <term>Aerarium: the public treasury</term>: since it is rather necessary to support them...

3. All Councilors should engrave upon their hearts and minds what *Rebuffus* <note>Pierre Rebuffi (1487–1557), a prominent French jurist</note> writes *on the law regarding the significance of words*: Those who advise a Prince to impose new Tributes and Taxes without great cause are to be tortured perpetually in Hell with Tartarean punishments. He cites that passage from *the second book of Maccabees, chapter 7, verse 31* (as I also mentioned above in chapter 4, number 2, verse 2): *And you, who have become the inventor of all malice, shall not escape the hand of the Lord.* <note>original Latin: "Et tu, qui Inventor omnis malitiæ factus es, non effugies manum Domini"</note> Think, therefore, that you shall die, and soon, and your generation shall quickly be extinguished. For how can they be pleasing to God, who, in order to flourish themselves, allow their neighbor to waste away in calamity with no hope of safety appearing? *Zephaniah* also speaks of these same people in *chapter 1, verse 9*: *I will visit [punishment] upon those who fill the house of their masters with robbery and deceit.* This is, as *Jonathan, the Chaldean Paraphrast* <note>Referring to the Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/interpretation of the Hebrew Bible</note> interprets it: with wealth acquired through fraud and plunder.

To this must certainly be added *Erasmus* in his *treatise On the Tongue, page 144*, where he relates an elegant story concerning a certain favor of exaction: In Paris, he says, there is shown in the grain market (if I am not mistaken) the mouth of a sewer, in which a certain man ordered himself to be buried, having too late repented of his evil counsel. He had seen the King sad and anxious. The cause of the sorrow was a shortage of money. To relieve the King, this man persuaded him to exact one or two small copper coins even from the tiny items that the peasants bring into the City, and this for a period of only two years. When they saw that a significant amount of money was collected from this in such a crowded City—evidently according to the sentiment of *Hesiod*: *from many small things, a huge heap is forged*—that which had once begun to be given was never released. *It is dangerous to let a dog taste the entrails* <note>original Greek: Χαλεπὸν χορίων κύνα γεῦσαι. A proverb suggesting that once someone gets a taste of easy profit, they cannot be stopped.</note>. Indeed, following this example, many more exactions were devised. When the man who had given the advice saw that he did not have the same authority in dissuading as he had in persuading, he took punishment upon himself for his ill-considered counsel, and simultaneously warned others not to strike against the same stone; he provided in his will to be buried in that sewer into which all the filth of that market flows, where the execution of that exaction remains even to this very day.

I also add what *Jovianus Pontanus* writes in *book 4 on obedience, chapter 7*: The rights of the treasury must be protected; however, the suspicion of avarice must be removed. *Petrus Bisuldunus*, a most mischievous man, while for the sake of enriching the Royal Treasury, [violated] divine and hu— <note>The text cuts off mid-word "humana" (human), continued on the next page.</note>

<margin>Giovanni Pontano, *On Prudence*, book 5.</margin>

This was despite seeing that the Treasury, exhausted by the profusion and bribes of the Emperors, was not sufficient to bear the Public expenses. For everything that **Leo** <note>Leo I, predecessor to Zeno</note> had left in the Treasury had been quickly exhausted by Zeno; both by giving unwisely to friends and by not exercising enough diligence to catch the thefts of others.

# On the Public Treasury, Chapter VII.

...under the guise of accounts, or in the name of expenses: as <note>George</note> Buchanan notes happened in the Kingdom of Scotland in Book 10, folio 333, under the 102nd King. Such individuals should be publicly and clearly marked. Nor should one imitate Augustus, who appointed Licinius, a freedman of Caesar, as governor of Gaul; when he had brought many losses upon the Gauls through various taxes and was heavily accused on that account, he did not doubt that his life was in danger. Then Augustus granted life to the man as he pleaded against death, but took for himself those riches which Licinius had accumulated over a long time. <note>See</note> Dio Cassius, Book 54; Aerodius, *On Adjudicated Matters*, Book 9, title 3, chapter 16, folio 759.

Indeed, what punishment is deserved by the ministers of Princes of this kind, who exceed the limits of their mandate or of justice in their exactions by increasing them at their own whim? This is shown by the laws passed by the Roman Emperors against <term>Superexactores</term> <note>over-collectors or those who extort more than the legal tax</note>: by which these men are punished not only with a double penalty to be paid to the harmed subjects, but even with capital punishment if they persist in the crime. <note>See</note> Law 1, Code, *On Over-exactions*, Book 10; Nicolaus Betsius, *On Family Pacts*, last chapter, folio 737.

There is no one who does not know how much audacity and recklessness is found in the factions of the <term>Publicani</term> <note>tax farmers or private collectors of public revenue</note>; therefore the Praetor, to restrain their boldness, proposed a singular edict, as Ulpian says in Law *Quantae* 12, Digest, *On Tax Farmers*. Certainly, officials and others to whom a matter is specifically entrusted, if they act treacherously in it, commit theft; indeed, an official in that case is not immune from <term>Peculatus</term> <note>the crime of embezzling public funds or property</note>. <note>See</note> Section *Item Lex Julia Peculatus* 9, where the interpreters discuss the Institutes, *On Public Judgments*; Law 1, Code, *On the Crime of Embezzlement*; Law 2, section 1, *On Guardianship and the Separation of Accounts*; Law *Tutor* 33, *On Theft*; Law *Tres Tutores* 55, section 1, *On the Administration and Risk of Guardians*. Petrus Friderus of Minden, *On Extraordinary Processes*, 2, chapter 13, penultimate and last numbers.

Nor can he escape the death penalty for that reason, especially if forgery, perjury, or other circumstances aggravate the crime. See Wesenbeck in the *Paratitla* on the Digest, *On Embezzlement*, numbers 7 and 9; Jean Papon, Book 22, title 2, arrest 1; Theodor Petreus, *Criminal Conclusions*, theses 47 and 53; and at length Jacob Alemannus, decision 2; and Berlichius, Volume 5, conclusion 57. I remember that this opinion prevailed after a laborious dispute among the most distinguished legal scholars. Although Matthias Coler, *Decisions*, Volume 1, decision 207; the compilers of the *Consultations of Saxon Decisions* revised by Petrus Friderus of Minden, part 5, question 70; and the Doctors of Law commonly seem to disagree. Indeed, Roman law subjects him who even lends out fiscal gold to the punishment of perpetual exile and deportation, with all his goods confiscated. Law 2, Code, *On those who have accepted a loan of money from public accounts*, Book 10.

...under the best of Princes, Trajan, of whom Gaius Plinius <note>Pliny the Younger, a Roman lawyer and author</note> writes as follows: <margin>Gyr. folio 72, edited by Justus Lipsius <note>A famous 16th-century Flemish humanist scholar</note></margin> "How pleasing it is to see the Treasury <note>original: *Aerarium*, the public fund of the Roman people</note> quiet, and in such a state as it was before the informers existed! Now that Temple is truly a God: it is no longer a place for the despoiling of citizens, nor a cruel receptacle for blood-stained spoils; nor is there any place in the whole world where, under the best Prince, good men are unequal to the wicked. The honor of the laws remains, and nothing of public utility has been torn away. Punishment has not been remitted for anyone, but rather added; only one thing has changed: now it is not the informers who are feared, but the laws. But perhaps you do not restrain the Imperial Purse <note>original: *Fiscus*, the private fund of the Emperor</note> with the same integrity as you do the Public Treasury? On the contrary, you restrain it with even greater care, believing that you have less license over what is yours than over what is public. An *Agent* is even summoned against your own Steward; 'Come to court,' he says, 'follow me to the Tribunal.' He assigns a judge to the Imperial Purse by lot. One is allowed to reject him, allowed to cry out: 'This man is timid and understands the blessings of the age too little; I want that man, for he loves Caesar boldly.' The Principate and Liberty use the same Forum. What is your chief glory is that the Imperial Purse is frequently defeated; it never has a bad case except under a good Prince. This is a great merit; but greater still is that you have such Stewards that, for the most part, your subjects would not prefer any other judges," etc.

## CHAPTER VIII. AND LAST.

Something must be added concerning the CENSUS. For it is established (especially for the distribution of Tributes) that wealth should be publicly known. <note>See the extensive writings of Jean Bodin, *Six Books of the Commonwealth*, book 6, chapter 1; Nicolas de Montand in *The Mirror of France*, folio 675; Keckermann, *Practical Disputations*, 34, problem 10.</note> Nor is it only useful if a valuation of goods is made, but also if the age, sex, and lands of the citizens are described. <note>Discussed at length by Philipp Hænon, *Political Disputations*, thesis 8 through 17.</note> Baptismal and death registers, tax books, assessments, and land registries <note>original: *Tauff- und Todtenbücher/ Steurbücher/ Æstimum, Catastrum*</note>. Birthdays and days of death are to be properly noted. And so the Roman citizens were accustomed (by the decree of Marcus Antoninus <note>The Emperor Marcus Aurelius</note>) so that the status of men should not be ambiguous, to declare their newborn children before the Prefect of the Treasury of Saturn <note>The temple where public records and funds were kept</note> within the third day. Which also serves for proof...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the administration of the public treasury and the legal frameworks governing the estates of the nobility and the common citizenry.</meta>

# On the Public Treasury, Chapter 8 & Last — Page 225

Francis I, King of the French, established in his more recent laws a more secure [legal status] for those of age. The Venetians likewise established the same law by a Decree of the Senate for the safer assertion of the nobility's rights. <term>Johannes Corasius</term> <note>Jean de Coras (1512–1572), a celebrated French jurist</note> on the Law of the Emperor, book 8 of the Digest regarding the status of men; <term>Conrad Rittershusius</term> <note>A German jurist and classical scholar</note> in his *Mirror of the Civilly Good Prince*, page 63. Inventories of feudal properties must also be drawn up, by which they may be exactly separated from those goods which vassals possess by <term>Allodial Right</term> <note>Land owned independently, without any superior feudal lord</note>; all of which things are most conducive to shortening legal disputes.

Since all collections of <term>Taxes</term> <note>original: "Vectigalium"</note> ought to be exacted according to the norm of equity; and since equity is chiefly to be considered and weighed according to the proportion of goods; and since proportion cannot be investigated unless the individual goods of citizens are examined, inquired into, and valued: therefore, the instrument of the <term>Census</term> was devised, by which the patrimonies of individual citizens are valued and assessed. This is nothing other than the publicly made valuation and designation of the goods of individual citizens: <term>Bornitius</term> <note>Jacob Bornitz, a writer on political economy</note> book 5, chapter 2. Hence among the Greeks it is called <term>valuation</term> <note>original Greek: "τίμημα"</note> or even <term>description/registration</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀπογραφή"</note>. And so <term>Theophilus</term>, the Greek translator of the *Institutes*, says in the penultimate section on the title of Freedmen: "The Census was a tablet in which the wealth of the Romans was described, so that if the situation required, each person might contribute a tribute according to his means."

This work is indeed very arduous, especially if a people is unaccustomed to it, as the <term>Emperor Claudius</term> testifies on the bronze tablet still existing at Lyon, and represented by <term>Guillaume Paradin</term> in the *History of Lyon*, book 1, chapter 19. But the public benefit outweighs the difficulty, as does the equity of private law. Hence, very few Republics are found which have not approved of the Census; and by the calculation of all political thinkers, it is judged a clearly most wholesome thing for a future great Empire. <term>Jean de Chokier</term>, *Political Aphorisms*, book 2, chapter 10, page 94, under number 3. Even the <term>Censorship</term> of the Romans itself was not originally invented for the correction of morals, but for the description of all citizens—their age, number, rank, condition, and the valuation of all fortunes and means. <term>Servius Tullius</term>, the sixth King of the Romans, first instituted the <term>Census</term>, by which things opportune for both peace and war might be provided. # Political Discourses

The Republic was born through the distribution of privileges and the supreme skill of the King, so that all distinctions of patrimony, dignity, age, arts, and offices were recorded in registers; it was as if the greatest State were managed with the diligence of the greatest Household. *See Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 4, my edition number 19 and following; Pierre Grégoire of Toulouse, book 3, chapter 4, number 7, etc.* Now William, Duke of Normandy, commonly surnamed the <term>Conqueror</term> <note>original: "questor", likely a typo or specific legal usage for "Acquirer/Conqueror"</note> on account of his occupation of England, among other methods of strengthening his Empire, caused all of England to be described and recorded in the Archives: how much land each of his Barons possessed, how many knights' fees, how many <term>plowlands</term> <note>original: "carrucas", a medieval measure of land</note>, how many villagers, how many animals, and indeed how much liquid money each person possessed in his entire Kingdom, from the greatest even to the least, and how much revenue each possession was able to yield, etc. *John Selden, in The Two Faces of the English Janus, book 2, number 1.*

2. Ulpian indicates what the form of the Census was in the past, *in law 4 of the Digest, on Censuses.* Today, it is generally observed that individuals declare how much they hold in Goods. In some places, that declaration is made by means of an oath: **Sworn Tax.** <note>original German: "Geschworne Steuer"</note> In such cases, however, it seems to be sufficient if one estimates one's property at the common price, even if one would not wish to sell it at that price due to personal affection. *Law on prices, 63, on the Falcidian Law.* However, concerning the "Unregistered"—that is, those who did not wish to be counted or have their goods appraised, or who in bad faith allowed them to be appraised for less than they were worth—according to the Law passed by Servius Tullius (as Livy witnesses), the penalty was chains and death, or (according to Dionysius of Halicarnassus) that they be beaten and sold after their goods were confiscated. Today, in some places, the custom is accepted <insert>that the Magistrate is authorized to purchase the property for the same high value at which it was appraised by the owner.</insert> <note>original German: "daß die Obrigkeit / das Vermögen / vmb so hoch es von jhm geschätzt würdt / an sich zulösen / befugt ist." This was a clever way to prevent under-reporting: if you valued your house too low to avoid taxes, the state could simply buy it from you at that low price.</note> Likewise, against one who does not declare goods subject to public Collections and Exactations, an <term>action of forfeiture</term> <note>original: "actio commissi"</note> is exercised according to some, as I said above. *last number.* And this is expressly provided for in Saxon Law. But in that case, if someone does declare the thing but fraudulently estimates it at a lower value, only that which exceeds the estimation—not the whole thing—falls into forfeiture. *Thomas Maullius, on Homage, chapter 9, number 136, etc.* In Lübeck Law, book 2, final title, paragraph 3, I find it decreed: <insert>He who has not acted rightly under the oath shall fall under the punishment of the Council, and shall additionally pay the tax.</insert> <note>original German: "Der nicht recht bey dem Eydt gethaan / der sol in des Rhats Straaff gefallen seyn / darzu den Schoß geben."</note>

# On the Public Treasury, Chapter VIII and Last

<margin>The Senate must be informed of the state of the treasury.</margin>
...by the authority of the Senate; so that it may be clearly understood by them how great the resources are, and how great the poverty of the Treasury may be; in order that the Republic may be more conveniently protected, and that immense gifts and expenditures may be countered. *Bodin, Book 6 of The Republic, chapter 2, number 672. Scipio Ammirato, book 1, discourse 4. Clapmarius, book 5 of Secrets of State, chapter 14. Caspar Ens, Apparatus for Banquets, book 2, title on the secrets of Princes, book 15, page 155. Bulenger, On Taxes, chapter 57, from the beginning.* **Princely Table Talk, book 1, chapter 1.** <note>Original: "Fürstliche Tischreden" - likely referring to a collection of political or moral anecdotes.</note> Regarding this matter, given the opportunity, I am inclined to expound more broadly.

<margin>Cicero on the duty of a Senator.</margin>
A Senator should uphold the causes of the People, and it is necessary for him to know the Republic; a subject which is broad in scope. He must know what Soldiers he has, what strength he possesses in the Treasury <term>Ærarium: the public treasury of ancient Rome, housed in the Temple of Saturn</term>: what Allies the Republic has, what Friends, what Tributaries; by what Law, condition, and treaty each one is bound? He must maintain the custom of decreeing and know the examples of the ancestors. All of this is a matter of knowledge, diligence, and memory, without which a Senator can in no way be prepared. *Cicero, Book 3 on the Laws, near the end, page 460, Gothofredus edition.* And of this industry, Cato the Younger can provide an example: of whom Plutarch writes thus, in his *Life, number 6:* Not out of a desire for glory, nor for wealth, nor by accidental chance, as some others are brought to handle public affairs, did he take up the work; he considered this to be the duty of a good man; that he ought to be more intent upon it than a bee is upon its honey. And so he even took pains that from his friends and hosts, whom he had everywhere, the administrations of the Provinces, the decrees, the judgments, and the principal deeds should be written out to him. And a Prince ought to know these same things all the more; because upon him alone falls as much of a burden as rests upon many Senators in a Republic. The Emperor Hadrian <note>Reigned 117–138 AD; known for his extensive travels and administrative reforms.</note> so embraced all public accounts that any diligent father of a family does not know his own private house as well. *Spartianus, in his Life [of Hadrian], page 132, Friedrich Sylburg edition.*

2. By the same reasoning, a Counselor <term>Consiliarius: a high-level political advisor or member of a prince's council</term> who assists the Prince, will also apply the greatest study and diligence to knowing all those things, even the smallest, which seem to pertain to the Principality in which he serves. He will investigate the Prince and the Court from every side; as well as the nature and character of the other Ministers and Counselors: what and how great is the entire dominion of the Prince, what Provinces, Cities, Towns, and Places are subject to that dominion? Indeed, how many miles the Provinces themselves have in length, and how many in circumference; the nature of the places...

I say, the extent and the location. Whether they are fortified by mountains, the sea, a river, a ditch, or a lake; what their advantages are, and whether supplies can be blocked; whether there is abundance or a scarcity of grain; and what advantages and disadvantages the Republic <note>Latin: *Respublica*; here referring to the state or commonwealth in general</note> possesses? What exactly is disputed in the Principality, with whom, and for what reasons: which provinces are to be administered, what the fundamental laws are, what specific laws and liberties they use, by what custom they are guided, or by what discipline, practice, and habit they are governed; in what things the Citizens delight, what sustains them, and how they are disposed toward the Prince? What is the revenue from those things imported or exported, from the pastures of public lands, from salt, wine, oil, grain, from trade, and from the Tributes of the Subjects? What is the Treasury <note>Latin: *Aerarium*; the public finances or storehouse of wealth</note>: whether the Subjects are pressed by excessive Taxes <note>Latin: *Vectigalia*</note> or other burdens? Whether they are devoted to trade: whether they abound in wealth? How great a number of soldiers can be levied in each Province? What is the Prince's family, what are his connections, affinities, and friendships; what treaties exist, and what is to be hoped from them; whose interests has the Prince undertaken to defend? And in short, he shall apply all study, care, thought, and skill to all things, even the most minute, which if neglected could be to the detriment of the public.

<margin>*Hippolytus a Collibus in The Counselor, folio 262, etc.* <note>Hippolytus a Collibus (1561–1612) was a noted legal scholar and diplomat.</note></margin>
Because if anyone is ignorant of these things, he cannot give prudent counsel: a point which Aristotle teaches in the *Rhetoric, Book 1, Chapter 4*, in the following words, which I shall set down (since they are most worthy of knowing); do not be loath to read them, O Best of Readers. > Generally, the things about which all men consult, and about which those who deliberate make an effort, are chiefly five in number. These are: the preparation of money <note>public finances</note>, war and peace; furthermore, the guarding of the Region, and those things which are imported and exported, and Legislation. Therefore, he who is to deliberate on the preparation of money must know the revenues of the City <note>Greek/Latin: *Civitas*; the state or political community</note>, how many and how great they are; so that if any is lacking, it may be added, and if any is too small, it may be increased. Furthermore, he must know all the expenses of the City, so that if any is superfluous, it may be removed; and if any is too great, it may be made smaller. For men become wealthier not only by adding to what is present, but also by subtracting from expenses. And it is possible to perceive these things not only from experience of one's own affairs; but it is also necessary to be a researcher of what others have discovered, for the sake of that deliberation which is held concerning these matters. But concerning war and peace, it is necessary to know the power of the City...

# On the Public Treasury: Chapter VIII and Last

How much wealth is currently present, how much might yet be acquired, what is the nature of that which is held, and what might be added to it? Furthermore, it is necessary to know how and what wars have been waged; and this must be known not only for one's own State, but also for neighboring states, or even those with whom it is glorious to contend. While peace should be maintained with the more powerful, the decision to go to war with the lesser should remain at one's own discretion. One must also know if their resources are similar or dissimilar to our own, for it is in this comparison that we determine whether we possess the advantage or are inferior. For these reasons, it is necessary to have observed not only our own wars but also those of others, and what their outcomes were; for similar causes naturally produce similar effects.

Furthermore, regarding the defense of the Territory, one must not be ignorant of how it is guarded; one must know the size of the guard, its form, and the locations of the garrisons. This is impossible unless one is skilled in the geography of the Region, so that if the guard is too small, it may be increased; if any part is superfluous, it may be removed; and the strategic locations may be better preserved.

Regarding the food supply: how much expense is sufficient for the state, how much is produced there, and how much is imported? Which things require exportation and which importation, so that agreements and treaties may be made with those who are useful for these purposes? For it is necessary to keep the Citizens free from blame <note>original: "culpâ carentes," implying keeping the populace satisfied to prevent unrest</note> in relation to two kinds of people: both the more powerful and those who are useful for these commercial matters.

For security, it is necessary to be able to perceive all these things; but it is of no small importance to understand Legislation. For in the Laws consists the safety of the State. Therefore, it is necessary to know how many forms of Government <note>original: "Rerumpublicarum," referring to the Greek 'politeia' or systems of governance</note> there are, what is beneficial to each, and by what things they are naturally corrupted—both by factors internal to the State and by those external to it. I say "corrupted by internal factors" because, except for the best form of Republic, all others are corrupted both by being "loosened" or "tightened" <note>This is a musical metaphor often used by Aristotle to describe the tension in political systems</note>. For example, a Democracy becomes weaker not only if it is loosened, until it finally reaches an Oligarchy <note>Rule by the few</note>, but also if it is tightened too much. Just as with hookedness or flatness of the nose: if they are loosened, they return to a moderate shape, but if they become excessively hooked or flat, they are so disposed that they no longer even look like noses.

It is useful for Legislation not only to understand what benefits the Republic by observing the past, but also to know what exists among other peoples, and which forms are suitable for which groups. Therefore, it is manifest that for the purpose of Legislation, travels to foreign lands are useful. From this...

# Political Discourses

Indeed, one may take the laws of nations as a guide; but for civil deliberations, one should look to the histories of those who write concerning human actions.

**3.** All these matters (which are necessary for a Prince, a Senator, or a Counselor to know), if they cannot be safely entrusted to memory, should be consecrated to the eternity of writing. This follows the example of the most shrewd Princes. **Augustus** left behind a small book <note>original: "Libellum"</note> written in his own hand for his successor, which was a **Summary of the entire Empire** <note>original: "totius Imperii Breviarium"</note>. In it were contained the public resources: how many citizens and allies were under arms, how many military standards were everywhere; how many fleets, kingdoms, provinces, tributes, taxes, and necessities (public burdens) and grants? How much money was in the Treasury <note>The *Aerarium* was the public treasury of Rome</note> and the private imperial funds <note>The *Fiscus*</note>, and the remainders of the taxes? He had also added the names of the freedmen and slaves from whom an accounting was to be demanded. *Tacitus, Annals book 1, my page 5; Suetonius, last chapter on Augustus; Dio, book 56, Year of Rome 767.* Similarly, **Amurath III** <note>Murad III, Sultan of the Ottoman Empire (reigned 1574–1595)</note>, who ruled the Turks within recent memory, wished above all else that the state of his Empire be perfectly clear to him; and for this purpose, he kept his own Commentaries on all business that occurred, all revenues that reached him by any means, and the expenses for which each was spent, stored near him on a certain table; after his death, these came into the hands of his son, who also preserves them diligently. *Lazzaro Soranzo, The Ottoman, chapter 49. Bodin has other examples of Princes in the said chapter 2, book 6, number 672 and following.* Relevant here is the *Register of Both Empires* <note>The *Notitia Dignitatum*, a document of the late Roman Empire</note>, illustrated with commentaries by Pancirollus; as well as the *Themes* of Constantine Porphyrogenitus; likewise the book by the same author, *On Administering the Empire*, written for his son, which was sufficiently praised by Casaubon in his *Preface to Polybius*. Yet these books just named contain only one or two chapters of an Accounting Ledger. The creation and possession of such an **Accounting Ledger** <note>original: "Rationarium"</note> is so closely joined to Imperial power that when Augustus, weary from long illness, thought of restoring the Republic, he summoned the Magistrates and Senate to his house and handed the Ledger to them as the most certain symbol of the Realm. *Suetonius, Augustus, chapter 28.* For this purpose, it seems probable that after his father's death, when Tiberius was pretending to reject the succession of the Empire, he ordered the often-mentioned book to be brought forth and read aloud in the Senate. *Tacitus, in the place cited above.*

# On the Public Treasury: Chapter 8 and Last

It seems necessary that records be maintained and varied according to the diversity of the matters contained within them. We read that Charlemagne <note>original: "Carolum M." referring to Carolus Magnus</note> did not neglect this practice. <margin>Johannes Aventinus, Book 4 of the *Annals of the Bavarians*. Bernard de Girard, Lord of Haillan, Book 4 of the *History of France*, page 369.</margin> For whatever he heard, or whatever came to his mind that he judged worthy of memory, he would commit to wax tablets—which were always kept ready for this purpose—so that he might more easily remember them later. No less by ancient institution were the "Briefs of Census" <note>Summaries of tax and population records</note> sent annually to the Roman Emperors; for the diligence of a good age demands the reliability of public instruction. Indeed, it is fitting that Princes and the "parents of the human race" be informed of what new additions the venerable Order <note>The Senate</note> gains from the arrival of new Senators, or what is lost through exemptions. <margin>Symmachus, Book 10, Letter 60.</margin> Today, we see nothing more frequent or common than the unworthy being promoted while the worthy are oppressed and hidden; the chief cause of this is that Princes do not properly know either group. <margin>Caspar Ens, *The Second Banquet*, page 278, under the title: "Great men must maintain an accurate distinction among their ministers."</margin>

Above all, therefore, I believe it suits the wisdom and goodness of a Prince to form a mental picture of the brave and outstanding men of all the provinces subject to him (whom he may know by reputation) and their qualities: so that, surely, when some office becomes vacant, he may be mindful of them. Those who know they are included in this book will be more eager and will strive to conduct themselves as equals to the high opinion of their Prince; those, however, whose names are not yet inserted in this book, will flee from no danger in order to reach that status. Therefore, in this little book of ours, and in the Prince's manual, a specific title (or chapter) should be adapted for this matter, and it should be designated the **Title of Honor**. And when the Prince hears the excellent virtue of someone being commended, after proper inquiry, he should announce in a clear voice that this person has been enrolled in his Breviary <note>A concise record or handbook</note>. This is a practice that Louis XII also laudably followed in appointing judges. Indeed, upon the death of the President of the Consistory of Agen, he conferred this most honorable and distinguished office—free of charge—upon a certain studious youth whom he had heard speaking most elegantly at Orléans, and whose name he had noted in the manner we propose. He did the same in other instances when decreeing honors. <margin>Blaise de Monluc, *Military Commentaries*, Book 7, page 216.</margin> Alexander Severus knew his soldiers so well everywhere that he kept Briefs in his bedchamber containing the number and the service times of those campaigning; and whenever he was alone, he would review their accounts, their numbers,

There are, moreover, thirteen companies of Swiss. A Leader of War <note>original: "Belli Dux"</note> will observe this more easily. Odet de Foix <note>A French military leader, also known as Lautrec</note> not only held in recent memory the names of all the Centurions who fought under his banners and the principal soldiers, but he also noted their brave deeds. However, it is not enough to have noted those recommended to him; it is necessary that the Prince, according to the quality of each person and their merits, either promote those noted, or if that cannot be done conveniently at once, cheer them with gifts from his own hand and with gracious words. *Montlucius, as above, book 7, folio 217.* In this way, not only are the worthy promoted, but what is more, those who are so promoted will feel gratitude to the Prince alone, and not to vile brokers <note>original: "proxenetis" - middlemen or those who sell influence</note>.

# Political Discourses

It is also memorable what Nicetas <note>Nicetas Choniates, a Byzantine Greek historian</note> relates concerning Manuel Comnenus in *Book 6*. He ordered water to be drawn from a river flowing past, but after tasting it with the tips of his lips, he poured it out; having recognized by the unpleasant flavor that it was tainted by the gore of the dead, he said with a sigh: "Unhappily, I have tasted the blood of Christians." At that moment, a certain bold and troublesome man—more bitter even than those bitter times—remarked: "Not now, Emperor, not for the first time now, but long ago and often, you have drunk the blood of Christians even unto drunkenness, while you vexed and skinned your poor subjects with taxes." Manuel bore this rebuker with such a calm mind as if he were deaf.

*Page 114. Having fed on the blood of Christians, let them again be milked of their silver.*
Add: But there was a still more shameful profit, of which Melchior Adam <note>A German hagiographer and historian</note> writes in his *Lives of the Germans, page 42*, concerning Reuchlin <note>Johannes Reuchlin, a famous humanist and Hebrew scholar</note>: There was in the city of Cologne a certain Jewish impostor (called Pfefferkorn) who pretended to embrace the Christian religion and was an intimate of the monk known as the Inquisitor, Hoogstraten, and his friends. He showed these men that a great deal of money could be snatched from the Jews under an honorable pretext and without much effort, if the Emperor were to issue an edict: that all Jews should bring their books to the town hall in their respective towns, so that all books except the Bible might be burned by the Inquisitors as being ruinous to the Christian religion. That impostor did not actually want this to be carried out seriously; rather, he knew the Jews would immediately pay a great sum of money to redeem their books. He wanted the matter brought to that point so that the Jews would offer money. Therefore, the monks sought an edict from the Emperor, using religion as a pretext. The edict was issued, and at Frankfurt, the books were carried to the town hall. Meanwhile, as there are many Jews not ignorant of public life, they approached their own patrons in the Imperial Court, who brought the matter to the point where the Emperor inquired after the judgment of those learned in the Hebrew language. He therefore ordered Capnio <note>The Greek nickname for Reuchlin, meaning "smoky"</note> to write what he thought; from this arose that famous lawsuit against Capnio himself.

### *Nicolas de Clémanges, Treatise on the Fall and*
### *Restoration of Justice, Chapter 17.*

->What is a King without a Treasure, or a Kingdom without a public Treasury <term>Aerarium</term><note>The Aerarium was the name for the public treasury in ancient Rome, often housed in the Temple of Saturn.</note>, if not a City without walls, or a house without a foundation? Furthermore, every Prince ought to review the account of his daily expenses at least once a week; he must not, through an immoderate lifestyle or profuse bribery, reduce either himself to poverty or his fatherland to Tyranny. For what is more shameful than that he, who is the Administrator of a Kingdom, should not know how to preside over his own house?<-

### James Brocard, in the Mystical and Pro-
### phetical interpretation of Leviticus.
### Chapter 25.

IF each individual who shall belong to the Kingdom of Christ <note>original: "Regno Christi"</note> will strive to share their own possessions with those in need, then even he who is Prince shall waive his demands and taxes: he will be content with those things which are rightfully given to a Prince. For to let the land keep its Sabbath <note>original: "terram sabbathisare"; a reference to the Biblical Jubilee year where debts were forgiven and land rested</note> means that the land is not to be torn apart by the more powerful, nor held in subjection; but all must act in such a way that they recognize Christ is present in His Kingdom. He is one who would be indignant if He saw in His own family a man who abounds in goods allowing his brother to go in want—or saw him who is the Father of the People acting as a Tyrant; no longer shall the earth endure the greedy and the Tyrants!
